NRCS FAQ spec-sheet contrast (high-C wood vs poultry-manure char) is the extension-facing version of this design space (FAQ).

19. Analytical blind spots for farm labs

Standard KCl / water extracts underestimate micropore-captured nitrate (Kammann sequential washing >> EUF >> quick extract) (DOI).
Total ash P ≠ plant-available P — use agronomic soil tests after application, not only char totals (Ippolito availability framing DOI).
Liming equivalency must be measured, not assumed from pH alone (NRCS FAQ arithmetic).
EC on manure chars can dominate first-year risk even when NPK looks attractive (NRCS FAQ).
H:C_org and C_org remain the permanence/quality gates for CPS 336 and credits even when nutrients are the farm goal (Properties; CPS 336 PDF).


20. Worked planning scenarios (sourced numbers only)
Scenario A — Temperate fertile row crop, wood char, yield goal
Expect weak mean raw-char yield response (Jeffery 2017). Charge 1–3 weeks with compost (USBI) or use CPS 336 blend scenarios (FAQ). Co-apply fertilizer; Ye 2020 supports biochar+IF synergy (PDF).
Scenario B — Acid tropical sandy soil
Liming + WHC mechanisms more likely to reward even less-enriched char (Jeffery 2011; Jeffery 2017), but nutrient charging still improves FUE (Melo; Schmidt).
Scenario C — Low-dose BBF program
Target Melo-class rates (~1 t ha⁻¹) with documented enrichment (urine/NPK/compost) and root-zone placement (Schmidt 2015; Melo 2022).
Scenario D — CDR-primary with secondary agronomy
Meet H:C_org / eligible-use MRV; still inoculate for farm relations and to avoid year-1 drag (NRCS/USBI); Hagemann shows composting coating does not erase aromatic stability (DOI).

21. Glossary (nutrient chemistry)

AEC — anion exchange capacity (usually low on biochar vs CEC).
BBF / BCF — biochar-based fertilizer / biochar-based compound fertilizer.
CEC — cation exchange capacity.
COMBI — co-composted biochar–compost product (Antonangelo framing).
EUF — electro-ultrafiltration nutrient extraction (Kammann method).
FUE / NUE / PUE — fertilizer / nitrogen / phosphorus use efficiency.
SIN — soil inorganic nitrogen (NH₄⁺ + NO₃⁻).
Liming equivalency — % CaCO₃ neutralizing value of the amendment.

Applications/Co-composting-Science.title: Co-composting Science
Applications/Co-composting-Science.content:
Co-composting Science
Mechanisms and evidence for adding biochar into active composting (COMBI / co-composting) so char surfaces develop an organic coating, capture nutrients (especially nitrate), and the composting process itself often runs cleaner and faster. Practice logistics: Farm Co-composting Practice. Safety: Compost Blend Safety. Field blends & NRCS scenarios: Biochar Compost and Manure Blends. Charging continuum: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer. Credit pathways (cross-link only): Matrix Pathways for Credits.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Definitions






























TermWorking definitionPrimary URLCo-composting / COMBIBiochar mixed at the start (or early) of composting so surfaces age with the piledoi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2020.111443 · Antonangelo et al. 2021Post-blendFinished compost mixed with biochar after compostingContrast in Vandecasteele et al. 2016 doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2015.11.045Organic coatingPatchy organo-mineral layer on char surfaces/pores formed during co-composting; drives nutrient retention more than bulk aromatic oxidationdoi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-01123-0Nitrate captureEnrichment of NO₃⁻ in co-composted particles beyond what standard AEC predictsdoi.org/10.1038/srep11080 · doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0171214 · Kammann et al. 2015
Antonangelo et al. (2021) define COMBI as biochar added at the beginning of composting and conclude COMBI often outperforms using compost and biochar separately or mixing them after composting (DOI).

2. Why co-composting differs from post-blending
2.1 Landmark plant-growth contrast
Kammann et al. (2015): at 2% (w/w) in a nutrient-poor sandy substrate, untreated high-temperature wood biochar cut quinoa aboveground biomass to ~60% of control, while co-composted biochar at the same rate raised biomass to up to ~305% of control, with nitrate/phosphate capture central to the interpretation (DOI; PMC pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4460888/).
2.2 Before vs after composting
Vandecasteele et al. (2016) compare biochar added before vs after composting and document process and product differences that motivate treating co-composting as a distinct pathway (DOI). Pacific Biochar’s practitioner synthesis likewise prefers early addition of wood biochar at roughly 5–10% by weight (white paper PDF · Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023).
2.3 Coating chemistry (permanence-relevant)
Hagemann et al. (2017) Nature Communications: an organic coating—not bulk oxidation of aromatic carbon—explains enhanced nutrient retention after co-composting; bulk aromatic C speciation / stability is not substantially altered (DOI). That finding is why credit math still treats co-composted char C under standard persistence / F_perm rules rather than “compost C” rules—see Matrix Pathways for Credits, Permanence, Permanence Science for Credits. Nanoscale organo-mineral complexes on field-aged and co-composted surfaces: Archanjo et al. (2017) (DOI). Microstructural/chemical changes during composting of high-T biochar: Joseph et al. (2018) (DOI).

3. Nutrient capture and slow release






























FindingValue / claimURLNO₃⁻-N in co-composted particles~2.1 g kg⁻¹ (standard extraction) to ~5.2 g kg⁻¹ (sequential washing) in cited Kammann/Hagemann experimentsdoi.org/10.1038/srep11080 · doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0171214Plant availabilityCaptured nitrate partly plant-available; largely protected from leaching in those experiments; did not stimulate N₂O in the reported setupsdoi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0171214N loss during poultry-litter compostingNH₃ emission concentrations down up to 64%; total N losses down up to 52% at 20% pine-chip biochar vs 0%doi.org/10.2134/jeq2009.0337Practitioner synthesis (N losses)Cited studies >50% lower N losses with shift toward nitratepacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdf · Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023
Full N chemistry spine: Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry. Immobilization risk of raw wood char: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · NRCS FAQ (PDF · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026).

4. Process GHG and odor co-benefits (facility boundary)
These are composting-process emissions—not the same as soil N₂O/CH₄ after land application (GHG Fluxes, Nitrous Oxide Fluxes, Methane Fluxes).















































SourceGas / metricReported effectURLSteiner et al. 2010NH₃Up to −64% emission concentration at 20% BCdoi.org/10.2134/jeq2009.0337Yin et al. 2021 reviewCH₄, N₂O, NH₃Mitigation possible; ~10% (w/w) often discussed; feedstock, pyrolysis T, particle size matterdoi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149294Li et al. 2025 meta (123 studies)CH₄ / N₂O / NH₃ / CO₂Mean CH₄ −53.7%, N₂O −49.8%, NH₃ −35.9%; CO₂ not significant; dose key; recommend 10–20% w/w dry under stated compost parametersdoi.org/10.48130/nc-0025-0003Maturation meta 2025CH₄ / N₂O / NH₃ + maturityCH₄ −51.31%, N₂O −43.49%, NH₃ −47.59%; GI +25.57%; NO₃⁻-N +32.54%; NH₄⁺-N −34.96%; C/N −5.44%doi.org/10.48130/bchax-0025-0005Pacific white paper (cited studies)CH₄ / N₂O / NH₃Some studies CH₄ >80% ↓, N₂O >50% ↓, NH₃ up to 60% ↓ — best cases, not averagespacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdfEarth Foundries × Napa Recycling 2023Non-methane VOC−33% at 10% by volume biochar in green/food CASP composting; curing maturity ~1 week sooner; NPK +11%; Ca/Mg salts more than halvedwww.earthfoundriesinc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Earth-Foundries-Green-Compost-Biochar-Composting-Project-Report-2023.pdf · Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023
Yin et al. (2021) note crop-residue and woody biochars tend to mitigate CH₄/N₂O/NH₃ more strongly; high pyrolysis temperature (500–900 °C) favors CH₄/N₂O mitigation while low-T (200–500 °C) favors NH₃ mitigation; granular vs powdered forms trade off CH₄ vs NH₃ (DOI).

5. Loading rates in the literature















































Guidance bandLoadingNotesURLSanchez-Monedero et al. 20183–50% DW cited range; benefits from 3–5%; ~10% often discussed as practicalReview of biochar as composting additivedoi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2017.09.193Pacific Biochar white paperWood biochar 5–10% by weight, earlyPractitioner synthesispacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdfAntonangelo framing (vault use)10–15% w/w often treated as COMBI optimal band in secondary citationsVerify against full text before quoting as this paper’s recommendationdoi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2020.111443 · Antonangelo et al. 2021ABI Compost Guidelines 2026 draft5–10% by volume at start; >20–30% not recommended (can interfere with biodegradation)Industry org draftbiochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Compost-2026-Draft-V1.pdfEarth Foundries demo10% by volumeOne pile vs control, one cyclewww.earthfoundriesinc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Earth-Foundries-Green-Compost-Biochar-Composting-Project-Report-2023.pdfLi et al. 2025 meta recommendation10–20% w/w dry with C:N 20–30, moisture 55–65%, pH 7.5–8.5, EC <4 mS cm⁻¹Composting-process optimization framingdoi.org/10.48130/nc-0025-0003
Volume vs weight: Earth Foundries and ABI draft use volume; peer-reviewed metas and Pacific white paper often use weight. Convert with measured bulk densities—do not assume 1:1 (Application Rates and Methods unit caveats; NRCS FAQ dry weight of 1 yd³ biochar ~135–540 lb — FAQ).

6. Maturity, microbes, and product quality

Maturation meta (2025): germination index +25.57%, NO₃⁻-N +32.54%, NH₄⁺-N −34.96%, C/N −5.44% under biochar amendment of composting (DOI).
Sanchez-Monedero et al. (2018) review aeration, N conservation, and maturity pathways (DOI); Sánchez-Monedero et al. (2019) place biochar, compost, and biochar-blended compost across cropping systems (DOI).
Earth Foundries: low free ammonium reached ~1 week sooner; finished NPK +11% (PDF).
Habitat caveat for raw buried char remains (Quilliam et al. 2013 · DOI); co-composting is the reliable way to pre-load surfaces — Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology.

Pathogens, salts, immature compost: Compost Blend Safety.

7. Agronomic implications (pointer)
COMBI products often outperform raw char and sometimes outperform post-blends for plant growth in controlled and field contexts (Antonangelo et al. 2021; Oasis compost+biochar five-harvest mean +36% vs control — Oasis PDF · Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023). Field rates and economics: Field Rates by System, Agronomic Economics, Crop Yield Effects.


8. Evidence quality and limits













































Claim classStrengthWhyKammann untreated vs co-composted biomass contrastHigh (controlled experiment, open access)Clear same-rate contrast (DOI)Organic coating / aromatic stability preservedHighNature Communications full paper (DOI)COMBI “often beats post-blend”MediumNarrative review (Antonangelo et al. 2021); limited primary trialsComposting-gas meta means (CH₄/N₂O/NH₃)Medium–highLarge metas (DOI; DOI) but composting ≠ soilEarth Foundries VOC −33%DemonstrationOne pile, one cycle (Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023)Pacific white paper best-case % cutsPractitioner synthesisCite primary papers for diligence (Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023)Antonangelo 10–15% / 400–700 °C bandsNeeds full-textSource note flags abstract-only for those rows

9. Links to nutrient and microbe chapters

Nitrate / ammonium chemistry after charging: Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry (Nguyen SIN meta doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2016.11.004; Hagemann PLOS doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0171214).
Habitat vs sparse colonization: Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology · Quilliam et al. 2013 (DOI) · Lehmann biota review (DOI).
Immobilization risk framing for raw char: NRCS FAQ (PDF); Bruun et al. 2012 C/N turnover (DOI).


10. Decision summary

If you run a composting operation → add biochar early at roughly 5–10% (state volume vs weight) and cure to maturity (Farm Co-composting Practice).
If you need plant response from woody char → prefer COMBI or intentional charging over raw broadcast (Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer).
If you claim climate benefits → separate facility process GHG, soil N₂O/CH₄, and durable biochar C accounts (Matrix Pathways for Credits, GHG Fluxes).
Never skip EC / pathogen / metals gates (Compost Blend Safety, Contaminants and Quality).

Applications/Compost-Blend-Safety.title: Compost Blend Safety
Applications/Compost-Blend-Safety.content:
Compost Blend Safety
Pathogens, maturity, salts/EC, nutrient imbalance (esp. P), contaminants, and worker/dust risks when using biochar–compost / manure blends or co-composted products. Mechanisms: Co-composting Science. Practice: Farm Co-composting Practice. Contaminant chemistry of the char itself: Contaminants and Quality (do not duplicate that chapter). Specs: Product Standards EBC IBI, NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Immature compost and pathogens
NRCS CPS 336 FAQ warns to prefer mature compost and manage pathogen risk when using compost or manure with biochar (FAQ PDF · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026). Composting itself is used to reduce pathogens, weed seeds, and odor in manure systems—but only when the process reaches adequate time–temperature regimes (Steiner et al. 2010 frame poultry-litter composting that way — DOI).
Practice rules of thumb (sourced):

Do not treat unfinished, cool, anaerobic piles as “inoculated biochar ready for food crops.”
Document maturity indices your facility already uses (e.g., germination index, NH₄⁺/NO₃⁻ ratio). Maturation meta (2025) reports mean GI +25.57%, NH₄⁺-N −34.96%, NO₃⁻-N +32.54% when biochar is used in composting—useful as process evidence, not a substitute for site testing (DOI).
Earth Foundries demo: low free ammonium reached ~1 week sooner with 10% v/v biochar (PDF · Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023).


2. Salts and electrical conductivity (EC)






























GuidanceDetailURLNRCS FAQBiochar can intensify salinization at high rates; look for spec-sheet EC under 8 (FAQ guidance); manure-based biochars are higher in saltsnrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfNRCS FAQ examplesHigh-C wood char typically lower EC; poultry-manure char example extremely high in salts and nutrients—may suit very acidic, low-nutrient, high-rainfall soils; not neutral-to-basic soils with high P or saltssame FAQEarth Foundries finished compostCa and Mg salts down by more than half vs control pile in that demowww.earthfoundriesinc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Earth-Foundries-Green-Compost-Biochar-Composting-Project-Report-2023.pdfLi et al. 2025 composting metaHigh EC (>4 mS cm⁻¹) impaired mitigation effects of biochar on target gasesdoi.org/10.48130/nc-0025-0003
Soil test EC before and after high-rate manure-char or manure-blend applications. Pair with Field Rates by System.

3. Phosphorus, nutrient imbalance, and manure

NRCS FAQ discusses P-index / high-P soils when using manure-rich chars or blends; Northeast P-index discussion in FAQ (PDF).
Manure used only as inoculant under CPS 336 is unpaid; keep it under a nutrient management plan (FAQ).
Fresh wood char can immobilize nutrients and cut yields if applied raw (NRCS FAQ; Kammann untreated 2% w/w → ~60% of control biomass — DOI). Blends and co-composting are risk-management, not a license to skip soil tests (Biochar Compost and Manure Blends).


4. Feedstock and contaminant gates
CPS 336 / FAQ:

No biosolids or municipal-waste feedstocks under CPS 336 (PFAS concerns) (FAQ; 2022 standard).
Metals within Table 3 maxima; H:C_org <0.7; C_org >10% DW; production >350 °C limited oxygen.
IBI seal alone is not sufficient without a recent spec sheet (FAQ).
Residues that would normally stay on the land cannot be used as feedstock (FAQ).

Deep PAH/metals/PFAS discussion: Contaminants and Quality. Product labels: Product Standards EBC IBI · ANSI ASABE USBI S668.

5. Alkalinity / liming interactions
NRCS: biochar is usually alkaline; most useful as liming on acid soils; on soils already pH >7, check liming equivalency and add cautiously. Worked example: 1 t/ac biochar at 9% CaCO₃ equivalency offsets ~9% of a 1-ton lime recommendation (FAQ). Compost blends change the liming arithmetic—use lab sheets for both components.

6. Dust, handling, and placement safety

Surface-only applications on slopes risk wind/water loss of fine char (NRCS FAQ incorporation guidance — PDF).
Moist blends and co-composted products generally dust less than dry fines; still use PPE appropriate to lime/manure spreading norms.
Placement methods and equipment: Incorporation Topdress Banding, Equipment and Timing.


7. Credit / claim hygiene (safety of claims)
Do not claim soil N₂O reductions from facility VOC/NH₃ data. Earth Foundries VOC −33% is a composting-process metric (Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023); soil flux evidence lives in GHG Fluxes. Do not double-claim the same tonne as CPS 336 cost-share and voluntary CDR without contractual separation (Matrix Pathways for Credits, Double Counting and Credit Ownership).

Applications/Cost-Components.content:
Cost Components
Line-item cost building blocks for farm biochar budgets—only sourced figures. Parent chapter: Agronomic Economics. Fertilizer interactions: Fertilizer Displacement. Rates: Field Rates by System.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Cost stack (conceptual)








































ComponentWhat it coversSourced anchorsProductFOB or farmgate /t or /yd³ of biochar (± compost)Oasis 2016 delivered biochar 240/t** wet; compost **40/t wet — pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdf · Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023LogisticsShipping, loading, haulingBundled in Farmland Info ~$160/yd³ FY2023 scenario average — farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/12/biochar_funding_for_US_producers_quick_guide_.pdfApplicationSpreading / ripping / incorporatingSame Farmland Info scenario construction; Oasis used GPS rip + winged plow (ops cost not separately published)Inoculation / co-compostCompost, manure, labor, pile timeCompost price as above; CPS 336 manure inoculant unpaid — nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfMRV / creditSampling, audits, registry fees (if CDR stacked)Methodology-specific — Matrix Pathways for Credits, MRV Stack; not farmgate amendment priceOpportunity / tillageOne-time deep tillage vs no-till constraintsNRCS notes deep tillage as one-time vs multi-century C — FAQ PDF above
Do not treat CDR literature costs (~$70–360/tCO₂ in Fuss & Lunstrum 2026 — DOI) as bag retail prices (Market Volumes and Pricing, www.cdr.fyi/).

2. NRCS payment scenario construction
Farmland Info quick guide: FY2023 typical 60% biochar / 40% compost scenario built around ~$160 per cubic yard covering average purchase + shipping + loading + hauling + applying + incorporating; varies by state; not matched to actual invoices (PDF). Scenario quantities: Biochar Compost and Manure Blends, NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026.
ABI funding guide 2026: biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Funding-2026-final.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag.

3. Unit traps that break budgets

Wet vs dry tons — Oasis prices are wet as-applied (biochar 38% moisture, compost 49% in report) (Oasis PDF).
yd³ ↔ tons — NRCS dry weight 135–540 lb per yd³ (FAQ).
Banding vs broadcast — same in-band concentration can cut total tonnes (Incorporation Topdress Banding).
Supplier packaging — Wakefield cites 2 yd³ supersacks and 2–3 sacks/ac without a public $/t on that page (wakefieldbiochar.com/biochar-for-landscapers/).


4. Facility co-composting cost narrative (qualitative)
ABI Compost Guidelines 2026 draft: operators report fuel/labor savings from fewer turns and higher-value finished product; material costs more but may command better price (PDF). Treat as industry narrative pending site P&L—not a universal ROI.

Applications/Crop-Yield-Effects.title: Crop Yield Effects
Applications/Crop-Yield-Effects.content:
Crop Yield Effects
Yield responses to biochar are context-specific—stronger in acid, coarse-textured, degraded, and tropical soils; weaker or null on average in many temperate fertile systems. Biochar is not a universal fertilizer substitute. Pair with Soil and Agriculture, Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer, Application Rates and Methods, Biochar Compost and Manure Blends, and Agronomic Economics.
Meta-analytic estimates









































SourceDesignEffectURLJeffery et al. (2011) Agric. Ecosyst. Environ.Meta of productivity (yield or aboveground biomass)Grand mean ~+10%; subgroup means roughly −28% to +39%doi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015Jeffery et al. (2017) Environ. Res. Lett. 12:053001Tropical vs temperateTropical mean ~+25%; temperate mean little/no benefitdoi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bdYe et al. (2020) Soil Use Manage. 36:2–18Field studies; separate fertilizer controlsBiochar + inorganic fertilizer ~+15% vs fertilizer alone; biochar alone often weakwww.css.cornell.edu/faculty/lehmann/publ/SoilUseManage%2036%2C%202-18%202020%20Ye.pdfLehmann et al. (2021) Nat. Geosci.Synthesis citing Ye and related field workFertilised field contexts can show ~+15%-class responses not 1:1 correlated with fertilizer responsedoi.org/10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8Jia et al. (2023) Land Degrad. Dev.Global patterns GHG + crop yieldCrop yield +9.4% overalldoi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868
Mechanistic subgroups (Jeffery 2011)
From the 2011 meta (DOI):

Acidic soils ~+14%, neutral ~+13%; liming hypothesized as a major pathway.
Coarse ~+10%, medium ~+13% textures; water holding implicated.
100 t ha⁻¹ subgroup showed the largest positive mean (+39%) — research extreme, not a farm recommendation.
Poultry-litter feedstock subgroup strong positive (+28%); biosolids feedstock the only significant negative feedstock mean (−28%).

Tropical vs temperate (Jeffery 2017)
Jeffery et al. (2017) conclude biochar boosts tropical but not temperate mean crop yields, attributing tropical gains largely to liming and nutrient effects in acidic, nutrient-poor soils (DOI; open PDF mirror: ecoss.nau.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Jeffery_2017_Environ._Res._Lett._12_053001.pdf).
Field trials and real deployments (selected)
Details and more URLs: Real World Soil Projects.
Oasis Vineyard (Monterey County, CA) — multi-year
Pre-plant treatments on Pinot Noir (Oceano Sand / Garey Sandy Loam, ~0.7% OM): control; compost 15 t/ac; biochar 10 t/ac; compost+biochar. Same irrigation/fertilizer regime. Across five harvests, average yield increases vs control: compost+biochar +36%, biochar +25%, compost +29% (combined five-season totals 41.7 / 38.2 / 40.1 vs 31.7 t/ac). Quality not significantly degraded. Primary report: pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdf · Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023
Exomad Green field study (Santa Cruz, Bolivia) — 2025 reporting
Company report with CIAT at three Santa Cruz sites: one 4 t ha⁻¹ biochar application, beans then corn, under drought. Reported gains vs untreated control: corn +15% biochar alone, up to +32% with NPKS + microorganisms; beans +13% alone, up to +25% combined (PDF; Bioenergy International 2025-07-04). Caveats: the report’s own yield ANOVA is not significant (beans p = 0.4481, corn p = 0.924); there is no fertilizer-only arm; and recomputed against the control, bean gains are +14.9% alone and +34.2% combined. Aligns with tropical/acid-soil expectation from Jeffery 2017. Full breakdown: Exomad Green Corn and Bean Field Study. Facility/soil end-use: Puro Exomad Concepción.
Nepal — enriched biochar fertilizers (low dose)

Schmidt et al. (2015): urine-enhanced biochar + compost produced very large pumpkin yield responses relative to urine or biochar alone on a fertile tropical soil (DOI).
Pandit / Schmidt et al.: 21 field trials, 13 crop species, liquid nutrient–enriched biochar fertilizers (DOI · Schmidt et al. 2017).

These support the Soil and Agriculture point that charged / biochar-based fertilizers can work at ≪ bulk research rates.
Brazil — degraded pastures
Latawiec et al. (2019) evaluate biochar on degraded pasturelands with environmental and cost-benefit analysis (DOI; PDF: www.iis-rio.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Latawiec_et_al-2019-Scientific_Reports.pdf).
Inoculated / enriched vs raw (pointer)
Yield metas that mix raw and fertilized biochar understate the charging effect. Dedicated evidence:






























ContrastResultURLCo-composted vs untreated (Kammann 2015)Up to 305% vs ~60% of controldoi.org/10.1038/srep11080BBF meta (Melo 2022)+10% vs fertilized; +186% vs unfertilizeddoi.org/10.1007/s11104-021-05276-2Microbial inocula + biochar meta↑ productivity vs biochar alone (commercial inocula weak)doi.org/10.1002/saj2.20792 · Ross & Emery 2025Zheng BCF maizeGrain +10.7%; N-AE +43.1% vs ICFdoi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2017.02.034
Full tables, protocols, products: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer.
Application rates in yield literature vs farm practice













































ContextTypical rates citedURLHistorical research trials~5–50+ t ha⁻¹; extremes 100 t ha⁻¹doi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015Ye et al. field fertilizer setRates >10 t ha⁻¹ often no extra short-term yield vs lower (paper PDF)www.css.cornell.edu/faculty/lehmann/publ/SoilUseManage%2036%2C%202-18%202020%20Ye.pdfEnriched biochar fertilizersOften <2 t ha⁻¹doi.org/10.1002/ldr.2761Oasis vineyard (wet weight as applied)Biochar 10 t/ac; compost 15 t/acpacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdfDominus EstateBiochar 25 t/ac to 36”pacificbiochar.com/case-study-biochar-application-with-dominus-estate-in-napa-valley-after-2-years-fallow/NRCS CPS 336 planning start4–10 yd³/ac; scenario baseline 4 yd³/ac pure biocharnrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026Exomad ag guidanceSite-specific; volume-% examples; inoculatewww.exomadgreen.com/biochar
Practice detail: Application Rates and Methods.
When yields fail to rise

Temperate, already-fertile, near-neutral pH soils (Jeffery 2017).
Fresh, high-sorption char without compost/manure charge (NRCS FAQ).
Contaminated or inappropriate feedstocks (biosolids subgroup negative in Jeffery 2011; PFAS → biosolids excluded under CPS 336).
Alkaline soils with high-liming chars (FAQ).
Economics: even positive yield deltas may not repay purchase price without carbon finance — Agronomic Economics, Galinato et al. 2011.

Cross-links

GHG co-effects of the same applications: GHG Fluxes
Soil physical/chemical pathways: Soil and Agriculture
US cost-share: NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag
Numbers cheat-sheet: Quantitative Benchmarks
Hub: Applications Hub · Science Hub

Applications/Equipment-and-Timing.title: Equipment and Timing
Applications/Equipment-and-Timing.content:
Equipment and Timing
What to spread with and when to apply biochar and blends on farm. Placement geometry: Incorporation Topdress Banding. Rates: Field Rates by System. Trials: On-farm Trial Design. Hub: Application Rates and Methods.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Timing (NRCS + USBI)
NRCS FAQ: apply when ground is not frozen; common timing is early spring or post-harvest with cover crop so char equilibrates and erosion/nutrient loss is reduced; combining with other organic amendments or planned tillage improves efficiency (FAQ · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026).
USBI: right timing as part of 4R-style framing; allow equilibration in soil; charge 1–3 weeks before use when inoculating (Ag Guidelines · USBI Ag Guidelines 2023; ABI 2026 biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-for-Agriculture-Applications-2026.pdf).
Exomad/CIAT trial: apply 30 days pre-plant at 4 t ha⁻¹ (PDF · Exomad Green Corn and Bean Field Study).
Single vs repeated applications: CPS 336 practice lifespan 1 year, contractable up to 5 times (FAQ). USBI discusses single large vs repeated smaller applications in guidelines (PDF).

2. Equipment classes













































TaskTypical gear (sourced examples)Notes / URLBroadcast dry char or blendsManure / lime spreaders; USBI cites lime spreader + rototillfarmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/06/usbi-biochar-guidelines-for-ag-application.pdf · nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfIncorporateDisc, rotary tiller, field cultivator, winged plow (Oasis)Oasis winged plow to ~30” pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdfRow rip / trenchGPS ripper + mix (Oasis); excavator deep mix (Dominus)pacificbiochar.com/case-study-biochar-application-with-dominus-estate-in-napa-valley-after-2-years-fallow/No-till drillPrilled / screened productPlugging risk — FAQManure injectorsChar mixed into slurryFAQ + USBI slurry noteFertigationMicronized suspensionsFAQ; Exomad liquid injection www.exomadgreen.com/biocharCompost facilityExisting windrow/CASP loaders — add char as feedstockABI compost draft biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Compost-2026-Draft-V1.pdf · Earth Foundries CASP www.earthfoundriesinc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Earth-Foundries-Green-Compost-Biochar-Composting-Project-Report-2023.pdf
Particle size and binders
NRCS FAQ: particle size must match equipment; plugging if mismatched (FAQ). USBI notes binders/pelletizing to improve compatibility with existing spreaders (Guidelines; pelletizing literature example cited there: doi.org/10.3390/pr9091591).
Moist compost–biochar blends generally handle with compost spreaders—see Farm Co-composting Practice, Compost Blend Safety (dust).

3. Quality gates before the spreader rolls
From CPS 336 Table 3 / FAQ (2022 PDF; FAQ):

Production >350 °C, limited oxygen
C_org > 10% DW; H:C_org < 0.7
Metals within Table 3; report ash, liming equivalent, EC, nutrients
Prefer recent batch tests; IBI seal alone insufficient
No biosolids under CPS 336

NRCS tools landing: www.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/natural-resource-concerns/soil/soil-health/soil-carbon-amendments

4. Contracting calendar (US)
CPS 336 lifespan 1 year; up to 5 contracts over a contract life; ranking improves when stacked with cover crops, no-till, rotations (FAQ). Funding quick guides: farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/12/biochar_funding_for_US_producers_quick_guide_.pdf · ABI 2026 funding PDF biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Funding-2026-final.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag.

Applications/Exomad-Green-Corn-and-Bean-.title: Biochar Field Study: Corn and Beans in Controlled Plots
Applications/Exomad-Green-Corn-and-Bean-.content:
Exomad Green Corn and Bean Field Study
Study note on “Biochar Field Study — Corn and Beans in Controlled Plots”, a 13-page field report published by Exomad Green and run with CIAT (Centro de Investigación Agrícola Tropical) at three sites in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. Biochar was applied once at 4 t ha⁻¹ before a winter bean crop (2024); corn followed with no re-application (PDF). Exomad accounts for roughly 60% of biochar CDR tonnes sold since 2022 (CDR.fyi Snapshot 2025); this is one of the field-study PDFs on its R&D page. Report context: 2026-09-14.
Related notes: Crop Yield Effects · Real World Soil Projects · Soil and Agriculture · Application Rates and Methods · Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology · Supply Landscape · Applications Hub · Key Sources

Bottom line

Headline gains (as reported): biochar alone +15% corn and +13% beans; biochar + NPKS + microorganisms +32% corn and +25% beans vs an untreated control (PDF p.8; p.10). Direction fits meta-analyses of low-fertility tropical soils (Jeffery 2017 · DOI).
Yield differences are not statistically significant. The report’s own ANOVA gives yield p = 0.4481 (beans) and p = 0.924 (corn). Only bean plant height (p < 0.0001) and corn 100-grain weight (p = 0.014) differ significantly (same pages).
Only T2 vs T1 isolates biochar. There is no fertilizer-only arm, so the larger T3/T4 gains cannot be credited to biochar.
Bean percentages are understated. Against the control, beans gain +14.9% / +24.9% / +34.2% (T2/T3/T4), not the printed 12.94 / 19.90 / 25.47% — the report divided by treatment yield instead of control yield (§6.1).
Soil-health conclusions come without soil data. Better nutrient availability, porosity, moisture retention, leaching, CEC, and pH are asserted (PDF p.13), but no post-trial soil tests are shown.
Use it as supportive company case evidence with these caveats attached — not as proof of a yield response.

1. Study at a glance























































ItemDetailSourcePublisherExomad Green — in-house, not peer-reviewed; CEO Diego Justiniano called it “this latest study by our team”PDF p.1 · Bioenergy InternationalPartnerCIAT — Santa Cruz departmental agricultural research center (not the Colombia-based CGIAR CIAT); runs the Cañada Larga and Saavedra experimental stations, a Mairana regional center, and a soil–water–plant laboratoryPDF p.3 · ciatbo.orgSitesCL Cañada Larga, Chiquitania (map label: Pailón EECL) · EEAS Saavedra experimental station, Northern Zone · CRI Mairana regional research center, ValleysPDF p.3–4DesignFour treatments (§2). Layout figure shows 16 plots (4 × 4), each treatment once per row and column; site shown, replicates per site, plot size, and statistical model not statedPDF p.5Biochar dose4 t ha⁻¹ once, manual & mechanical, 30 days before bean planting; dry vs as-received basis not statedPDF p.6Crop sequenceBeans (winter; planted June 2024) → corn (summer) after bean harvest, no additional biocharPDF p.6 · p.13Weather”Severe drought” stated on the corn results page; no rainfall or irrigation dataPDF p.11PublishedUndated PDF; press coverage 2025-07-04 (§9)Carbon HeraldFilesCanonical exomadgreen.com PDF · same file on Wix’s file host (filesusr link); SHA-256 identical (checked 2026-09-14)—
2. Treatments






























CodeTreatment (as printed)Adds vs previous armT1Control (no intervention)—T2Single application of biochar without microorganismsRaw biocharT3Biochar + NPKS fertilizers+ fertilizerT4Biochar + NPKS + microorganisms+ microbial inoculant
Source: PDF p.5. Exomad says its biochar is “usually activated” with microbes including Rhizobium, Pseudomonas, Azospirillum, and mycorrhizae (PDF p.2); the T4 inoculant’s product, dose, and timing are not given.
Missing arms: fertilizer only, microbes only, and fertilizer + microbes without biochar. For contrast, Ye et al. (2020) measure the ~+15% biochar effect against fertilizer alone (PDF) — the comparison this design cannot make.
3. Biochar used (as reported)



































ParameterValueBenchmarkOrganic carbon86.3%NRCS CPS 336 requires C_org > 10% (CPS 336 PDF · NRCS CPS 336 Standard 2022)H:C_org0.24Under the 0.7 limit in the IUPAC definition and NRCS (Bilias 2024 · DOI); under Isometric soil < 0.5 (module) and CSI ≤ 0.40 for GPC (CSI 3.3)Ash8.6%—pH7.2Near-neutral; NRCS notes biochar is usually alkaline and valued for liming acid soils — liming equivalence not reported (NRCS FAQ · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026)Moisture18%Dose basis matters (below)
Values: PDF p.2. Not reported: feedstock, pyrolysis temperature, particle size, lab or method, sampling date, or whether H:C_org is molar. Exomad’s Concepción facility listing describes sawmill hardwood residues pyrolyzed at ~600 °C (Puro facility page), but the report doesn’t say which facility supplied the trial char. Persistence context: biochars with H/C_org < 0.5 retained a mean ~82% of C after 100 years in Lehmann et al. (2021) (DOI) — see Permanence and Properties.
Applied carbon (vault arithmetic, not a credit figure): 4 t ha⁻¹ × 86.3% C ≈ 3.45 t C ≈ 12.7 t CO₂ ha⁻¹ gross if the dose is dry-basis; ≈ 2.83 t C ≈ 10.4 t CO₂ ha⁻¹ if it is as-received at 18% moisture. Credited tonnes apply persistence factors and life-cycle deductions — Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025, Permanence Science for Credits.
4. Site soils (baseline, CIAT lab)











































































ParameterUnitsCRI (Mairana)CL (Cañada Larga)EEAS (Saavedra)pH (H₂O)–6.086.46.3CECcmolc kg⁻¹6.5410.14.9N%0.040.180.1Pppm164718Kmeq 100 g⁻¹0.210.170.18Organic matter%1.082.81.7Sand / clay / silt%76 / 22 / 221 / 61 / 1949 / 16 / 35Texture (printed)–LSCCLLSUSDA class from printed fractions (vault check)–sandy clay loamclayloam
Source: PDF p.4 (CIAT Water, Soil and Plant Laboratory). Sampling depth and date are not given. CL fractions sum to 101%. The printed texture codes don’t match the USDA triangle for CL (61% clay is “clay”) or EEAS (“LS” usually means loamy sand; 49/35/16 sand/silt/clay is loam), so treat the codes as unverified.
Reading: CRI and EEAS are mildly acidic, low-OM, low-CEC soils — the tropical low-fertility setting where meta-analyses report larger yield responses (Jeffery 2017; Jeffery 2011 · DOI). CL is a high-clay, higher-P soil. Results are not broken out by site, so these contrasts can’t be tested from the report.
5. Agronomy by crop


















































ItemBeansCornBiochar4 t ha⁻¹, 30 d before plantingNone added (residual from bean season)Planting date (as printed)Jun 2 (CRI), Jun 5 (EEAS), Jun 20 (CL) 2024Nov 24 (EEAS), Dec 8 (CL) 2023; Jan 2 (CRI) 2024 — see §8Row spacing20 cm45 cmSeed50 kg ha⁻¹20 kg ha⁻¹Crop cycle110–120 d120–130 dP₂O₅ / K₂O / SO₄18.32 / 66 / 15 kg ha⁻¹”Applied with bean crops” (no new P/K/S)Zn–B–Cu1 L ha⁻¹—NN/A100 kg ha⁻¹
Source: PDF p.6. The fertilizer rows presumably apply only to the fertilized arms (T3/T4); the table doesn’t say.
6. Results
6.1 Beans (harvest)




































































TreatmentHeight (cm)FlowersYield (kg ha⁻¹)Δ vs T1 (kg ha⁻¹)% vs T1 (recomputed)% printedT1 Control44.5521.601,189.10———T2 Biochar47.0522.301,365.94+176.84+14.9%+12.94%T3 + NPKS51.5824.401,484.66+295.56+24.9%+19.90%T4 + NPKS + microbes56.9825.151,595.48+406.38+34.2%+25.47%CV %17.3228.923.47ANOVA p< 0.00010.30020.4481
Source: PDF p.8. Each printed percentage equals (T − T1) ÷ T, not ÷ T1. The 58-day “preliminary assessment” lists T1–T4 with blank descriptions and shows one photographed plant per treatment (PDF p.7).
6.2 Corn (harvest; drought season, no new biochar)





























































TreatmentHeight (cm)100-grain weight (g)Yield (kg ha⁻¹)Δ vs T1 (kg ha⁻¹)% vs T1 (printed ≈ recomputed)T1 Control15624.51,962.27——T2 Biochar16527.52,249.90+287.63+14.7%T3 + NPKS16929.02,259.11+296.84+15.1%T4 + NPKS + microbes12830.52,590.67+628.40+32.0%CV %7.957.957.49ANOVA p”<0.44” (as printed)0.0140.924
Source: PDF p.10; ear photo and drought statement on p.11. T4 plants were ~18% shorter than the control yet highest-yielding; the report doesn’t explain why. A 57.49% yield CV implies a residual SD of ~1,300 kg ha⁻¹ on a ~2,270 kg ha⁻¹ mean (vault arithmetic) — consistent with site or drought variation left in the error term, but the model isn’t described.
6.3 What each contrast isolates (vault arithmetic from table means)









































ContrastIsolatesBeansCornT2 − T1Raw biochar+176.8 kg ha⁻¹ (+14.9%)+287.6 (+14.7%) — second-season residualT3 − T2NPKS fertilizer, given biochar+118.7 (+8.7%)+9.2 (+0.4%)T4 − T3Microbial inoculant, given biochar + NPKS+110.8 (+7.5%)+331.6 (+14.7%)T3 − T1Biochar + NPKS combined (no fertilizer-only arm to split them)+295.6 (+24.9%)+296.8 (+15.1%)T4 − T1Whole package+406.4 (+34.2%)+628.4 (+32.0%)
No yield difference is backed by a significant ANOVA in either crop (§6.1–6.2). In corn, 100 kg N ha⁻¹ added almost nothing on top of biochar (T3 vs T2 +0.4%). That would fit water rather than nutrients limiting a drought season, but the report gives no rainfall or soil-moisture data to check.
7. How it fits the vault’s evidence













































QuestionThis studyWider evidenceDoes raw biochar raise yields?+15% in both crops, not significantTropical mean ~+25% (Jeffery 2017); grand mean ~+10% (Jeffery 2011); +9.4% (Jia 2023 · DOI) → Crop Yield EffectsDid uncharged char cause yield drag?No sign in T2 (numerically positive)NRCS warns fresh char can immobilize nutrients and reduce yields (FAQ) → Biochar Inoculation for FertilizerDo microbes add value?T4 − T3: +7.5% beans, +14.7% corn; inoculant unspecifiedInocula beat biochar alone on average, but commercial products are weak and field effects are smaller than greenhouse (Ross & Emery meta · Ross & Emery 2025) → Biochar Microbes and Soil BiologyIs 4 t ha⁻¹ a typical rate?One 4 t ha⁻¹ dose carried into a second cropResearch trials often ~5–50+ t ha⁻¹ (Jeffery 2011); enriched biochar fertilizers often < 2 t ha⁻¹ (Schmidt 2017 · DOI) → Application Rates and MethodsDrought resilience?Claimed for corn; no water dataLargest water-retention gains in coarse soils — FC +23.8% / AWC +25.6% (Wei 2023); AWC +15.1% overall (Omondi 2016) → Soil and AgricultureDoes it pay?No costs or revenue reported; Exomad donates char to local communities (Puro facility page)→ Agronomic EconomicsCredit relevanceNot a credit document; yield effects don’t enter CORC quantificationExomad’s CORCs rest on soil end-use and persistence (Puro facility page) → Supply Landscape · Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025 · Real World Soil Projects (credit project ≠ agronomic trial)
8. Data-quality issues

Non-significant yields (beans p = 0.4481; corn p = 0.924), with no mean-separation tests; replication, plot size, and statistical model undescribed (PDF p.8; p.10).
Confounded treatments — no fertilizer-only or microbes-only arms (§2).
Mixed percentage bases — beans ÷ treatment, corn ÷ control (§6.1). Press coverage repeated the understated bean figures (Bioenergy International; Carbon Herald).
Date conflict — corn is printed as planted Nov 2023–Jan 2024, before the June 2024 bean crop it followed. June planting + 110–120 days puts bean harvest around late Sep–mid Oct 2024, so Nov 2024–Jan 2025 is the likely intent — unconfirmed (PDF p.6).
Charts disagree with tables — e.g., corn 100-grain-weight bars read ≈19 / 28 / 37 / 37 g against 24.5 / 27.5 / 29.0 / 30.5 g in the table (PDF p.12 vs p.10); bean flower bars also drift (p.9). Use table values.
Soil-health claims without data — no post-trial pH, CEC, OM, bulk density, or moisture measurements (PDF p.13).
Not reported — per-site results, bean species or variety, corn hybrid, incorporation depth, particle size, inoculant product and dose, weather, yield moisture basis.
Conflict of interest — a producer and credit seller reporting its own trial; CIAT is named as collaborator, but no CIAT authors, sign-off, or raw data appear in the PDF.

9. Press coverage and related Exomad material

Applications/Farm-Co-composting-Practice.title: Farm Co-composting Practice
Applications/Farm-Co-composting-Practice.content:
Farm Co-composting Practice
How farms and compost facilities actually run biochar co-composting and compost–biochar blends: ratios, timing in the pile, equipment, NRCS payment scenarios, and named facility/field examples. Mechanisms: Co-composting Science. Safety: Compost Blend Safety. Charging without a compost facility: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer. Rates after the product leaves the pile: Field Rates by System, Application Rates and Methods.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Decision tree (practice)

Have an active composting operation? → Prefer early co-composting (COMBI) over mixing finished compost with raw char alone (Antonangelo et al. 2021 · DOI; Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023).
No compost facility, but need agronomic response? → Charge/inoculate 1–3 weeks with compost, manure, tea, fertilizer, urine, or microbes (USBI Ag Guidelines · USBI Ag Guidelines 2023; NRCS inoculate language CPS 336 2022 PDF).
Seeking EQIP/CSP CPS 336? → Match a published blend scenario quantity table and state payment schedule (NRCS FAQ · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026; NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag).
Stacking voluntary CDR? → Lock ownership / no-double-claim language (Matrix Pathways for Credits, Double Counting and Credit Ownership).


2. Target loadings (facility and farm piles)















































SourceTargetWhen to addURLABI Compost Guidelines 2026 draft5–10% by volume; avoid >20–30%Start of composting, like any feedstockbiochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Compost-2026-Draft-V1.pdfPacific Biochar white paperWood biochar 5–10% by weightEarlypacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdfSanchez-Monedero 2018Benefits from 3–5%; literature 3–50% DWReview synthesisdoi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2017.09.193Li et al. 2025 meta (process gases)10–20% w/w dry under stated C:N / moisture / pH / EC windowsProcess optimization framingdoi.org/10.48130/nc-0025-0003Earth Foundries Napa demo10% by volume forestry-residue charMixed into green/food waste CASPwww.earthfoundriesinc.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Earth-Foundries-Green-Compost-Biochar-Composting-Project-Report-2023.pdf · Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023Steiner et al. 2010 (poultry litter)5% and 20% pine-chip BC treatmentsLab/bioreactor composting 42 ddoi.org/10.2134/jeq2009.0337
Convert volume ↔ mass with measured bulk density and moisture. NRCS: dry weight of 1 yd³ biochar roughly 135–540 lb depending on material (FAQ).

3. Pile management checklist

Char quality gate before mixing: production >350 °C limited O₂; C_org >10% DW; H:C_org <0.7; metals within CPS 336 Table 3; report ash, liming equivalent, EC, nutrients (CPS 336 2022; FAQ). No biosolids feedstocks under CPS 336 (PFAS).
Screen/crush as needed so particle size matches turning/spreading gear (plugging risk noted in FAQ for drills/injectors).
Add early, mix thoroughly with wet feedstocks (ABI draft; Pacific white paper).
Moisture / C:N / aeration — stay in the composting window your facility already uses; Li et al. 2025 recommend C:N 20–30, moisture 55–65%, pH 7.5–8.5, EC <4 mS cm⁻¹ when optimizing gas mitigation (DOI).
Cure to maturity before farm sale or field use — immature compost pathogen/weed risk (NRCS FAQ maturity caution; Compost Blend Safety).
Document batch IDs, % biochar (state volume vs weight), feedstock, and lab sheets for both CPS 336 and any CDR offtake (Matrix Pathways for Credits).

ABI draft economic narrative (qualitative): operators report shorter processing, fewer turns (fuel/labor), and higher nutrient value product (PDF). Rexius case in that draft: 5% by volume windrow comparison with higher moisture/nitrates/nutrients vs control pile.

4. NRCS CPS 336 field blend scenarios (FY2024)
These are payment scenarios (acres unit), not universal agronomic optima. From FAQ Table 1 (PDF):








































ScenarioCompostBiochar20% biochar / 80% compost4.4 tons/ac0.8 yd³/ac40% biochar / 60% compost3.3 tons/ac1.6 yd³/ac60% biochar / 40% compost2.2 tons/ac2.4 yd³/ac80% biochar / 20% compost1.1 tons/ac3.2 yd³/ac100% biochar—4 yd³/acCompost off-site3 tons/ac—
Payment rates are state-specific. Farmland Info quick guide example: FY2023 typical 60/40 scenario constructed around ~$160 per cubic yard average cost components (purchase, shipping, loading, hauling, applying, incorporating)—flat scenario rate, not invoice match (PDF).
Manure as inoculant (paid vs unpaid)
NRCS allows mixing biochar with raw manure as inoculant; CPS 336 does not pay for the manure—contract the 100% biochar scenario and mix at producer expense under a nutrient management plan; only biochar counts toward minimum quantity (FAQ). Watch P index / high-P soils when using manure-rich chars or blends.
Practice lifespan: 1 year; may be contracted up to 5 times; ranking improves when stacked with other soil-health practices (FAQ).

5. Named facility and field examples

6. Charging without co-composting (bridge)
If you cannot co-compost: USBI 1–3 week inoculation/charging window (PDF); urine 1:1 volume ≥1 h protocols (Schmidt et al. 2015 · DOI); multi-crop liquid enrichment (Schmidt et al. 2017 · DOI). Full protocols: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer.

Applications/Fertilizer-Displacement.title: Fertilizer Displacement
Applications/Fertilizer-Displacement.content:
Fertilizer Displacement
When biochar, blends, or biochar-based fertilizers (BBFs) change fertilizer need or fertilizer-use efficiency—sourced evidence only. Parent: Agronomic Economics. Chemistry: Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry. Practice: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer.
Report context: 2026-09-16. This note does not invent $/ac fertilizer savings without a cited trial that measured them.

1. What “displacement” can mean






























MeaningEvidence typeCautionHigher yield at same fertilizer rateField metas / trialsNot the same as cutting fertilizerEqual yield at lower fertilizer rateExplicit N/P rate factorialsRare in public farm demosNutrient carrier replacing some soluble fertilizer massBBF / urine-char / co-compost productsStill a nutrient input—track total NPKReduced losses (leaching, NH₃) improving effective fertilizerProcess and soil studiesMay not show on fertilizer invoice
Oasis Vineyard explicitly held irrigation and fertilizer constant across treatments—so its revenue gains are not fertilizer-displacement dollars (Oasis PDF · Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023).

2. Sourced productivity interactions








































SourceFindingURLYe et al. 2020Biochar + fertilizer ~+15% yield vs fertilizer alone in field setwww.css.cornell.edu/faculty/lehmann/publ/SoilUseManage%2036%2C%202-18%202020%20Ye.pdf · Ye et al. 2020Melo et al. 2022BBFs +10% productivity vs fertilized controls at mean 0.9 t ha⁻¹doi.org/10.1007/s11104-021-05276-2 · Melo et al. 2022Schmidt et al. 2015 / 2017Urine- / liquid-enriched low-dose chars outperform urine or biochar alonedoi.org/10.3390/agriculture5030723 · doi.org/10.1002/ldr.2761Kammann et al. 2015Co-composted char loads nitrate/phosphate; untreated char can cut biomassdoi.org/10.1038/srep11080Nguyen et al. 2017Soil inorganic N meta: mean ~−11% NH₄⁺ / −10% NO₃⁻ (first-year class of evidence)doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2016.11.004Steiner et al. 2010Co-composting poultry litter: total N losses down up to 52%doi.org/10.2134/jeq2009.0337
Jeffery temperate null mean for raw char (Jeffery et al. 2017 · DOI) implies fertilizer displacement is unlikely as a standalone temperate story without blends/BBFs or liming value on acid soils.

3. Practical budgeting rules

Credit fertilizer savings only if the trial measured reduced fertilizer or equal yield at lower NPK.
When using co-compost or manure blends, count compost/manure NPK toward the nutrient budget (Compost Blend Safety, P-index).
Prefer banding + enrichment when the goal is cutting total biochar tonnes while maintaining root-zone nutrients (Incorporation Topdress Banding, Field Rates by System).
NRCS still expects nutrient management plans when manure inoculates char (FAQ).

Applications/Field-Rates-by-System.title: Field Rates by System
Applications/Field-Rates-by-System.content:
Field Rates by System
How much biochar (and blends) to plan by system type—NRCS scenarios, research spans, enriched fertilizers, vineyards, pastures, and CDR-inventory thresholds. Placement: Incorporation Topdress Banding. Gear/calendar: Equipment and Timing. Trials: On-farm Trial Design. Hub: Application Rates and Methods. Economics: Agronomic Economics.
Report context: 2026-09-16. Every rate below is sourced; convert units with measured bulk density.

1. Principles before picking a number

Soil- and product-specific (soil tests + amendment lab sheets) — NRCS FAQ · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026.
Charge / inoculate when agronomic response is a goal (CPS 336 2022; USBI).
Separate CDR mass goals from agronomic optimum (Agronomic Economics, Matrix Pathways for Credits).
Unit caveat: dry weight of 1 yd³ biochar roughly 135–540 lb (FAQ).


2. US NRCS CPS 336 planning rates

4. Matching rate to climate / soil expectation
Yield metas (full tables Crop Yield Effects):

Stronger mean responses in acidic, coarse, tropical/subtropical, low-fertility soils (Jeffery et al. 2011 · DOI; Jeffery et al. 2017 tropical ~+25% vs temperate little mean benefit — DOI).
Temperate fertile systems often need blends, banding, or policy/CDR stack to pencil (Agronomic Economics, Galinato et al. 2011 DOI).
Biochar + fertilizer field synergy ~+15% vs fertilizer alone (Ye et al. 2020 · PDF).


5. Co-compost / blend rates (pointer)
Facility loadings 5–10% (v/v or w/w depending on source) — Farm Co-composting Practice, Co-composting Science. Field blend payment scenarios — §2 above and Biochar Compost and Manure Blends.


6. Converting yd³/ac ↔ t/ac (method, not a universal factor)
NRCS FAQ dry weight of 1 yd³ ≈ 135–540 lb (FAQ).
Example arithmetic (illustrative bounds, not a recommendation):

At 135 lb/yd³ dry: 4 yd³/ac ≈ 540 lb/ac ≈ 0.27 t/ac
At 540 lb/yd³ dry: 4 yd³/ac ≈ 2,160 lb/ac ≈ 1.08 t/ac

Wet as-applied masses (Oasis biochar 38% moisture) are higher than dry tonnes (Oasis PDF). Always use the batch bulk density and moisture.
Woolf’s 10 Mg C ha⁻¹ N₂O threshold is carbon mass, not biochar mass—divide by FC (e.g. wood FC ~0.7–0.81 in Woolf Table 2) to estimate biochar tonnes (DOI · Woolf et al. 2021).

CDR credit math is still dominated by stable biochar carbon (Permanence, Biochar as Durable CDR); flux co-benefits are secondary and highly variable.

Deep chapters: Nitrous Oxide Fluxes · Methane Fluxes · Priming and SOC Interactions.

N₂O — one-paragraph pointer
Cayuela et al. (2014) classic meta ~−54% (DOI); Cayuela 2015 H:C_org moderator (DOI); Jia 2023 −26.8% (DOI); Woolf optional −23% year 1 only above 10 Mg C ha⁻¹ (DOI). Full mechanisms and rate reality check: Nitrous Oxide Fluxes.

CH₄ — one-paragraph pointer
Jeffery et al. (2016): mitigation in flooded/acidic systems; possible sink weakening in non-flooded neutral–alkaline soils (DOI). Jia 2023 mean −13.0% (DOI). Woolf default: no net CH₄ change (DOI). Composting-process CH₄ cuts are a different boundary: Methane Fluxes, Co-composting Science.

Priming — one-paragraph pointer
Wang et al. (2016) overall −3.8% (CI includes zero); short-term negative priming; sandy soils positive +20.8% (DOI · Wang et al. 2016). Weng et al. (2017) decade-scale negative priming (DOI). Detail: Priming and SOC Interactions.
NRCS FAQ contrasts biochar’s multi-century C persistence framing (~60–80% remaining at 100 years in their cited range) with compost (~2–14%) (FAQ PDF · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026). Cross-check F_perm in Permanence / Quantitative Benchmarks (IPCC 2019 appendix · IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix).

Interactions with rate, blends, and management

Rate: Woolf’s optional N₂O inventory term only at >10 Mg C ha⁻¹ year 1 — far above many CPS 336 planning rates (~4 yd³/ac baseline) (Woolf; NRCS FAQ).
Compost / manure blends: change labile C, moisture, and N — Biochar Compost and Manure Blends; facility VOC −33% at 10% v/v biochar (Earth Foundries PDF) is not soil N₂O.
Fertilizer N: Ye et al. 2020 (PDF); Fertilizer Displacement.


Real-world projects noting GHG / CDR co-benefits
These claim climate benefits primarily via soil C storage; flux claims should be read as supplementary:

Applications/Incorporation-Topdress-Band.title: Incorporation Topdress Banding
Applications/Incorporation-Topdress-Band.content:
Incorporation Topdress Banding
Where biochar goes in the soil profile and row: broadcast + tillage, banding / seed-row, deep incorporation, no-till / drill / injection, pasture topdress, and composting co-batching. Rates: Field Rates by System. Gear: Equipment and Timing. Hub: Application Rates and Methods.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Why placement matters
NRCS FAQ: incorporate “the same ways soil amendments are normally incorporated” including tillage, trenching, no-till drill, permanent beds, surface apply, or mixed into water; best results with incorporation; surface-only applications risk wind/water loss, especially on slopes (FAQ · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026). USBI: incorporate when possible to limit wind erosion (Ag Guidelines · USBI Ag Guidelines 2023).
Root-zone placement lets low doses of enriched chars work (Schmidt et al. 2015 · DOI).

2. Broadcast + incorporation
Standard manure/lime spreaders followed by disc, rotary, or other tillage. USBI photo/case language includes Iowa corn broadcast then incorporate (Guidelines). Gady Farm WA: lime spreader then rototill to 4-inch depth before winter wheat at 8 t/ac biochar (same PDF).
NRCS notes deep tillage is a one-time disturbance relative to multi-century char C (FAQ).

3. Banding / seed-row / planting-row
Concentrate char where roots explore.






























ExamplePlacementURLOasis VineyardGPS-ripped delve down vine row; winged plow to ~30” in bowl ~2 ft wide × 2.5 ft deeppacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdf · Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023USBI perennial guidanceIncorporate directly into planting rowfarmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/06/usbi-biochar-guidelines-for-ag-application.pdfExomadPlanting-row incorporation and trenching for perennialswww.exomadgreen.com/biocharNepal urine-biocharLocalized root-zone pits with compostdoi.org/10.3390/agriculture5030723
Banding cuts total tonnes vs whole-field broadcast at the same in-band concentration—central to Agronomic Economics and Fertilizer Displacement.

4. Deep incorporation / redevelopment
Dominus Estate: excavator / earthworks cultivating biochar to 36” after fallow redevelopment at 25 t/ac (case study). Appropriate for vineyard/orchard redevelopment—not annual no-till.

5. No-till / drill / prills / injection / fertigation

Crush/screen or compress to prills for drills; inject biochar–manure mixes; fertigate micronized suspensions (NRCS FAQ).
Plugging risk if particle size mismatches equipment (FAQ).
Exomad lists liquid injection / fertigation for perennials (Exomad).
USBI: incorporate into liquid slurry before field application where manure systems allow (Guidelines).


6. Pasture topdress
CPS 336 may be planned on pasture; not on native rangeland except to facilitate CPS 550 or 342. Surface topdress without incorporation increases loss risk—follow slope/runoff restrictions (FAQ). Brazil pasture research + CBA: Latawiec et al. 2019. USBI notes grazing can help incorporation of surface applications in some forage systems (Guidelines).

7. Composting facility co-batching
Add biochar into composting (not only field blend). Earth Foundries: 10% by volume (PDF). SEC/Napa pathway: sonomabiocharinitiative.org/sec-and-napa-recycling-pyrolysis-startup/. See Biochar Compost and Manure Blends, Farm Co-composting Practice.

Materials and Built Uses
Brief hub contrasting soil application with biochar in concrete, asphalt, composites, and other matrices. Existing vault depth is mostly soil/CDR; this page frames the domain and links credit-relevant notes without inventing materials-science claims.
Soil vs built storage (conceptual)




















PathwayTypical framing in vault todayCredit / MRV angleSoil / agricultureYields, GHG fluxes, permanence in soilDominant historical research; NRCS CPS 336; most BCR volumeBuilt / materialsChar locked in construction or productsMethodologies may allow non-soil sinks with different monitoring and leakage rules
Soil pathway notes: Soil and Agriculture, Crop Yield Effects, GHG Fluxes, Permanence.
Why materials matter for CDR
If biochar is incorporated into long-lived products, storage can be argued via the product lifetime and disposal pathway rather than soil biogeochemistry alone. Registries differ on eligible uses, characterization, and monitoring—compare methodologies rather than assuming equivalence.

Applications/Matrix-Pathways-for-Credits.title: Matrix Pathways for Credits
Applications/Matrix-Pathways-for-Credits.content:
Matrix Pathways for Credits
How compost blends, co-composting, and soil application sit inside voluntary biochar CDR methodologies and US practice payments—cross-links only. Deep methodology chapters stay in Carbon Markets; this note maps application-matrix choices growers and project developers actually face. Do not use this note as a substitute for Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025, Verra VM0044, Isometric Biochar Protocol, or MRV Stack.
Report context: 2026-09-16. Out of scope here: CSI deep rewrite (other stream); permanence science deep rewrite (Permanence, Permanence Science for Credits remain the homes).

1. Two different money streams























StreamWhat it pays forBiochar–compost relevancePrimary URLNRCS CPS 336 (EQIP/CSP etc.)Practice cost-share for soil carbon amendmentBlend scenarios (biochar ± compost quantities); inoculate language; not a carbon creditnrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026Voluntary CDR (Puro / Verra / Isometric / …)Eligible durable biochar C after eligible end-useSoil amendment pure or mixed often eligible; quantification follows methodology persistence rules on biochar C, not compost CRegistry/methodology links below
A text search framing in vault notes: CPS 336 FAQ does not discuss carbon credits as part of the practice (FAQ). Stacking requires explicit ownership / no-double-claim language (Double Counting and Credit Ownership).

2. Soil / agriculture end-use families (pointers)
Puro.earth

Edition 2025 agriculture/soil (AF*) pathways include soil amendment pure or mixed (AF1–AF2), cultivation/planting substrates (AF3–AF4), seed coatings (AF5) — see vault summary Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025 and official PDF: 7518557.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/7518557/Puro%20Biochar%20Methodology%20-%20Edition%202025%20%28version%202%29%20-%20For%20Publication.pdf
Point of CORC creation = first durable eligible use (ex-post relative to application) — Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025.
Overview cluster: Puro.earth Overview · Puro Project Cycle and MRV · Puro CORC200+.

Verra VM0044

Soil and non-soil utilization methodology: verra.org/methodologies/vm0044-biochar-utilization-in-soil-and-non-soil-applications-v1-2/
Vault cluster: Verra VM0044 · Verra VM0044 Methodology and Eligibility · Verra VM0044 Permanence and Quantification · Verra VM0044 Project Cycle and MRV.

Isometric

Biochar Protocol v1.3: registry.isometric.com/protocol/biochar/1.3
Soil storage module v1.3: registry.isometric.com/module/biochar-storage-soil-environments/1.3
Vault: Isometric Biochar Protocol · Isometric Modules Soil Built Burial · Isometric Project Cycle and MRV.

Comparison hub
Verra vs Isometric vs Puro · Carbon Markets Hub · Biochar as Durable CDR.

3. Does co-composting erase permanence?
No — not in the chemistry framing used by this vault. Hagemann et al. (2017) find co-composting does not substantially change bulk carbon speciation; aromatic stability underpinning persistence is not erased by the organic coating (DOI). Credit quantification still follows each methodology’s persistence / F_perm / monitoring rules on measured biochar carbon (Permanence, Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI; Permanence Science for Credits, MRV Stack).
NRCS FAQ contrast (practice education, not a credit equation): roughly 60–80% of biochar C remaining at 100 years vs 2–14% of compost C in their cited research summary (FAQ). Do not paste that FAQ range into a credit calculator without the methodology’s own tables.

4. What composting-process GHG cuts are not
Facility reductions such as:

Earth Foundries non-methane VOC −33% at 10% v/v biochar (PDF),
Composting CH₄/N₂O/NH₃ metas (e.g. Li et al. 2025 mean CH₄ −53.7%, N₂O −49.8%, NH₃ −35.9% — DOI),

are process-boundary benefits. They are not automatically soil-storage CORCs and are not interchangeable with Woolf’s optional soil N₂O inventory term (Nitrous Oxide Fluxes, GHG Fluxes, Woolf et al. 2021). Separate MRV if claiming facility emission reductions under a different instrument.

5. Grower / developer checklist

Decide end-use evidence early (soil application records, GPS, invoices, photos per methodology).
Keep batch identity of biochar (feedstock, T, lab sheet, mass) through co-composting so biochar C remains auditable.
State whether compost is a carrier/inoculant vs a separately claimed soil-C practice.
If CPS 336 cost-share is used, put CDR ownership in writing (Double Counting and Credit Ownership).
Do not budget multi-year soil N₂O co-benefits into credit NPV unless the methodology explicitly credits them—and most biochar CDR tonnage is stable C, not flux (GHG Fluxes, Agronomic Economics).

Applications/Methane-Fluxes.title: Methane Fluxes
Applications/Methane-Fluxes.content:
Methane Fluxes
How soil-applied biochar changes methane (CH₄) exchange in agricultural systems—especially the contrast between flooded paddies and upland / non-flooded soils. Hub: GHG Fluxes. Sisters: Nitrous Oxide Fluxes, Priming and SOC Interactions.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Why CH₄ is messy
Soils can be CH₄ sources (methanogenesis in anaerobic microsites / paddies) or sinks (methanotrophy in oxic soils). A positive Hedge’s d can mean either a weaker sink or a stronger source—Jeffery et al. (2016) spell out that ambiguity explicitly (DOI; author manuscript PDF on file under /workspace/biochar-research/jeffery-2016-ch4-meta.pdf).
Global agricultural CH₄ is net positive because rice cultivation sources dwarf upland sinks—so paddy mitigation can matter even if upland sink strength sometimes drops (Jeffery 2016 abstract conclusion).

2. Jeffery et al. 2016 meta-analysis (core)
Jeffery, Verheijen, Kammann & Abalos (2016), Soil Biology & Biochemistry 101:251–258 (DOI):





































ItemValueScreened / included62 studies screened → 42 included; 189 pairwise comparisonsMetricHedge’s d (standardised mean difference)Flooded (management includes flooding)d = −0.87 — increased sink / reduced source strengthNon-floodedd = +0.65 — decreased sink / increased source strengthAcidic soils (pH < 6)d = −1.56 — strongest mitigation directionNeutrald = +1.17Alkalined = +0.44
Practice reading: biochar is most promising for CH₄ in flooded / paddy / acidic systems; in non-flooded neutral–alkaline uplands it may weaken the CH₄ sink. Do not paste a single global % onto every farm.

3. Jia et al. 2023 global mean
Jia et al. (2023): mean CH₄ emissions −13.0%; CH₄ uptake unchanged in that analysis; pools incubation, pot, and field (DOI · Jia et al. 2023). GHG intensity −14.3% overall (−18.7% upland, −14.5% paddy) in the same paper. Field responses were weaker than lab/pot—treat headline % cautiously.

4. Inventory default (Woolf 2021)
Woolf et al. (2021) assume no net CH₄ change for national inventory–style accounting—too few field data to predict size or direction reliably (DOI · Woolf et al. 2021). Farm NPV and credit calculators should not invent a CH₄ co-benefit unless the methodology and site data support it.

5. Composting-process CH₄ (different boundary)
During composting, biochar often cuts CH₄ strongly (anaerobic pockets / methanogen–methanotroph balance):






























SourceCH₄ effectURLLi et al. 2025 composting metaMean −53.7%doi.org/10.48130/nc-0025-0003Maturation meta 2025−51.31%doi.org/10.48130/bchax-0025-0005Pacific white paper (cited studies)Some studies >80% lowerpacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdfYin et al. 2021 reviewMitigation possible; ~10% w/w often discussed; granular form favors CH₄ cutsdoi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149294
These are facility emissions—not soil CH₄ after land application (Co-composting Science, Matrix Pathways for Credits).

6. Related management notes

Hydrology and iron redox chemistry matter in paddies (mechanistic literature cited inside Jeffery 2016 discussion).
Rate and product quality still matter for the whole GHG package (Nitrous Oxide Fluxes, Application Rates and Methods).
Named projects: Real World Soil Projects.



7. Mechanisms (qualitative, from the CH₄ meta discussion)
Jeffery et al. (2016) synthesize literature mechanisms without claiming a single pathway dominates (DOI):

Improved aeration / redox shifts in flooded soils may favor methanotrophs or suppress methanogens.
pH rises from alkaline chars can alter methanogen/methanotroph balance (acidic soils showed the strongest sink-strengthening d).
Labile C additions can temporarily fuel methanogenesis—another reason to prefer matured co-composted products when CH₄ is a concern (Co-composting Science).
In oxic uplands, biochar effects on the CH₄ sink may reverse the flooded-system story (positive d in non-flooded classes).

Pair with N₂O mechanisms (Nitrous Oxide Fluxes) and priming (Priming and SOC Interactions) when building a full GHG narrative.

8. Farm decision rules

Paddy / flooded acidic soils: CH₄ co-benefit is plausible per Jeffery 2016—still measure if claiming.
Temperate upland neutral soils: do not assume CH₄ mitigation; sink weakening is possible.
Inventory / credit defaults: follow Woolf no net CH₄ unless the methodology says otherwise (DOI).
Compost facilities: process CH₄ cuts can be large—account under composting MRV, not soil CORCs (Matrix Pathways for Credits).

Applications/Nitrous-Oxide-Fluxes.title: Nitrous Oxide Fluxes
Applications/Nitrous-Oxide-Fluxes.content:
Nitrous Oxide Fluxes
Agricultural framing of how soil-applied biochar changes nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions. Hub: GHG Fluxes. Sisters: Methane Fluxes, Priming and SOC Interactions. CDR tonnage is still dominated by stable biochar C (Permanence, Biochar as Durable CDR).
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Summary numbers



































SourceMean / ruleScopeURLCayuela et al. 2014−54%30 studies, 261 treatments; lab + field mixed (2007–2013 window)doi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2013.10.009 · Cayuela et al. 2014 · author PDF digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/273052/4/Cayuela2014AgricEcosysEnv.pdfJia et al. 2023−26.8%Global meta; 3,883 paired obs / 220 studies; pools incubation, pot, and fielddoi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868 · Jia et al. 2023Woolf et al. 2021 inventoryOptional −23% (95% CI 5–41%), year 1 only, only if >10 Mg C ha⁻¹; field-fitteddoi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c02425 · Woolf et al. 2021Woolf weighing of prior metasCites Cayuela −54%; Verhoeven −12.4%; Borchard −38%; Verhoeven reanalysis −9.2% nssame §3.3.2same
Farm takeaway: treat −54% as an early lab-heavy ceiling, −26.8% as a broader modern mean (still mixing study types), and Woolf’s −23% as a conservative inventory option that most CPS 336 planning rates do not unlock.

2. Mechanisms
2.1 Electron shuttling / denitrification
Cayuela et al. (2013) Scientific Reports examine biochar’s role in soil denitrification pathways (DOI).
2.2 H:C_org as a product moderator
Cayuela et al. (2015): molar H:C_org is a key factor—more aromatic / lower H:C_org chars tend to mitigate N₂O more strongly (DOI). This is one scientific reason NRCS and EBC/IBI stress H:C_org < 0.7 (NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag, Product Standards EBC IBI, Properties).
2.3 Rate, texture, N form
Cayuela 2014: application rate directly correlated with N₂O reductions; soil texture and chemical form of N fertilizer strongly influence emissions (DOI). Jia 2023: biochar-induced soil pH change was the strongest driver of GHG responses in that analysis (DOI).
2.4 Fertilizer N baselines
Ye et al. 2020 emphasize fertilizer interactions for yield (PDF); N rate also modulates N₂O baselines. Nutrient chemistry: Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry.

3. Inventory / MRV conservatism (Woolf 2021)
Woolf et al. (2021) greenhouse-gas inventory method for biochar soil additions:

Optional N₂O adjustment −23% for the first year only
Only when application exceeds 10 Mg C ha⁻¹
Fitted excluding pot/incubation studies
Assume no net CH₄ change for inventory simplicity
Mineral soils only — organic/forest soils with organic horizons out of scope (positive priming possible)
Priming of native SOC not credited (net negative priming not statistically robust in metas they cite)

(DOI; open PDF open-science.canada.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/112fc297-0352-4683-ae0e-dd1271f59d77/content · Woolf et al. 2021)
Rate reality check: CPS 336 planning often starts at 4–10 yd³/ac (FAQ). With dry bulk density ~135–540 lb/yd³, many farm rates are below 10 Mg C ha⁻¹—so the optional inventory N₂O term often does not apply. Credit programs primarily remunerate durable C, not flux co-benefits (MRV Stack, Matrix Pathways for Credits).

4. Interactions with blends and management

Compost / manure blends change labile C, moisture, and N availability that drive N₂O — Biochar Compost and Manure Blends.
Facility composting N₂O cuts (e.g. Li et al. 2025 mean composting N₂O −49.8% — DOI) are not soil flux results.
Earth Foundries VOC −33% is a composting-process metric (PDF).
Co-composted particles that capture nitrate did not stimulate N₂O in Hagemann PLOS experiments (DOI)—context-specific.


5. Real-world claim hygiene
Projects that mention N₂O co-benefits (e.g. Exomad facility language puro.earth/cdr-credit-suppliers/facilities/exomad-green-concepcion/) should be read as supplementary to soil C storage claims. Full list: Real World Soil Projects.


6. Comparing the three “headline” numbers

























NumberWhat it averagesWhen to use it−54% (Cayuela 2014)Early literature; lab + field; 261 treatmentsHistorical benchmark; upper-end illustration−26.8% (Jia 2023)Broader modern corpus; still mixes incubation/pot/fieldPrefer for “recent global mean” language−23% year 1 (Woolf 2021)Field-fitted inventory option at >10 Mg C ha⁻¹ onlyNational inventory / conservative MRV — usually not CPS 336 rates
Author PDF for Cayuela 2014: digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/273052/4/Cayuela2014AgricEcosysEnv.pdf. Open Woolf PDF: open-science.canada.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/112fc297-0352-4683-ae0e-dd1271f59d77/content.

7. What not to do in farm NPV

Do not multiply Cayuela −54% by fertilizer N₂O emission factors for 10-year cash-flow models without site data.
Do not apply Woolf’s optional term below 10 Mg C ha⁻¹ or beyond year 1 (DOI).
Do not treat composting N₂O metas as soil results (DOI).
Do not ignore H:C_org — low-aromatic chars may underperform Cayuela 2015 expectations (DOI).
Prefer on-farm chambers if flux co-benefits are in a contract (On-farm Trial Design).

Economics framing: Agronomic Economics. Credit ownership: Double Counting and Credit Ownership.

Applications/On-farm-Trial-Design.title: On-farm Trial Design
Applications/On-farm-Trial-Design.content:
On-farm Trial Design
How to structure credible on-farm biochar trials so results can inform rate, blend, and economics decisions—without inventing statistics. Pair with Field Rates by System, Crop Yield Effects, Agronomic Economics, and named precedents in Real World Soil Projects.
Report context: 2026-09-16.

1. Why design matters
Meta-analyses show large context dependence (soil pH, texture, climate, fertilizer co-application) (Jeffery et al. 2011 · DOI; Jeffery et al. 2017 · DOI; Jia et al. 2023 · DOI). A single unreplicated strip cannot overturn those patterns—but a well-logged strip trial can answer “does this char × this blend × this rate work here?”
Jeffery et al. (2016) CH₄ meta required randomised, replicated designs for inclusion (42 of 62 screened studies; 189 pairwise comparisons) (DOI)—a reminder that weak designs get filtered from science, and weak farm demos get filtered from lenders.

2. Minimum viable farm trial













































ElementSourced rationale / exampleURLControlSame fertility, irrigation, timing minus biocharOasis four-way: control / compost / biochar / combo pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdfReplicationGady Farm USBI case: 4 replicates × 2 seasonsfarmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/06/usbi-biochar-guidelines-for-ag-application.pdfRandomisation / blockingSteiner poultry composting: complete-block, 3 repeats of 3 treatmentsdoi.org/10.2134/jeq2009.0337Rate chosen a prioriTie to NRCS scenario or literature analogueField Rates by System · FAQ nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfCharge state documentedRaw vs inoculated vs co-composted is a treatment, not a footnoteBiochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Kammann contrast doi.org/10.1038/srep11080Multi-yearOasis needed 5 harvests for economics narrative; Woody persistence claims cite WoolfOasis PDF · doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c02425Same inputs otherwiseOasis held irrigation/fertilizer constant (so did not monetize water/fertilizer savings)Oasis PDF · Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023
Earth Foundries facility demo used one pile per treatment, one cycle—treat as demonstration, not inferential stats (Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023).

3. Treatment ideas that answer real questions

Raw vs charged vs co-composted at equal biochar mass (Kammann logic — DOI).
Broadcast vs banded at equal total t/ac (placement efficiency — Incorporation Topdress Banding).
Biochar ± fertilizer factorial (Ye et al. 2020 synergy framing — PDF).
NRCS scenario rates vs half-rate enriched BBF (Melo mean 0.9 t ha⁻¹ — DOI).
Compost alone / biochar alone / combo (Oasis design).


4. Measurements worth logging








































DomainExamplesWhyYield / qualityCrop yield, grade, pruning weight (Oasis)EconomicsSoilpH, EC, OM, P, moisture; depth of incorporationSafety + mechanisms Compost Blend SafetyAmendmentSpec sheet, moisture, bulk density, % blendUnit conversionOpsSpreader settings, fuel/timeCost ComponentsOptional GHGChamber N₂O/CH₄ if claiming flux co-benefitsGHG Fluxes — do not inventCreditsApplication evidence pack if CDR offtakeMatrix Pathways for Credits

5. Statistics without overclaiming

Prefer confidence intervals / paired contrasts over single-year % without error bars.
Report absolute yields alongside % vs control (Oasis cumulative t/ac table is a model — PDF).
For economics, stress-test crop price and zero yield response (Galinato caution for temperate wheat — DOI; Agronomic Economics).
Do not average unreplicated strips into a “meta.”


6. Templates from published farm cases
