Compare: Puro Project Cycle and MRV · Verra VM0044 Project Cycle and MRV
Primary sources: Biochar Production and Storage v1.3; Soil Environments v1.3.

End-to-end cycle
PDD (protocol + modules + ESS + additionality)
        ↓
Validation (Isometric-approved VVB; site visits)
        ↓
Produce → characterize (Method A/B) → store
        ↓
Reporting Period GHG Statement
        ↓
Verification (ex-post after durable storage)
        ↓
Credit issuance on Isometric Registry / Certify
        ↓
Transfer / retirement (± buffer contribution if applicable)

Critical rule: Credits issued only after CO₂ is durably stored — not at factory gate alone (protocol).

Documentation & validation





























ArtifactRolePDDLocations (biomass, pyrolysis, storage); feedstock counterfactual; reactor design diagrams; characterization plan; models; ESSGHG StatementNet removal quantification for Reporting PeriodVVBValidate feedstock module; verify storage module; verify quantification; ESS; Isometric Standard complianceMateriality5% threshold (protocol)UncertaintySensitivity analysis; parameters <1% impact may be omitted from uncertainty analysis
Site visits
Minimum: site visits during first Validation/Verification to biomass pyrolysis site and biochar application site (ISO 14064-3 framing). Representative sampling of multiple application sites allowed (protocol).

Batches and sampling





























ConceptRuleProduction batchProject-defined but ≤ 1 month; consistent feedstock/processStorage batchOne or multiple production batches blended before storageMethod ASample every batch (≥3 samples preferred) until statistical basis for Method BMethod BAfter ≥ 30 samples (example: 3×10 batches), conservative mean − SEM for unsampled; refresh every ≤10 batches; 6-month sample eligibility windowOutliers (Method B)Winsorize beyond ±3σ after ≥30 measurements
Mass: preferred weighbridge at delivery; alternative documentation only with Isometric pre-approval. Retain carbon analyses and scale tickets ≥ 5 years after monitoring period.

Pyrolysis emissions MRV
Two quantification options (protocol §10):

Direct continuous measurement of flow + composition (CH₄, N₂O, CO, CO₂) upstream of emission point — preferred
Accredited periodic emissions testing (≥ annually) when continuous not feasible

Permissible gas end-uses: venting; venting after control system; combustion for process energy; provision to third party (allocation rules). N₂O concern elevated for low C/N feedstocks (manure, biosolids, seaweed) — justify if not monitoring.
Reactor design diagrams, materials, pressure-vessel standards (e.g., 2014/68/EU), and maintenance plans required in PDD.
Production variants: mobile / distributed / combustion co-product modules referenced in protocol §9.

End-use proof & chain of custody (soil)
From soil module §8:
Direct soil application

Geotagged photos/videos: stockpile, spreading, incorporation
GIS / maps of application boundaries + dated quantity logs

Mixing with organic matrices (crediting at mix + transfer)

Biochar < 50% v/v of final product; product unsuitable as fuel
Defined eligible end-use pathway
Verified transfer of custody to third party
Burden of proof that product goes to land (not incineration-dominant jurisdictions without soil proof)

Third-party sales

Purchaser affidavit (intended use, geography for soil-T conservatism, evidence retention)
Invoices / BOLs / delivery proof
Mixing process evidence

CoC hygiene

Unique batch IDs
Documentation at every handoff
Retain records ≥ 5 years
Stockpile ≤ 12 months unless agreed; store wet/covered; keep away from waterways

Fuel-diversion risk: if material picking risk is non-negligible, ≥95% by weight ≤ 10 mm particle size (module).

Additionality dynamics

Project-specific baseline/counterfactual per Isometric Standard
Reassess when regulations or financials change (tipping fees, farmer payments, cheaper capital, co-product revenue)
Finding of non-additionality stops future crediting only — does not claw back past/current periods (protocol)

Contrast Verra v1.2 VT0008 investment analysis + activity method (Verra VM0044 Project Cycle and MRV); Puro facility/output audits (Puro Project Cycle and MRV).

Data transparency
Evidence for quantification and ESS generally public on Isometric’s platform (PDD, GHG Statement, measurements, EFs, literature, permits). Limited confidential carve-outs (e.g., licensed EF databases) with buyer/registry/VVB access (protocol Data Sharing).

Buffer contributions (by module)





















ModuleTypical buffer framingSoil Environments0% (No Observable Risk; discount in (F_{durable}))Low Oxygen Burial0% (same framing)Built Environment2% (Very Low Risk)
Confirm live project pages for actual buffer pool contributions (e.g., Charm registry counters).

Example projects (MRV archetypes)























ArchetypeProjectMRV flavorSourceSoil / land applicationCharm Range & PlainsBiochar trucked to land application sitesregistryLandfill burialCarba BurnsvilleDaily cover → low-oxygen burial; Microsoft offtakeregistry; Carba

US producer practical path

Choose storage module early (soil vs burial vs built) — locks lab suite (Ro or not)
Define production batch ≤ 1 month; write Method A→B sampling plan into PDD
Contract ISO 17025 labs; if pursuing 1000y, secure petrography (≥500 R₀ points) + TGA
Instrument pyrolysis emissions (continuous or accredited annual)
Build geotag / GIS / affidavit CoC before first offtake season
Allocate credit ownership contractually across feedstock, pyrolyzer, applicator
Budget VVB site visits to both plant and fields/landfill

Carbon-Markets/Methodologies/Puro-Biocha.content:
Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025
Parent concept: Puro CORC200+
Operator: Puro.earth Overview
Project ops / audits: Puro Project Cycle and MRV
Comparison: Puro vs Other Standards
This is the vault’s exhaustive note on Puro’s current biochar methodology: Edition 2022 → 2025 evolution, permanence modeling, eligibility, feedstock, end uses, LCA boundaries, and phase-out dates. Facts below are drawn from the Puro deep-dive research (2026-09-14) and primary PDFs/URLs cited there — not invented.
Primary PDF: Edition 2025 v2 — For Publication
Transition PDF: Methodology Transition Plan for Biochar Edition 2025 (2025-08-10)
Science cross-links while reading: Permanence · Permanence Science for Credits · Properties · Production · Contaminants and Quality · MRV Stack

Versions at a glance




















VersionApprovalPublishing / notesEdition 2025 V112 Jun 2025 (Advisory Board)Published Document Library 30 Jun 2025. Introduces CORC200+, revised power-law permanence model, stricter Biomass Sourcing Criteria, mobile facility rules, Table 3.2 overhaul. Retail Category R3 initially not CORC-eligible.Edition 2025 v227 Nov 2025Makes retail-to-individuals (Category R3) CORC-eligible under product controls + country-level RDF. (retail update)
Launch (earliest Facility Audit under Edition 2025): 1 Nov 2025 (extended from 15 Aug 2025 per transition plan).

Exact transition timeline (2022 → 2025)





































MilestoneDatePublic consultation3–28 Apr 2025Advisory Board approval (Ed. 2025 V1)12 Jun 2025Publishing (Document Library)30 Jun 2025Launch (earliest Facility Audit under 2025)1 Nov 2025End of transition (last Ed. 2022 Audit Package for pre-launch registrations)15 Dec 2025Edition 2022 termination12 Jun 2030 (max 5-year crediting from approval of new edition)Edition 2025 v2 (retail R3 eligible)Approved 27 Nov 2025
Implications by facility stage (transition PDF)

























Facility stageRuleAlready certified under 2022May finish current crediting period; renew only against latest edition; optional early upgrade at next Output AuditRegistered before Launch, not yet auditedEncouraged to use 2025; allowed 2022 only if complete Audit Package submitted by End of Transition (15 Dec 2025)Registered on/after LaunchMust use Edition 2025Preliminary Assessments against 2022Do not carry over as assessments for 2025
Crediting period under Edition 2025: 10 years, renewable twice (via new Facility Audit against latest rules) — contrasted in transition docs with prior 5-year framing often cited for older facilities.

What changed (Edition 2022 → 2025)
Documented changes (methodology intro, permanence post, retail post, transition plan):







































































#ThemeEdition 2022Edition 20251Durability claimCORC100+CORC200+ (“several centuries”)2Permanence modelWoolf 2021 multi-pool exponentialRevised power model over 200 years, then soil-depth protection assumed for further centuries; 80% confidence interval lower bound; H/C_org domain 0–0.7; soil T floor 7 °C; open-source on GitHub3Random reflectance (Ro)—Reporting encouraged; does not affect quantification yet4Biomass sourcingPrior rulesStricter alignment with Puro Biomass Sourcing Criteria (category A MSW excluded; category J food crops excluded; category P land-clearing processable but no CORCs; etc.)5Mobile pyrolyzersLimited treatmentExplicit Stationary vs Mobile facility definitions; spatial extent within one host country; fleet rules6Baselines—New Facility / Retrofit / Charcoal Repurpose7Crediting periodOften cited as 5y for legacy facilities in transition docs10 years, renewable twice8Use pathwaysPrior TableTable 3.2 overhaul; retail R3 initially not CORC-eligible, then v2 adds safeguards9LCA / leakage / uncertaintyPrior sectionsExpanded quantification (project emissions, leakage, monitoring, measurement uncertainty)10Reversal buffer—No default buffer for reversal risk (eligibility + evidence; supplier liability if reversal from non-compliance)
Concept note for the durable-credit claim (without repeating this whole method): Puro CORC200+
Permanence science debate: Permanence Science for Credits · Risks and Controversies

Who can list (supplier eligibility)

CO₂ Removal Supplier = biochar producer or contracted representative with sole CORC claim rights and end-to-end data access (rules 2.1.1–2.1.3)
Must comply with methodology + Puro Standard General Rules + local law
Path: Facility Audit (initial, typically on-site) → Certified Facility → Output Audits (at least annually) → CORC issuance

Operational detail: Puro Project Cycle and MRV

Feedstock rules (Biomass Sourcing Criteria)
Categories that can potentially generate CORCs (non-exhaustive)
Allowed categories potentially generating CORCs include:





























































CodeDescription (high level)BSorted food wasteCSorted MSW fractions other than foodDGreen wasteEAnimal wasteFMunicipal sludge / biosolidsGForest biomass meeting BSCHPulp/paper sludgeINon-food ag crops with land-use limitsKIn-field residuesLNon-field processing residuesMPalm residualsNConservation / invasive biomassOAquatic biomass
Not allowed / no CORCs





















CodeRuleAMixed unsorted MSW — not allowedJFood / feed crops — not allowedPLand-clearing biomass — may be processed but shall not issue CORCs
Additional operational feedstock rules

No co-firing with fossil coal/oil in feedstock
Impurity & fossil-C accounting (plastics, paints, sludge fossil C)
Stockpiling CH₄ controls
Biohazard treatment (≥500 °C × 3 min if relying on carbonization)

Cross-link: MRV Stack · Contaminants and Quality · Production

Production requirements

Thermochemical conversion: pyrolysis / gasification / modified combustion / other
H/C_org < 0.70 mandatory (rule 3.5.1) — hard gate for quantification eligibility
Reactor categorization: mode, process, heating, streams, co-product fate
Combustion of volatiles: design for complete combustion; ≥95% normal combustion operating time; flameout procedures; CH₄/N₂O monitoring rules
Fossil fuel use allowed for ignition/support if no fossil C enters biochar and LCA includes emissions (coal as process fuel not allowed)

Additionality / baseline
Three components (rule 3.3.1):

Carbon additionality
Regulatory additionality
Financial additionality

Per Puro Additionality Assessment Requirements + Baseline and Additionality Questionnaire (made public after successful Facility Audit).

Biochar sales prices
Co-product revenues
Cost structure

Pitfall: waste-treatment cost-saving projects may fail financial additionality if savings alone make the project viable without CORCs (rule 3.3.4). See Puro Project Cycle and MRV · Risks and Controversies.

Lifecycle emissions, leakage, and net CORCs
Overall equation (5.2.1):
[
\mathrm{CORCs} = C_{\mathrm{stored}} - C_{\mathrm{baseline}} - C_{\mathrm{loss}} - E_{\mathrm{project}} - E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
]





























TermMeaning(C_{\mathrm{stored}})Stored biochar C as CO₂e: (Q_{\mathrm{biochar}} \times C_{\mathrm{org}} \times 44/12) (Eq. 6.1)(C_{\mathrm{baseline}})Removals that would have occurred anyway (incl. retrofit / charcoal-repurpose deductions via Eqs. 6.6–6.9)(C_{\mathrm{loss}})Expected decay losses via persistence fraction PF (Eq. 6.3 conceptually: (C_{\mathrm{stored}} \times (100 - PF)/100) with PF in %)(E_{\mathrm{project}})Full LCA operational + embodied emissions; allocation to co-products; cut-offs(E_{\mathrm{leakage}})Identify, mitigate, quantify residual market/activity-shifting leakage
Net CDR logic in words: Stored biochar C (as CO₂e) minus expected decay losses minus baseline removals that would have occurred anyway minus project LCA emissions minus unmitigated leakage — only for biochar proven in an eligible end use.

Puro’s permanence stance vs millennial claims
Puro explicitly stopped at centuries, not millennia, pending integration of inertinite/Ro science (permanence post). Ro is encouraged for reporting but does not change CORC quantification under Edition 2025. Contrast with Isometric Biochar Protocol (200y or Ro≥2% → 1000y) and CSI Global Biochar C-Sink (upper GPC path via Ro≥3.8% or HyPy≥90%). Concept note: Puro CORC200+.

Reversal policy

No default buffer deduction (rule 4.2.1)
Risks managed via use eligibility + evidence
Supplier liable for reversals caused by non-compliance

Critics may prefer pooled buffers — see Risks and Controversies · Puro vs Other Standards.

Crediting period and renewals

Capacity expansion of similar reactors may be possible without resetting period (rules 3.1.6–3.1.8 — detail in Puro Project Cycle and MRV).

ICVCM status for this methodology
As of ICVCM announcement 2025-12-11 and research date 2026-09-14:

Puro program is CCP-Eligible (General Rules v4.2+)
Biochar methodology is not yet CCP-Approved

Buyers wanting CCP-labelled credits today may prefer Verra VM0044 until Puro’s category assessment completes. Re-check ICVCM Assessment Status before relying on this. See Puro.earth Overview · Puro vs Other Standards.

When this methodology is the right fit
Prefer Edition 2025 / CORC200+ when you want:

Mature BCR buyer recognition + CORCCHAR price signal + Nasdaq registry infrastructure
Flexible baselines (New / Retrofit / Charcoal Repurpose) and explicit mobile fleet rules
A centuries-scale (200+) permanence claim with open-source PF model

Consider alternatives when you need CCP methodology labels today (Verra VM0044), a 1000-year Ro path (Isometric Biochar Protocol), or EBC/WBC-native GPC/SPC (CSI Global Biochar C-Sink). Full chooser: Puro vs Other Standards.

One-sentence definition
CORC200+ is Puro’s Edition 2025 biochar credit label asserting net durable CDR with a permanence framing of several centuries (≥200 years), quantified with a revised power-law decay model (H/C_org + soil temperature, 80% CI lower bound), and issued ex-post only after biochar reaches a durable eligible use.

Why the rename matters commercially

Buyers and offtake term sheets increasingly distinguish 100-year, 200-year / centuries, and 1000-year / millennial claims (Puro vs Other Standards · Buyers and Offtakes).
Marketing baseline CORCs still often say “100+ year durability” across pathways; biochar Edition 2025 specifically issues CORC200+ — do not conflate pathway-generic CORC marketing with the biochar label.
CCP methodology labels are a separate integrity layer: Puro program eligible ≠ biochar method CCP-Approved (Puro.earth Overview).


Permanence claim — what is asserted, what is not
Asserted

Quantification horizon of 200 years under a power-law persistence model.
After 200 years, deeper-soil protection is assumed for further centuries → marketing/label claim of several centuries / CORC200+.
Conservatism via the lower bound of an 80% confidence interval.
Soil temperature from Puro dataset with a 7 °C floor; H/C_org domain 0–0.7.

Not asserted (yet)

Millennial / 1000+ year inertinite-equivalent permanence as a quantified CORC factor.
That Ro (random reflectance) changes the number of CORCs — it is encouraged reporting only.
That program CCP-Eligibility equals a CCP credit label on biochar CORCs.

Puro explicitly stopped at centuries, not millennia, pending integration (permanence post). Contrast:

Common confusions (quick FAQ)
Is every CORC a CORC200+?
No. CORC200+ is the biochar Edition 2025 label. Other Puro methodologies use other durability labels (100+ / 200+ / 1,000+ depending on pathway).
Is CORC200+ the same as a 1000-year credit?
No. Puro stopped at centuries. Millennial claims live elsewhere (e.g., Isometric Ro path, CSI GPC upper class).
Does Ro unlock more CORCs under Puro?
Not yet. Encouraged reporting only; does not change quantification under Edition 2025.
Does CCP-Eligible program status put a CCP label on my biochar CORCs?
Not by itself. Methodology-category approval is separate; as of 2025-12-11 biochar was not yet CCP-Approved.
When is the credit created?
At first durable eligible use + successful Output Audit — not at the kiln door alone.

Recommended sequence

Map end-use channel to Table 3.2 before promising buyers CORC volumes (farm contracts vs retail R3).

Budget annual €1,400 + volume service tiers + retirement €0.25 (or offtake waiver).

Why comparison matters
Biochar carbon removal (BCR) buyers often diligence MRV stringency, permanence claim, and integrity labels more than brand alone. Choosing a pathway early locks feedstock rules, end-use evidence, and offtake narratives for years — especially under Puro’s Edition 2022 → 2025 transition through 2030.

Puro.earth Overview
Puro.earth is an engineered carbon dioxide removal (CDR) standard, registry, and market-infrastructure company based in Helsinki (Puro.earth Oy). It does not operate as a conventional multi-sector offset registry: CORCs are framed exclusively as durable removals, with avoidance kept out of CORC accounting.
This note is the map of the Puro cluster in the vault. Open child notes for depth; do not treat this overview as a substitute for the methodology or MRV chapters.
Why it matters for biochar
Biochar carbon removal (BCR) has been one of Puro’s longest-running pathways. Under Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025, biochar CORCs are labelled CORC200+ (“several centuries,” ≥200 years), with public price discovery via Nasdaq × Puro  CORCX indexes. For a US producer choosing among registries, start here, then read Puro vs Other Standards and Puro Project Cycle and MRV.
Related vault concepts: Biochar as Durable CDR · Permanence Science for Credits · MRV Stack · Market Hub · Market Volumes and Pricing · Buyers and Offtakes · Historical Deals · Price Indexes and Benchmarks · Risks and Controversies

What a CORC is
A CO₂ Removal Certificate (CORC) = 1 metric tonne CO₂e net removal, independently verified under a Puro methodology, recorded in the Puro Registry, transferable, and retired when applied to a climate claim (CORC page).
General marketing still frames “100+ year durability” as the baseline CORC definition across pathways. Biochar Edition 2025 specifically issues CORC200+.

Removal-only product. CORCs are engineered-CDR certificates; they are not a general-purpose offset unit mixing avoidance and removal.

Public price signal. Unlike most BCR pathways, Puro publishes Nasdaq-methodology indexes (CORCX, CORCCHAR) — see Puro Pricing and CORC Indexes · Market Volumes and Pricing.

Liquidity trend. CDR.fyi (citing Puro Aug 2025 report): biochar CORC issuance→transfer/retirement time improved from 95 days (2021) to 22 days (mid-2025).

This chapter covers rules of the road: what facilities, feedstocks, technologies, and end uses qualify under VM0044. Quantitative permanence factors live in the Permanence note. Facts prefer the v1.1 PDF plus v1.2 public announcements; confirm against the live v1.2 PDF on Verra’s methodology page before submission.

Active rule set

























ItemStatusSourceActive methodologyVM0044 v1.2 since 27 Jun 2025methodology pageWhat v1.2 addedInvestment analysis (step 3) under VT0008; Errata & Clarifications; tool version refsrevision announcementv2.0Consultation only (Jul–Aug 2026) — not activeconsultation
Verra’s public one-liner: quantifies removals from waste biomass → biochar at new facilities; soil (crop/grassland) and non-soil (e.g., biochar-amended concrete) (methodology page).

Facility newness — greenfield gate
VM0044 v1.1 states the project must install and operate a new (greenfield) biochar production facility(ies) (v1.1 PDF).

























ImplicationDetailExisting / retrofit plantsOut of scope under current active framing until v2.0 expands eligibilityv2.0 draftExplicitly proposes expansion to existing facilities (consultation)Contrast PuroPuro Edition 2025 allows New / Retrofit / Charcoal Repurpose baselines — see Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025Contrast IsometricProject-specific; not framed as Verra-style greenfield lock — Isometric Biochar Protocol
For US producers with an already-operating kiln: Verra v1.2 may be a non-starter until v2.0 is approved and adopted — watch the consultation outcome.

Thermochemical scope















EligibleExcludedSourcePyrolysis, gasification, biomass boilers (terms used interchangeably for this methodology)Torrefaction and hydrothermal carbonizationv1.1 §4 — excluded because solids are not significantly more persistent than feedstock (Woolf et al. 2021)
Health & safety program protecting workers from airborne pollutants is required (v1.1 applicability).

High-tech vs low-tech (four-condition gate)
High technology facilities must meet all of the following (v1.1 definitions, adapted from EBC Production Guidelines):

























#Condition(a)Pyrolytic GHGs recovered or combusted — not allowed to escape to atmosphere(b)≥ 70% of pyrolysis heat energy used (accounting for heat-transfer inefficiencies)(c)Pollution controls (e.g., thermal oxidizer) meeting local / national / international emission thresholds (strictest where overlapping)(d)Production temperature measured and reported
Fail any condition → low technology production facility (different quantification / monitoring defaults). See Verra VM0044 Permanence and Quantification and Verra VM0044 Project Cycle and MRV.
Non-soil applications are restricted to high-tech biochar only (v1.1 applicability condition 11).
v2.0 consultation flags “detailed criteria for high-technology biochar production facilities” as a revision theme (consultation).

Feedstock — waste biomass only
Core tests (must all hold)
From v1.1 §4:

Purely biogenic waste biomass — not purpose-grown
Otherwise left to decay or combusted for purposes other than energy production (Appendix 2 demonstration procedures)
Not imported from other countries
Meets Table 1 sustainability criteria for its sourcing category

Table 1 categories (non-exhaustive examples)













































CategoryExample themes (v1.1 Table 1)Notable safeguardsAgricultural waste biomassPrunings; straw/leaves/stalks/husk/pomace; fruit/veg residuesField residues: document no decline in soil C / productivity or baseline open burning; else remove ≤ 50% of residuesFood processing residuesWash/peel/centrifuge residues; expired food; coffee/tea/cocoa/tobacco processingResidue production per output must not increase to chase biocharForestry & wood processingOff-cuts, sawdust, mill by-products; sustainable forest sourcesForest-sourced wood must not drive deforestation/degradationRecycling economyUrban/rural green waste; biosolids; paper mill sludgeContaminant thresholds per IBI/EBCAquaculture plantsSeaweed/algae waste; aquatic invasive (Plantae)No purposeful introduction of invasives for feedstockAnimal manureSwine, cattle, horse, poultry wastesBy-products of husbandryHigh-carbon fly ash (HCFA)Bioenergy cogeneration by-product≤ 5% of annual waste biomass throughput; affirmative extraction tech; no fossil makeup for diverted calories; meet IBI
Mixed feedstocks must still meet IBI Biochar Testing Guidelines or EBC Production Guidelines (v1.1).
Transport of feedstock / biochar

Non-road (ships/boats/other) allowed up to 200 km
Distances > 200 km must use road vehicles per CDM Tool 12 framing (v1.1)

Mineral additives
Lime, rock minerals, ash ≤ 10% dry mass without extra proof; above 10% requires lab evidence against IBI/EBC contaminant thresholds (v1.1).
Appendix 2 — waste demonstration
Credible evidence of baseline fate (decay / non-energy combustion): government records, disposal facility records, production records; else literature / surveys of similar industries (v1.1 §6 / App. 2 themes). This is a frequent project failure mode called out by practitioner checklists — treat as validation-critical, not deferrable.
v2.0 proposes expanding eligible feedstocks (invasive species; other new non-purpose-grown streams) (consultation).

End-use eligibility
Timing
Biochar must be utilized in soil or non-soil applications within one year of production (v1.1 condition 9) — decay math is calibrated to 100-year permanence from application, not from multi-year stockpiles.
Soil applications

































RuleDetail (v1.1)Eligible landCropland, grassland, vegetated urban soils, forest — not wetlandsPlacementSurface or subsurfaceSurface ruleMust mix with compost, manure, or anaerobic digestateSubsurfaceMay be pure or mixedContaminantsIBI Testing Guidelines or EBC Production Guidelines (or relevant national regs)Chemistry gateMolar H:Corg ≤ 0.7
Contrast Isometric soil module: H/Corg < 0.5 and O/Corg < 0.2 (soil module) — tighter aromaticity gate. See Isometric Modules Soil Built Burial.
Non-soil applications





























RuleDetail (v1.1)ExamplesCement, asphalt, other long-lived productsTech restrictionHigh-tech onlyCarbon contentBiochar ≥ 50% C dry weightLongevity proofLab results, peer-reviewed papers, or third-party product assessment including lifetimeEnd-of-lifeMust demonstrate biochar in the product is not combusted at end of life
Isometric’s dedicated built-environment module adds Ro-based 1000y math and demolition/abrasion reversal modeling — different architecture than Verra’s non-soil PR_de path.

Additionality

























VersionApproachSourcev1.1Standardized activity method / positive list (activity penetration) + regulatory surplusv1.1 §7v1.2Adds mandatory investment analysis (step 3) following VT0008 Additionality Assessment, v1.0 — ICVCM Core Carbon Principles alignmentrevision announcementv2.0 draftReplace positive list with project method additionalityconsultation
Practical: v1.2 projects must budget for investment analysis documentation, not only the activity-penetration / positive-list narrative.

Baseline framing
Baseline: continuation of pre-project waste handling where waste biomass would be left to decay or combusted for non-energy purposes (v1.1). Default net baseline emission avoidance at sourcing stage treated conservatively as zero in the methodology’s BESS framing (v1.1 §8.1.1) — removal claim centers on durable biochar C, not methane avoidance stacking.
Related: Biochar as Durable CDR · Double Counting and Credit Ownership.

Product quality standards referenced

IBI Biochar Testing Guidelines (methodology cites latest version)
EBC Production Guidelines
Vault: Product Standards EBC IBI · Contaminants and Quality · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink (EBC/WBC prerequisite track — different program)


US / ag design notes (no invented Prairie facts)





























Design choiceVM0044 implicationNew kiln vs retrofitGreenfield required under current active rulesAg residues from fieldsSoil-C / productivity documentation or ≤50% residue removalCompost / manure “matrix” pathwaysAligns with surface-application mixing ruleConcrete / asphalt offtakeHigh-tech + ≥50% C + longevity evidenceWant existing facility creditedWatch v2.0; consider Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025 or Isometric Biochar Protocol in parallel diligence
Policy adjacency (not a credit method): NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · Policy Hub.

Carbon-Markets/Methodologies/Verra-VM004.content:
Verra VM0044 Permanence and Quantification
Parent hub: Verra VM0044
Eligibility rules: Verra VM0044 Methodology and Eligibility
Science context: Permanence Science for Credits · Permanence · Woolf et al. 2021 · IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix
Compare: Isometric Permanence Pathways 200y and 1000y · Puro CORC200+ · Verra vs Isometric vs Puro
This chapter covers how much carbon is credited and over what horizon under VM0044. Numbers below are taken from the public VM0044 v1.1 PDF unless labeled otherwise. Active program version is v1.2 (methodology page) — confirm Table 3 / equations unchanged in the live v1.2 PDF before locking a project model.

Horizon claim




















ItemVM0044 (v1.1 PDF)Peer contrastCrediting permanence window100 yearsPuro CORC200+ (several centuries); Isometric 200y or 1000yFraming“100-year permanence value … based on 100-year global warming potential horizon”Puro CORC200+ · Isometric Permanence Pathways 200y and 1000y
Utilization must occur within one year of production so pre-application decay does not undermine the 100-year factor (v1.1 applicability).

Core high-tech stored-carbon equation
For Option P.1 — High Technology Production Facility (v1.1 §8.2.2.1):
[
CC_{t,k,y} = \sum_p \left( M_{t,k,p,y} \times FC_{p,t,p} \times PR_{de,k} \right)
]
Then organic carbon is converted to CO₂e with the stoichiometric factor 44/12.

























SymbolMeaning(CC_{t,k,y})Organic C (dry) for biochar type (t), application (k), year (y) (tonnes)(M_{t,k,p,y})Dry mass of that biochar from facility (p)(FC_{p,t,p})Organic carbon content (dry weight percent) — lab analysis for high-tech(PR_{de,k})Permanence / decay adjustment factor for application type (k)
Lab methods: latest IBI Biochar Testing Guidelines or EBC Production Guidelines or other internationally/nationally accredited standards (v1.1).
Net removals also subtract project emissions at production (pre-treatment, conversion, auxiliary energy) and account for leakage / transport per methodology tools — see Verra VM0044 Project Cycle and MRV and MRV Stack.

Table 3 — default (PR_{de,k}) for soil
Table 3 (v1.1) provides default permanence adjustment factors drawn from IPCC (2019) Table 4AP.2 and Woolf et al. 2021 framing, keyed to production temperature (T_{prod}):





















Temperature classDefault (PR_{de,k})High temperature pyrolysis / gasification (> 600 °C)0.89Medium temperature pyrolysis (450 – 600 °C)0.80Low temperature (350 – 450 °C)0.65
Sources: VM0044 v1.1 PDF; IPCC 2019 App. 4 PDF; Woolf et al. 2021.
Important clarification — Table 3 vs H:Corg

















ConceptRole in VM0044 v1.1Table 3 (PR_{de,k})Temperature-class default fraction of organic C treated as remaining over 100 yearsH:Corg ≤ 0.7Soil eligibility gate (aromaticity / quality), not the Table 3 lookup key
Do not conflate with Isometric’s continuous H/Corg + soil-temperature decay function or CSI’s H/Corg ≤ 0.40 GPC split. Science map: Permanence Science for Credits.

Non-soil (PR_{de,k})
If scientifically robust permanence information for the non-soil product is unavailable, use the soil Table 3 default for the production temperature class (v1.1).
Project proponents may propose an alternate (PR_{de,k}) with evidence meeting VCS Methodology Requirements default-factor rules (peer-reviewed). If literature conflicts, adopt the lower value. White papers / non-peer-reviewed research are not accepted (v1.1).
Only high-tech biochar qualifies for non-soil pathways; biochar must be ≥ 50% C dry weight (Verra VM0044 Methodology and Eligibility).

Low-technology quantification path
Facilities that fail the four-condition high-tech definition use the low-tech option (v1.1):

Organic carbon content may rely on IPCC default tables/figures (e.g., Table 4 / Figure 4Ap.1 themes in methodology) rather than full batch lab (FC)
CH₄ / soot minimization must still be demonstrated (convection-zone kiln examples discussed in §8 narrative)
Generally less flexible / more conservative than high-tech lab path

High-tech definition (recap): GHG recovery/combustion; ≥70% heat use; pollution controls; measured temperature — full text in Verra VM0044 Methodology and Eligibility.

Project emissions at production (high-tech sketch)
[
PE_{PS,p,y} = (PE_{D,p,y} + PE_{P,p,y} + PE_{C,p,y}) \times \frac{\sum_t\sum_k M_{t,k,p,y}}{M_{p,y}}
]





















TermMeaning (v1.1)(PE_D)Pre-treatment of waste biomass (drying, pelletizing, etc.)(PE_P)Conversion / pyrolysis-related accounted emissions(PE_C)Auxiliary energy for pyrolysis
Biogenic CO₂ from biomass is treated within the carbon-cycle framing of the methodology; CH₄ and soot remain material because of higher GWP (methodology narrative citing Amonette et al. 2021). High-tech condition (a) (combust/recover pyrolytic gases) underpins de minimis treatment of some direct process emission categories — see PDF footnotes.
Full boundary GHG table: v1.1 Table 2 (confirm in PDF).

H:Corg eligibility vs other programs






























ProgramChemistry gatePermanence modelVerra VM0044Soil H:Corg ≤ 0.7Table 3 temperature defaults @ 100yIsometric soilH/Corg < 0.5, O/Corg < 0.2Woolf-style 200y function or Ro≥2% 1000yPuro Ed. 2025H/Corg domain in power model (see method)CORC200+ power decay + 80% CICSI C-Sink 3.3H/Corg ≤0.40 → 75% GPC; Ro≥3.8% or HyPy≥90% → 90% GPCGPC / SPC pools
Sources: v1.1 PDF; Isometric soil module; Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025; CSI Global Biochar C-Sink.

What VM0044 does not do (as of v1.x)

Does not issue millennial inertinite / Ro credits like Isometric Option 2 or CSI upper GPC
Does not use soil temperature as a continuous decay input in Table 3 defaults
Does not (yet) make H/Corg the Table 3 lookup key — though v2.0 consultation proposes enhanced H/Corg & moisture monitoring (consultation)


Worked intuition (illustrative only)
Suppose high-tech biochar, dry mass 1.0 t, lab organic C = 80%, produced at 650 °C → (PR_{de}=0.89):
[
CC = 1.0 \times 0.80 \times 0.89 = 0.712\ \text{t C}
]
[
CO_2e\ \text{before PE/leakage} \approx 0.712 \times 44/12 \approx 2.61\ \text{tCO}_2e
]
Then subtract project emissions, leakage, and apply any VCS buffer rules. Do not use this as a credit quote — it ignores PE, transport, application evidence, and verification findings.

Science anchors

IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix — temperature-class (F_{perm}) inventory guidance
Woolf et al. 2021 — DOI
Sanei et al. 2024 — DOI (used by Isometric/CSI, not VM0044 Table 3)

This note is the map of the Verra VM0044 cluster. Open child notes for depth; do not treat this overview as a substitute for eligibility, permanence math, or MRV chapters.
Research dump: /workspace/biochar-research/verra-vm0044-deep-dive.md (2026-09-16). Cross-standards: Verra vs Isometric vs Puro · Puro vs Other Standards · Puro.earth Overview · Isometric Biochar Protocol.

Why it matters for biochar
VM0044 is the main VCS pathway to issue removal VCUs from waste biomass → biochar → eligible soil or durable non-soil use. As of mid-2025 it is also one of the few biochar methodologies with an explicit ICVCM CCP-Approved category decision (ICVCM M43 PDF; Verra announcement).
For a US / Prairie-leaning producer comparing registries: start here for CCP-labelled VCU demand, then compare permanence horizons and facility rules against Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025 and Isometric Permanence Pathways 200y and 1000y.

What it credits (one paragraph)
CO₂ removals from converting waste biomass into biochar at new (greenfield) production facilities, then using that biochar in eligible soil applications (e.g., crop and grasslands) or durable non-soil applications (e.g., biochar-amended concrete and building materials) (methodology page).

Carbon-Markets/Risks-and-Controversies.title: Risks and Controversies
Carbon-Markets/Risks-and-Controversies.content:
Risks and Controversies
Permanence science divergence
Decomposition-model camp (IPCC, Woolf 2021, Puro CORC200+, Isometric 200y) vs inertinite/Ro camp (Sanei et al.; Isometric 1000y; CSI upper class). Critiques argue inertinite proxies can overstate absolute permanence or that two-pool models mis-specify chemistry. See Permanence Science for Credits and Consensus vs Debates.
Leakage & land-use

Market leakage if biomass is diverted from higher-carbon uses (timber, mulch, animal feed)
Harvesting that depletes ecosystem carbon stocks (non–waste biomass) undermines net removal
Residue removal can harm soil protection (also flagged in NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag)

Contamination & agronomic harm
PAHs, dioxins, heavy metals, high salts (manure chars), excessive liming on alkaline soils; dust/albedo/erosion on slopes. Standards respond with EBC/WBC limits; NRCS excludes biosolids chars over PFAS concerns. See Contaminants and Quality.
Double counting
Same tonne claimed as product footprint reduction, voluntary credit, and compliance instrument; unclear ownership along grower → pyrolyzer → farmer → buyer chain; overlap with soil-carbon farming methodologies. See Double Counting and Credit Ownership.
Overstated yields / MRV gaps
Crediting before application; weak retail chain-of-custody; optimistic permanence factors; ignoring CH₄ from pyrolysis or biomass storage. Delivery vs contracted volume gaps create expectation risk (CDR.fyi(www.cdr.fyi/blog/biochar-carbon-removal-market-snapshot-2025)).
Greenwashing critiques
NGOs (e.g., Fern, Carbon Market Watch) criticize carbon-removal certification frameworks—including biochar under EU CRCF drafts—for weak life-cycle boundaries, land-sector interactions, or insufficient safeguards. Marketing “carbon-negative fertilizer” without retired, unique registry tonnes is a separate risk.
Buyer concentration
Microsoft and a few others dominate BCR volume—see Buyers and Offtakes · Market Volumes and Pricing · Historical Deals. Q1 2026 intermediaries facilitated 74% of contracted tonnes (CDR.fyi).

Industry/US-Biochar-Initiative.content:
US Biochar Initiative (now American Biochar Institute)
North America’s long-running nonprofit hub for biochar education, technical assistance, market development, and standards. The organization founded in 2009 as the U.S. Biochar Initiative (USBI) now operates as the American Biochar Institute (ABI) after a March 2026 rename. This note is the vault’s org home for both the legacy USBI brand and current ABI publications.
Primary URLs: biochar.org/usbi · About ABI · biochar.org home · legacy usbi.biochar-us.org
Related vault notes: USBI Guidance vs Vault Notes · USBI Ag Guidelines 2023 · Industry Hub · Application Rates and Methods · Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Biochar Compost and Manure Blends · NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · Product Standards EBC IBI · Policy Hub · Market Volumes and Pricing · Key Sources

1. Identity, legal history, and rebrand



































MilestoneWhat sources sayURLFoundedEstablished 2009 as U.S. Biochar Initiative; formally incorporated 2010 to accelerate biochar use/production in North Americabiochar.org/about-abi/2024 transitionWork moved into North American Biochar Council, dba USBI; IRS recognition as 501(c)(3) public charity noted on About pagebiochar.org/about-abi/March 2026 renameNorth American Biochar Council adopted the name American Biochar Institute to reflect a maturing industrybiochar.org/about-abi/Public welcome“The U.S. Biochar Initiative is now the American Biochar Institute (ABI)”biochar.org/usbi/Legacy siteStill presents USBI branding, Learning Center, directory, and conference promousbi.biochar-us.org/
Leadership (named publicly): Executive Director Myles Gray is quoted on the USBI→ABI welcome page and featured on the legacy home (biochar.org/usbi; usbi.biochar-us.org).
Funders / partners called out on About: USDA Forest Service Wood Innovations Program; United States Endowment for Forestry and Communities (About). Earlier USFS Wood Innovations grants also funded USBI fact-sheet / market-roadmap work (historical newsletters / NFS partnership context).
Flagship convening: North American Biochar Conference 2026 — November 16–18, 2026, Ernest N. Morial Convention Center, New Orleans, hosted by ABI in partnership with the U.S. Biochar Coalition (biochar.org; legacy home).

2. Mission, vision, and positioning
Current ABI framing

Mission: “To deliver independent science-based information, technical assistance, and standards on biochar.” (About)
Vision: “We envision a world in which biochar is a sustainable material valued by agriculture, industry, and the built environment.” (About)
Positioning: Neutral infrastructure — standards, technical assistance, knowledge sharing — so producers can differentiate and buyers can procure with confidence (biochar.org).

ABI’s own values language emphasizes Focus, Trust, Efficacy, Collaboration (About).
Legacy USBI framing (still on legacy site)

Mission: Advance production and use of biochar in industrial, agricultural, and infrastructure markets to reduce biomass waste, grow the economy, and mitigate climate change (usbi.biochar-us.org).
Vision: Thriving biochar industry supporting resilience and decarbonization while sequestering carbon and building circular systems (usbi.biochar-us.org).

Gray’s rebrand quote stresses durable end-use markets and trusted standards as biochar becomes a circular waste-to-value solution (biochar.org/usbi).

5. Guidance highlights (sourced numbers)
5.1 Application rates (Ag Guidelines 2026)
From biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-for-Agriculture-Applications-2026.pdf:

No universal rate — field-by-field to address a specific constraint.
Literature-framed field band: 1–10 tons/acre with “consistent positive impacts” in numerous studies.
Practical starts: 1 ton/ac ≈ 4 cu yd/ac (lowest effective for soil-organism habitat); 3 ton/ac ≈ 12 cu yd/ac (SOM improvement).
Containers / planting holes: 5–25% by volume.
Economics: higher rates of “ideal” char often better agronomically but not cost-effective; points farmers to USDA / NRCS assistance.

Cross-walk: Application Rates and Methods · NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · USBI Guidance vs Vault Notes.
5.2 Charging / inoculation (Ag Guidelines 2026)
Same PDF:

Terms bundled: inoculating / charging / activating / blending / mixing.
Purpose: fill surface functional groups with nutrients and microbes; reduce nutrient immobilization and first-year yield drag.
Media: compost, manure, compost tea, fertilizer, urine, microbial inoculants.
Time: 1–3 weeks “has been recommended” (varies).
Links practice to biochar-based fertilizers (BBFs) via pre-/post-pyrolysis nutrient loading.

Cross-walk: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · USBI Ag Guidelines 2023 · Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry.
5.3 Compost co-processing (Compost 2026 Draft V1)
From biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Compost-2026-Draft-V1.pdf:

Recommended addition: 5–10% by volume at the start of composting.
Sheet claims include ~20% faster composting (aeration / microbial activity), odor capture, and higher nutrient retention (N).
Caution: >20% or 30% by volume not recommended — can interfere with biodegradation.

Cross-walk: Biochar Compost and Manure Blends · Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023.
5.4 Lab interpretation & standards pointers
From biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Lab-Report-2026.pdf:

No federal product-spec standard; incentive programs (e.g. NRCS CPS 336) and IBI criteria often set practical bars.
Other pathways may require state/local rules, stormwater specs, or carbon-removal methodologies (sheet discusses Puro.earth, Verra, and European Biochar Certificate context).
Points practitioners to IBI lab lists and IBI Standards v2.1.

IBI Standards: biochar-international.org/ · CPS 336: www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/336-NHCP-CPS-Soil-Carbon-Amendment-2022.pdf
5.5 NRCS funding (ABI + AFT 2026)
From biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Funding-2026-final.pdf:

Practice: CPS 336 Soil Carbon Amendment; financial assistance via EQIP (and possibly RCPP).
Criteria summary includes heating biomass >350 °C under limited oxygen; IBI Certified seal or IBI-criteria lab methods; documentation of origin, production method, moisture, particle size, pH, EC, etc.
Example scenario language includes 60% biochar / 40% compost or manure blends and ~$160 payment construction (FY2023 scenario framing in guide — state rates vary).
Points to Web Soil Survey “Dynamic Soil Properties Response to Biochar” and PNW Biochar Atlas (www.pnwbiochar.org/).

Cross-walk: NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026 · NRCS CPS 336 Standard 2022.

USBI Guidance vs Vault Notes
Explicit comparison between U.S. Biochar Initiative / American Biochar Institute practitioner guidance and this vault’s Science / Applications / Carbon Markets / Policy notes. Org context: US Biochar Initiative. Report date: 2026-09-16.
Method: Only claims that appear in cited USBI/ABI URLs or PDFs are attributed to USBI/ABI. Vault claims keep their existing outbound URLs / DOIs. Where USBI is thinner or stronger, that is about coverage depth, not a judgment that one side is “wrong” without a sourced conflict.

Snapshot TLDR

























VerdictDetailOverall agreementStrong on charging/inoculation, site-specific rates, compost co-addition bands, NRCS CPS 336 as the U.S. farm incentive pathway, and IBI-aligned lab specs for soil use.What’s new / stronger at USBI–ABIPackaged practitioner PDFs (2026 suite), ANSI/ASABE/USBI S668 testing standard, ABI+AFT NRCS funding FAQ packaging, 2025 U.S. Biochar Market Report survey benchmarks, stormwater/poultry/concrete library breadth.What’s stronger in the vaultPeer-reviewed mechanisms (immobilization, coatings, nitrate capture), BBF chemistry/biology chapters, registry MRV (Puro/Verra/Isometric/CSI), CDR.fyi deal/volume tracking, permanence science debates.Conflicts?No hard numerical contradiction found on the core farm practices. Unit-basis differences matter (USBI tons/acre & % volume vs NRCS yd³/acre scenarios; compost % volume vs some literature % w/w). Market figures from ABI survey ≠ CDR.fyi credit deliveries.

1. Where USBI agrees with existing vault notes
1.1 Charging / inoculation is critical






























ClaimUSBI / ABI sourceVault notesFresh char can immobilize nutrients / cause first-year yield dragAg Guidelines 2026: inoculation “critical” to minimize immobilization — biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-for-Agriculture-Applications-2026.pdfBiochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026 — nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdfCharge with compost, manure, tea, fertilizer, urine, microbesSame Ag Guidelines PDFUSBI Ag Guidelines 2023 · Application Rates and Methods · Biochar Compost and Manure Blends1–3 week activation window commonly recommendedSame PDF; USBI Ag Guidelines 2023Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Application Rates and MethodsNRCS practice language requires inoculation with compost / tea / manureABI Funding Guide cites CPS 336 pathway — biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Funding-2026-final.pdfNRCS CPS 336 Standard 2022 — www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/336-NHCP-CPS-Soil-Carbon-Amendment-2022.pdf
Mechanistic agreement (vault goes deeper): Vault cites Kammann et al. untreated vs co-composted contrast (DOI · Kammann et al. 2015) — same “don’t apply hungry char” conclusion USBI states in practice language.
1.2 Application rates — same order of magnitude





















USBI Ag Guidelines 2026Vault Application Rates and MethodsField 1–10 t/ac as literature band with consistent positive impacts — biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-for-Agriculture-Applications-2026.pdfResearch literature historically ~5–50+ t ha⁻¹ (not farm default) — doi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015; vault treats high rates as research, not defaultStart 1 t/ac (4 cu yd/ac) habitat; 3 t/ac (12 cu yd/ac) SOMNRCS FAQ “good place to start” 4–10 yd³/ac — nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026Containers / holes 5–25% v/vCompatible with Exomad-style 5–10% of cultivated top layer examples linked in rates note — www.exomadgreen.com/biochar
Agreement with nuance: USBI’s 1 t/ac ≈ 4 yd³/ac start sits at the low end of NRCS’s 4–10 yd³/ac planning band — consistent once bulk density/moisture variation is acknowledged (NRCS FAQ: ~135–540 lb dry per yd³ — same FAQ URL).
1.3 Compost co-addition













USBI Compost 2026 DraftVault5–10% by volume at start; avoid >20–30% — biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Compost-2026-Draft-V1.pdfBiochar Compost and Manure Blends: Pacific Biochar practical 5–10% wood biochar; Antonangelo COMBI band; Earth Foundries 10% by volume VOC trial — pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdf · Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023 · Earth Foundries Co-Composting Report 2023

3. Where the vault is stronger (USBI thinner)













































TopicVault strengthUSBI / ABI coverageImmobilization / coating / nitrate-capture mechanismsBiochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Kammann et al. 2015 · Hagemann coating DOI doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-01123-0States the practice rule; does not walk mechanisms at paper depthMicrobial habitat debateBiochar Microbes and Soil Biology · Quilliam sparse colonization doi.org/10.1016/j.soilbio.2013.06.004Habitat narrative in Ag Guidelines; limited counter-evidenceBBF chemistry / FUE metasBiochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry · Melo/Ndoung DOIsMentions BBFs; points to pellet/prill literature via Gao cite in 2023 guide (USBI Ag Guidelines 2023)Permanence science & IPCC accountingPermanence · CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting · IPCC 2019 Biochar AppendixBeyond Application discusses H/Corg–stability narrative and points to carbon Learning Center materials; not an IPCC deep diveCredit methodologies & MRVPuro.earth Overview · Verra VM0044 · Isometric Biochar Protocol · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink · MRV StackNames Puro/Verra/EBC in lab-report context; no protocol walkthroughDeal-level market trackingHistorical Deals · Buyers and Offtakes · CDR.fyi links in Key SourcesSurvey-based industry report, not offtake ledgerDouble counting NRCS vs creditsDouble Counting and Credit OwnershipFunding guide focuses on conservation payments, not credit stacking law

4. Apparent tensions / unit traps (not true contradictions)

Tons vs cubic yards: USBI leads with t/ac; NRCS payment scenarios lead with yd³/ac. Convert only with measured bulk density/moisture (NRCS FAQ).
Compost % volume vs % weight: USBI compost sheet is volume-based (Compost PDF); some vault literature bands are w/w (Pacific / Antonangelo). Same intent, different basis — don’t mix without density.
“1–10 t/ac consistent positives” vs temperate meta-analyses: Vault yield metas show context dependence (weaker mean temperate responses — Jeffery et al. 2017 doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bd). USBI’s own poorer-soil framing and the vault’s inoculation chapter reconcile this: raw high-C wood char on fertile temperate soils is exactly where charging matters most.
Market numbers: ABI 151 kt physical biochar (2025 survey) ≠ CDR.fyi credit tonnes delivered. Keep ABI 2025 US Biochar Market Report and Market Volumes and Pricing side-by-side, not merged.
IBI seal vs CPS 336: ABI funding guide emphasizes IBI seal/criteria; NRCS FAQ stresses spec sheet still required even with certification — vault already captured (FAQ).


5. Carbon markets — side-by-side






























QuestionUSBI / ABIVaultIs BCR important to U.S. producers?2025 report: carbon finance major/maturing; bimodal revenue dependence — biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2025-United-States-Biochar-Market-Report.pdfYes — Biochar as Durable CDR · Market HubHow do you issue a credit?Mentions methodologies exist (lab PDF)Full stacks: Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025 · Verra VM0044 · etc.U.S. physical supply growth86.9 → 151.3 kt (2023–2025), 32% CAGR — same market PDFUse as industry survey complement to CDR.fyiIntegrity / CCPNot ABI’s laneKey Sources ICVCM links

6. Practical reading order

Org & library map → US Biochar Initiative
Farm how-to → Ag Guidelines PDF + Application Rates and Methods + Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer
U.S. payments → ABI Funding PDF + NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag
Testing → ANSI ASABE USBI S668 + Product Standards EBC IBI
Industry survey vs credit markets → ABI 2025 US Biochar Market Report + Market Volumes and Pricing

Policy-and-Programs/NRCS-CPS-336-and-US-.content:
NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Conservation Practice Standard 336 — Soil Carbon Amendment: EQIP/CSP (and related) cost-share for applying biochar and/or compost to improve soil health and store carbon. This is a conservation practice standard, not a carbon-credit methodology. Pair with Soil and Agriculture, Application Rates and Methods, Biochar Compost and Manure Blends, Double Counting and Credit Ownership.
Official documents (outbound)

































DocumentURLNational CPS 336 page (downloads + state links)www.nrcs.usda.gov/resources/guides-and-instructions/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-conservation-practice-standardNational standard PDF (Nov 2022)www.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/336-NHCP-CPS-Soil-Carbon-Amendment-2022.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 Standard 2022Planning FAQ (April 2026)nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdf · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026Soil Carbon Amendments overview / toolswww.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/natural-resource-concerns/soil/soil-health/soil-carbon-amendmentsProducer funding quick guide (Farmland Info hosting)farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/12/biochar_funding_for_US_producers_quick_guide_.pdfABI / biochar.org funding guidelines PDF (2026)biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-Funding-2026-final.pdf
What CPS 336 is for
Stated purposes include improve/maintain SOM, sequester/enhance soil C stocks, improve aggregate stability, and improve habitat for soil organisms; producers may also seek moisture and productivity co-benefits (FAQ). Sandy, acidic, less-healthy soils are called out as more likely to respond.
Biochar eligibility specs (practice)
From national standard Table 3 / narrative (2022 PDF):

Produced >350 °C under limited oxygen (pyrolysis or gasification)
Organic carbon (C_org) > 10% dry weight
H:C_org < 0.7 (molar) — lower preferred for sequestration
Metals and pathogens within Table limits; report ash, liming equivalent, nutrients, etc.
IBI Certified seal or documented Table 3 methods — but FAQ: certificate alone is not enough; planner still needs the spec sheet (FAQ)

Explicit exclusions / restrictions

No biosolids / municipal waste biochar or compost under 336 (PFAS and related concerns) (FAQ)
Residues that should remain for soil cover or forest health cannot be diverted into paid 336 feedstock pathways (FAQ)
Humic/fulvic products are not stand-alone carbon amendments under 336 (may be inoculants) (FAQ)

Planning rates and FY2024 scenarios
FAQ: 4–10 cubic yards per acre is a general starting range; characteristics of soil and amendment drive the final rate (FAQ).








































FY2024 scenario (FAQ Table 1)CompostBiochar100% Biochar (acres unit)—4 yd³/ac20% biochar / 80% compost4.4 t/ac0.8 yd³/ac40% biochar / 60% compost3.3 t/ac1.6 yd³/ac60% biochar / 40% compost2.2 t/ac2.4 yd³/ac80% biochar / 20% compost1.1 t/ac3.2 yd³/acCompost off-site3 t/ac—
Cubic-yard and small-area (ft²) scenarios exist for non-standard rates. Dry weight of 1 yd³ biochar ≈ 135–540 lb (FAQ).
Payment construction example: FY2023 60/40 blend scenario ~$160/yd³ average-cost build (state-varying; not invoice-matched) (Farmland Info guide).
Application practice (NRCS)

Incorporate when possible (tillage, trench, drill, beds, fertigation); surface-only risks wind/water loss (FAQ)
Inoculate with compost, compost tea, or manure (2022 PDF)
Pasture OK; native rangeland only if facilitating CPS 550 or 342 (FAQ)
Lifespan 1 year; up to 5 applications over a contract (FAQ)
Ranking improves when bundled with other soil-health practices (cover crops, no-till, rotations, etc.) (FAQ)

Full methods note: Application Rates and Methods.

Ag pathway checklist (operator-oriented)

Feedstock: Prefer documented wastes/residues; respect residue-retention rules.
Produce & test: Meet CPS 336 Table 3 / EBC-WBC / IBI-style specs; target low H:C_org for CDR eligibility.
Choose registry early if also selling credits: Verra VM0044 · Puro CORC200+ · Isometric Biochar Protocol · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink.
Secure offtake & credit ownership in farmer / applicator contracts.
Stack carefully: NRCS payments ≠ carbon credits; prevent double claiming (Double Counting and Credit Ownership).
Apply: Incorporate; watch pH, EC, P loading, slope; prefer compost blends (Biochar Compost and Manure Blends).
MRV: Batch IDs, weigh tickets, geotagged application, multi-year records (MRV Stack).

Policy Hub
Public programs, practice standards, and product certification that sit beside voluntary carbon markets. Distinct from registry methodologies (Carbon Markets Hub): policy here means government ag programs, inventory rules, and quality labels that shape how biochar is produced and used.
Domain purpose

Practice / incentive programs (e.g. US NRCS) can pay for soil application without issuing tradable CDR credits.
Product standards (EBC, WBC, IBI) define material quality and safety thresholds used by markets and buyers.
Inventory / climate policy (IPCC appendix; regional frameworks mentioned in market notes) affects national accounting—not the same as project-level credits.

Keep these layers separate when reading methodologies or offtake contracts.

Production/Biochar-Quality-from-Process.title: Biochar Quality from Process
Production/Biochar-Quality-from-Process.content:
Biochar Quality from Process
Chapter mapping process settings → material quality: elemental ratios, pH, surface area, volatile matter, nutrients, and contaminant risk. Bridges Production / Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures to Properties and Contaminants and Quality. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: H-Corg and O-Corg · Permanence · PAHs · Heavy Metals and Ash · Testing EBC IBI S668 · Production Hub · Key Sources

1. Causal chain
Feedstock chemistry + Peak T + Residence + Heating rate + Vapor path
        → molecular structure (Keiluweit transitions)
        → H/C_org, O/C_org, FC, ash%, pH, SA, VM
        → permanence proxies + agronomic behavior + contaminant load

Molecular transitions with charring temperature: Keiluweit et al. 2010. Inventory mapping of T / H/C → (F_\mathrm{perm}): Woolf IPCC Fperm.

2. Carbonization intensity


























Process directionH/C_org & O/C_orgAromatic condensationTypical (F_\mathrm{perm})Mass yieldMilder / shorterHigherLowerLowerHigherHarsher / longerLowerHigherHigherLower
(Keiluweit 2010; Woolf 2021). EBC uses H/C_org < 0.7 as the universal carbonization gate; < 0.4 for FeedPlus / manure safety proxy (EBC 10.5E §7.2, §10.4).
FC sensitivity to T is weak for high-ash feedstocks because ash concentration offsets organic C enrichment (Woolf 2021 §3.1)—measure FC directly when ash is high.

3. pH, surface area, volatile matter

pH / liming: many lignocellulosic biochars become alkaline as acidic functional groups are lost and ash oxides/carbonates remain (Properties; agronomic liming narrative in Soil and Agriculture).
BET surface area: generally rises with T into mid/high range, then can collapse at very high T as pores sinter (Properties; measurement caveats in S668 §11.3 and EBC §7.9).
Volatile matter / labile C: higher at low T → more short-term mineralization and immobilization risk (Zimmerman 2010 pattern via DOI; inoculation context Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer).


4. Contaminants as process quality signals






























Contaminant classProcess leverFeedstock leverPAHsVapor residence, condensation on cooling char, quench designWeak (EBC: negligible influence)Heavy metalsMostly conserved/concentrated (Hg volatilizes)DominantDioxins/PCBsSame vapor-condensation pathway as PAHs; test if Σ8 EFSA PAH highCl-rich / contaminated feedsPFASHigh T + residence can remove from solid; may transfer to liquids/gasBiosolids / contaminated wastes
Deep chapters: PAHs · Heavy Metals and Ash · PFAS and Emerging Contaminants. EBC PAH narrative: EBC 10.5E §7.11.

5. Homogeneity and batch control
Quality is only as good as batch definition: same feedstock blend (±20% composition), same T window, documented interruptions (EBC §5). Solid-phase electrical conductivity helps compare within-batch homogeneity (EBC §7.8). Start-up/shut-down char may need segregation from Agro/Feed grades (EBC §5.5).

6. Practice takeaway

Specify T, residence, feedstock, vapor path in specs—not “biochar” alone.
Release products against H/C_org + contaminant package + FC, not temperature warranty alone (Testing EBC IBI S668).
For CDR contracts, pair process logs with Woolf/IPCC permanence inputs (Permanence).

Production/Contaminants-and-Quality.title: Contaminants and Quality
Production/Contaminants-and-Quality.content:
Contaminants and Quality
Hub for environmental contaminants and product-quality framing of biochar: PAHs, heavy metals/ash, PFAS and emerging organics, and the testing stack (EBC / IBI / ANSI S668). Not a carbon-credit methodology. Report context: 2026-09-16.

Companion chapters (2026-09-16): PAHs · Heavy Metals and Ash · PFAS and Emerging Contaminants · Testing EBC IBI S668. This note is the spine—risk map, standards roles, and practice takeaway.

Related notes: Properties · Production · Biochar Quality from Process · Product Standards EBC IBI · ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · MRV Stack · Risks and Controversies · Production Hub · Key Sources

1. Why quality control matters
Biochar’s climate and soil value collapses if products introduce PAHs, heavy metals, dioxins/PCBs, or PFAS into soils, feed, or materials beyond regulatory and certification limits. Consensus in the science report and EBC practice: clean process design + batch testing against recognized limits (EBC; IBI; science report §3.4). Market-side safeguards also appear in MRV Stack and Risks and Controversies.

2. Contaminant map



































ClassPrimary driverDeep chapterPAHsVapor condensation / process design (feedstock secondary)PAHsHeavy metals & ashFeedstock load + mass-loss concentration; Hg volatilizesHeavy Metals and AshPCBs / PCDD/FContaminated feeds + vapor pathway; EBC triggers on high PAHPAHs · Testing EBC IBI S668PFAS & emergingBiosolids/waste feeds; pyrolysis may remove from solid but transfer to liquids/gasPFAS and Emerging ContaminantsSalts / ECManure/ash-rich charsHeavy Metals and Ash · Properties

3. Standards layers (do not confuse)






























LayerExamplesRoleProduct standardsEBC / IBIPass/fail material classes, H/C_org, contaminant limitsTest methods (U.S.)ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · PDFHow to measure (incl. PFAS EPA 1633A)—not pass/fail by itselfCarbon methodologiesVerra / Puro / Isometric / CSIMay require EBC/IBI or equivalent characterizationFarm practiceNRCS CPS 336 and US AgEligibility, not tradable credits
CSI Global Biochar C-Sink requires EBC- or WBC-certified biochar—see CSI Global Biochar C-Sink. Detail: Testing EBC IBI S668 · Product Standards EBC IBI.

4. Elemental-ratio quality gates (reminder)

H/C_org ≤ 0.7 (EBC/IBI/IUPAC biochar definition); FeedPlus / manure < 0.4 (EBC 10.5E; Bilias et al. 2024 · DOI)
O/C_org often / should be ≤ 0.4 (Properties · H-Corg and O-Corg)

These are quality/definition gates; permanence factors are separate (Permanence).

5. Headline EBC contaminant numbers (v10.5E)
From EBC Guidelines 10.5E (14 Aug 2025):






























ParameterFeedPlus / Agro / AgroOrganic (indicative)NotesΣ16 EPA PAH6.0 ± 2.4 mg kg⁻¹ DMAnalytical accuracy caveat in EBC textΣ8 EFSA PAH1.0 mg kg⁻¹ DM (also Urban/Materials)Basic allows 4 mg kg⁻¹ Σ8Heavy metalsClass-specific Table 2 (Pb, Cd, Cu, Ni, Hg, Zn, Cr, As)Basic: declaration onlyPCB / PCDD/FTriggered if Σ8 EFSA PAH > 1 mg kg⁻¹Limits 0.2 mg kg⁻¹ PCB; 20 ng kg⁻¹ I-TEQ PCDD/F
Full discussion: PAHs · Heavy Metals and Ash · Testing EBC IBI S668.

6. Practice takeaway

Design reactors for vapor–char separation before cooling; then test every batch.
Match certification class to end use (feed ≠ materials ≠ basic industrial).
For biosolids/manure routes, budget metals + PFAS analytics up front.
Use S668/EPA methods in North America; EBC-endorsed labs for EBC PAH methods (matrix matters).

Production/Feedstocks.title: Feedstocks
Production/Feedstocks.content:
Feedstocks
Hub for biomass inputs to biochar: taxonomy, property consequences, logistics, and sustainability screens. Deep contrast chapter: Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks. Process coupling: Production · Biochar Quality from Process · Gasification Residues. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Contaminants and Quality · MRV Stack · Product Standards EBC IBI · NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · Production Hub · Key Sources

1. Why feedstock choice matters








































DimensionWhy it mattersWhere detailedCarbon yield & permanence proxiesSets durable C per tonne feedstock/productWoody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · PermanenceContaminantsPAH process risk + metals/PFAS feedstock riskContaminants and QualityNutrients / ashFertilizer value vs salinity/metalsProperties · Heavy Metals and AshCompeting usesFuel, feed, soil OM, materialsThis note §4LogisticsMoisture, density, seasonality, transportThis note §5Additionality / baselineWould biomass have decayed, burned, or been landfilled?Methodology notes via MRV Stack

2. Taxonomy (practical classes)
Aligned with Woolf Table 1–2 classes and EBC positive-list culture (Woolf 2021; EBC 10.5E §4):

Woody — forest residues, mill residuals, untreated wood chips (sustainability proof for virgin forest wood: FSC/PEFC/EU-RED etc. per EBC §4.7)
Herbaceous ag residues — straws, stovers, grasses, bagasse
High-silica residues — rice husks/straw (high ash)
Nut shells / pits / stones — high lignin, often high FC
Manures & digestates — high ash/nutrients; EBC H/C_org < 0.4
Biosolids / paper sludge — metals/PFAS scrutiny; often materials-grade only
Dedicated crops — e.g. miscanthus, SRF; EBC requires soil-C and input sustainability (§4.6)
Invasive / landscape biomass — project-specific contamination checks

EBC positive list governs which biomasses enter which certification classes; fossil carbon generally banned (limited EBC-Basic exceptions with tracking) (EBC §4).

3. Property consequences (already quantified in vault)

FC extremes and class means: Production · Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · Woolf et al. 2021
Ash concentration effect on metals: Heavy Metals and Ash
Gasification of high-ash feeds → FC ~0.10–0.14: Gasification Residues

C_org of finished biochar commonly <20% to ~95% DM depending on feedstock/process (EBC §7.1); wood/nutshell chars often 70–90%, straw often 40–50% (same section).

4. Sustainability screens (research checklist — not invented criteria)
Before claiming climate benefit:

No deforestation / clear-cuts for feedstock (EBC §4.7; Lehmann et al. 2021 energy/land framing · DOI)
Plastic/rubber contamination limits (EBC: ≤1% for soil classes; up to 10% materials with approval — §4.5)
Food vs fuel competition and ILUC — evaluate in LCA; do not invent vault thresholds
Baseline fate (decay, open burn, landfill CH₄) dominates system GHG (CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting)

Registry feedstock rules: point to Puro Biochar Methodology Edition 2025, Verra VM0044 Methodology and Eligibility, Isometric Biochar Protocol, CSI Global Biochar C-Sink rather than duplicating.

5. Logistics & preprocessing

Moisture: drying is often the largest energy sink before pyrolysis; EBC energy-efficiency calculus includes drying energy (EBC §8.5).
Particle size: chipping/grinding for reactor feed; FeedPlus may recommend grinding char <3 mm to reduce stone/glass injury risk (EBC §10.3).
Seasonality & density: herbaceous residues bulky/seasonal; woody more storable if dry.
US farm context: NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · USBI Ag Guidelines 2023.


6. Practice takeaway

Classify feedstock with Woolf/EBC vocabulary before modeling CDR tonnes.
Run contaminant risk by class (metals/PFAS for manures/biosolids; PAH for all via process).
Document sustainability proof at procurement—not only at kiln exit.

Production/Gasification-Residues.title: Gasification Residues
Production/Gasification-Residues.content:
Gasification Residues
Chapter on solids from biomass gasification—often high-ash, lower organic-carbon materials that may still qualify as biochar when organic C meets definitional and permanence criteria. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Production · Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · Biochar Quality from Process · Heavy Metals and Ash · Woolf IPCC Fperm · Production Hub · Key Sources

1. What gasification leaves behind
Gasification converts biomass with a limited oxidant supply to prioritize syngas (CO, H₂, CO₂, light hydrocarbons). The solid residue retains ash plus whatever organic carbon did not gasify. Woolf notes these materials may be described as “ash with biochar” or “high-ash content biochar”—no universal naming standard (DOI §3.1).
IPCC App. 4 and Woolf include gasification solids in the biochar inventory method when they meet the >350 °C limited-oxidant definition (IPCC PDF; Woolf §2.1.1). EBC likewise allows gasification within its technology spectrum if quality and sustainability rules are met (EBC 10.5E §2).

2. Carbon fractions (Woolf Table 2 gasification column)



































FeedstockGasification FC (mean)Contrast: pyrolysis mean FCWood0.630.76Herbaceous0.380.64Manure0.140.39Sewage sludge0.100.37Rice residues0.200.47
(open PDF Table 2). Abstract extremes: gasified biosolids C content as low as ~7% (DOI).
If ash has been partially removed from a gasification solid, Woolf Table 2 defaults must not be used—measure FC directly (§3.1).

3. Permanence paradox (low FC, possibly high persistence)
Gasification typically runs hot → low H/C_org → organic C that remains can be highly condensed and score well on Woolf H/C_org permanence regressions (§3.2). IPCC high-T class explicitly contemplates high-T gasification for (F_\mathrm{perm}) 0.89 (PDF).
Accounting implication: tonnes of product are ash-diluted; tonnes of durable organic C may still be valuable. Always multiply (M \times F_C \times F_\mathrm{perm}), never assume wood-like FC.
Hansen et al. (2015) discuss gasification biochar as a co-product for sequestration and soil amendment in the broader literature Woolf cites (DOI).

4. Agronomy and contaminants

Ash / salts / liming: can supply K, Ca, Mg and raise pH—but salinity and heavy-metal concentration risks rise (Heavy Metals and Ash).
Nutrients: manure/sludge gasification residues concentrate P/K relative to woody pyrochars but may fail EBC-Agro metal limits (EBC §4.9).
PAHs: still process-dependent; poor vapor handling can contaminate residues (PAHs).
Naming for buyers: disclose FC, ash, H/C_org, and feedstock—avoid selling “biochar” without ash context.


5. Practice takeaway

Treat gasification solids as first-class inventory materials only with measured FC + H/C_org (or documented high-T class).
Expect CDR per tonne product ≪ woody slow-pyrolysis char.
Screen metals/PFAS before soil use—ash concentration amplifies feedstock contamination.

Production/Heavy-Metals-and-Ash.title: Heavy Metals and Ash
Production/Heavy-Metals-and-Ash.content:
Heavy Metals and Ash
Chapter on ash and trace metals in biochar: concentration during pyrolysis, feedstock drivers, EBC class limits, and agronomic salinity/micronutrient issues. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Contaminants and Quality · Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · Gasification Residues · Properties · PFAS and Emerging Contaminants · Testing EBC IBI S668 · Key Sources

1. Ash conservation and concentration
Biomass ash is largely conserved into the solid while C/H/O leave as volatiles, so metal and mineral concentrations in biochar exceed those in the parent biomass (EBC 10.5E §7.5; Woolf 2021 eq. 2). Woolf Table 1 mean ash: wood 2.2% vs manure 28.5% vs sewage sludge 39.4% (open PDF).
Exception: mercury (and some semi-volatiles) can leave in the gas phase at pyrolysis temperatures (EBC §7.5).
High ash → lower FC (Gasification Residues, Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks) and harder O/C_org analytics (H-Corg and O-Corg; S668 §14).

2. EBC heavy-metal limits (v10.5E Table 2)
Indicative dry-matter limits from EBC 10.5E (FeedPlus/AgroOrganic often on 88% DM basis for some elements):



























































MetalFeedPlus / AgroOrganic (stricter)Agro / Urban / MaterialsBasicPb5 g t⁻¹ (88% DM)45 / 120 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationCd0.5 g t⁻¹ (88% DM)0.7 / 1.5 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationCu70 g t⁻¹ DM70 / 100 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationNi25 g t⁻¹ DM25 / 50 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationHg0.1 g t⁻¹ (88% DM)0.4 / 1 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationZn200 g t⁻¹ DM200 / 400 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationCr70 g t⁻¹ DM70 / 90 g t⁻¹ DMDeclarationAs2 g t⁻¹ (88% DM)13 g t⁻¹ DMDeclaration
Aligned with EU fertiliser regulation and national soil/chem ordinances as cited by EBC (§7.5). Cu/Zn exceedances may be marketed as micronutrient fertilizers if labeled and rate-guided—not as ordinary Agro biochar.
Biosolids chars often fail Agro/Urban metal limits; EBC channels them toward EBC-Basic unless a country annex allows nutrient-to-metal ratio approaches (§4.9).

3. Salts, EC, and agronomy
Leachate electrical conductivity estimates salt content—a feedstock contamination / manure signal (EBC §7.6). Ash-rich chars can lime and fertilize but also salinize sensitive soils. Pair with nutrient declaration (N, P, K, Mg, Ca, Fe mandatory in EBC — §7.4).

4. Testing

EBC: endorsed labs, class-specific packages.
U.S.: EPA trace-metal methods per ANSI ASABE USBI S668 §12.2 · PDF.
Always report on stated moisture basis (DM vs 88% DM for feed).


5. Practice takeaway

Metals track feedstock cleanliness more than kiln brand.
Concentration math: >50% mass loss roughly doubles non-volatile metal content—plan feedstock specs accordingly.
Separate micronutrient labeling from general soil-amendment claims when Cu/Zn are high.

Production/PAHs.title: PAHs
Production/PAHs.content:
PAHs
Chapter on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in biochar: formation, process controls, toxicity framing, and EBC/IBI/S668 testing. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Contaminants and Quality · Biochar Quality from Process · Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures · Testing EBC IBI S668 · Heavy Metals and Ash · Product Standards EBC IBI · Key Sources

1. Formation and process dependence
Pyrolysis of organic materials generates PAHs (EBC 10.5E §7.11). Content depends primarily on:

Peak temperature and vapor residence
Separation of biochar from pyrolysis gases
Post-pyrolysis condensation of PAH-laden vapors onto cool porous char

EBC states feedstock type has a negligible influence relative to process conditions (§7.11). Clean combustion of pyrolysis gases usually destroys PAHs in the gas phase; contamination rises when gases adsorb or condense on the solid. Controlled vapor quenching and high-T separation help.
Even simple flame-curtain kilns can achieve low PAH with correct operation; some industrial designs have historically produced elevated PAH as a process-quality signal (EBC §7.11; Kon-Tiki emissions/char study Cornelissen et al. 2016).

2. Which PAH lists matter





















ListRole16 EPA PAHClassic monitoring suite; EU fertiliser regulation uses Σ16 = 6 mg kg⁻¹ DM for soil amendments (EBC citing EU 2019/1009)8 EFSA PAHCarcinogenic subset used for tighter EBC controlsREACH extrasBenzo[e]pyrene & benzo[j]fluoranthene ≤ 1 mg kg⁻¹ each for all EBC classes
EBC analysis of 936 certified samples found non-carcinogenic PAHs usually >80% of Σ16; 99% of samples meeting Σ16 ≤ 6 mg kg⁻¹ also had Σ8 EFSA < 1 mg kg⁻¹—motivating the dual limit to stop post-treatments that strip light PAHs while leaving heavy carcinogens (EBC §7.11).

3. EBC limit summary (v10.5E)

























ClassΣ16 EPA PAHΣ8 EFSA PAHFeedPlus, Agro, AgroOrganic6.0 ± 2.4 mg kg⁻¹ DM1.0 mg kg⁻¹ DMUrban, MaterialsDeclaration of Σ16 to CSI1.0 mg kg⁻¹ DMBasicDeclaration4 mg kg⁻¹ DM
(EBC 10.5E Tab.1 / §7.11). Units in EBC tables also appear as g t⁻¹ (= mg kg⁻¹).

4. Bioavailability and risk posture
Hilber and co-workers (cited extensively in EBC) show soil-applied low-PAH biochar often acts as a net sink for environmental PAHs rather than a source; bioavailability of biochar-bound PAHs is typically very low—but rumen studies showed substantial desorption of PAHs from high-PAH chars, motivating strict FeedPlus limits (EBC §7.11). Absent biochar-specific risk assessments, regulators applied compost/digestate-like limits (precautionary).
PCB / PCDD/F: EBC requires quantification when Σ8 EFSA PAH > 1 mg kg⁻¹; limits 0.2 mg kg⁻¹ PCB and 20 ng kg⁻¹ I-TEQ PCDD/F (§7.10). FeedPlus has stricter dioxin/PCB packages (§10.7).

5. Testing notes

Standard soil PAH methods often under-extract biochar—use EBC-endorsed methods/labs (EBC §7.11).
North American method pointers: ANSI ASABE USBI S668 §12.1.1 · PDF (EPA extraction/analysis pathways).
IBI standards similarly require PAH declaration/limits by grade—see IBI standards portal · Product Standards EBC IBI.


6. Practice takeaway

Engineer no cool-down in PAH-rich vapor.
Dual-track Σ16 and Σ8 (plus REACH pair) for soil/feed grades.
Treat elevated PAH as a process failure, not a feedstock inevitability.
