Production/PFAS-and-Emerging-Contaminant.title: PFAS and Emerging Contaminants
Production/PFAS-and-Emerging-Contaminant.content:
PFAS and Emerging Contaminants
Chapter on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and related emerging organics in biochar systems—especially biosolids and waste-derived feedstocks. Distinguishes solid-phase removal from true destruction. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Contaminants and Quality · Heavy Metals and Ash · Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · Testing EBC IBI S668 · ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · Risks and Controversies · Key Sources

1. Why PFAS shows up in biochar conversations
PFAS are ubiquitous and especially elevated in wastewater treatment plant biosolids. Pyrolysis is explored both as a biosolids management path and as a potential PFAS treatment. ANSI ASABE USBI S668 §12.1.4 states PFAS are more common in biochar from high-PFAS feedstocks such as WWTP biosolids and recommends periodic analysis when those feeds are used (PDF).
EBC allows biosolids for EBC-Basic with worker-safety plans and minimum >500 °C for 3 min, noting metals usually block Agro/Urban soil use (EBC 10.5E §4.9). PFAS is an additional emerging constraint beyond metals.

2. Removal ≠ destruction (critical distinction)





























FindingSourcePyrolysis can remove >99% of targeted PFAS from the solid (biochar) phaseMcNamara et al. 2023 — DOISome PFAS / precursors can increase in py-liquid (e.g. NEtFOSE, NMeFOSE masses rose >100× vs influent biosolids across 500–800 °C trials)Same studyPyrolysis + thermal oxidizer on off-gas achieved 99.4% molar PFAS removal in a lab system resembling full-scale; short-chain PFAS dominated residual flue gasThomsen et al. / Water Environ. Res. — DOIBench pyrolysis/co-pyrolysis at 600 °C reported 99.4% PFAS destruction efficiency under long residence (~10 s gas / 1 h solids) with residual char PFAS meeting proposed unrestricted land-app limits in that studyRathnayake et al. 2025 — DOIReviews: destruction efficacy depends on PFAS structure, T, O₂, residence; incomplete combustion products are a concernLongendyke et al. 2022 — DOI
Vault takeaway: low PFAS in biochar is necessary but not sufficient for a clean process claim—track liquids and stack gas, and use thermal oxidation where required.

3. Testing guidance (methods, not pass/fail)
ANSI ASABE USBI S668 (PDF §12.1.4):

Analyze per EPA Method 1633A when testing biochar for PFAS.
Standard does not set pass/fail criteria—use jurisdictional guidance (e.g. EPA interim biosolids limits, state soil screening levels).
Matrix challenges: high organic C and inorganics affect extraction; contamination control is essential; science is still emerging.

Pair with metals and PAH packages for biosolids-derived chars (Heavy Metals and Ash, PAHs).

4. Other emerging / regulated organics (brief)

Dioxins/furans & PCBs: covered under PAH-triggered EBC rules and FeedPlus packages (PAHs; EBC §7.10, §10.7); S668 lists EPA 8082A / 8290A pathways (§12.1.2–12.1.3).
Pharmaceuticals / micropollutants in manures: EBC uses high carbonization (H/C_org < 0.4) as a destruction proxy for animal by-products (§4.8, §10.4).
Microplastics in feedstock: EBC mass limits and possible C-sink deductions (§4.5).


5. Practice takeaway

Any biosolids → biochar pathway needs a PFAS mass-balance story (solid + liquid + gas), not only a clean char certificate.
Prefer feeds with low PFAS when targeting soil grades; reserve contaminated feeds for tightly engineered systems with thermal oxidizers.
Cite method (EPA 1633A) and jurisdiction when reporting PFAS results.

Production Hub
Map of notes on how biochar is made, what feedstock and process choices control, and how material quality is judged before application or credit issuance. Sits between raw biomass and the science of permanence / agronomy / markets. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Domain purpose
Production is the controllable step that turns biomass into a carbon-rich solid. Peak temperature, residence time, heating rate, reactor type, and feedstock chemistry jointly set:

Mass yield of char vs oil/gas
Carbon content and aromatic condensation (persistence proxies such as H/C_org, O/C_org)

Production/Production.title: Production
Production/Production.content:
Production
Spine note on how biomass becomes biochar: thermochemical modes, product slate, carbon fraction, and links into the deeper production chapter set. Companion chapters (2026-09-16): Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures · Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · Biochar Quality from Process · Gasification Residues · Feedstocks. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Production Hub · Properties · Permanence · Contaminants and Quality · Overview and Definition · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. Process definition
Thermochemical decomposition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin under oxygen-free or oxygen-limited conditions yields:

Solid — biochar (pyrogenic carbon-rich porous solid)
Liquids — bio-oil / pyroligneous fractions
Gases — CO₂, CO, H₂, light hydrocarbons (syngas when oxidant is present at gasification levels)

IPCC inventory definition: solid from heating biomass >350 °C under controlled/limited oxidant so it does not combust (pyrolysis or gasification), for mineral soils in cropland/grassland (IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix · PDF).
IUPAC (Bilias et al. 2024): solid multifunctional porous carbonaceous product of agricultural biomass pyrolysis typically 350–1000 °C, with molar H/C_org < 0.7 and O/C_org < 0.4 (Bilias et al. 2024 · DOI).
Not biochar under these definitions: torrefaction / HTC solids (typically <350 °C or wet pressurized; not sufficiently persistent for Woolf/IPCC methods — Woolf 2021 §2.1.1), fossil chars, open wildfire charcoal without process control.
EBC treats gasification as within the pyrolysis technology spectrum when optimized for biochar and otherwise compliant (EBC 10.5E §2).

2. Typical modes





























ModeTemperature / rateFavorsDeep noteSlow pyrolysis~300–700 °C, low heating rate, minutes–hoursBiochar yieldPyrolysis Systems and TemperaturesFast / flash pyrolysisHigher heating rates, secondsLiquids (bio-oil)SameGasificationHigher T, limited oxidantSyngas; solid often high-ash / lower FCGasification Residues
Controls on properties: feedstock class, peak temperature, residence time, heating rate, reactor design, ash (Biochar Quality from Process; Keiluweit et al. 2010).

3. Carbon content (FC) — Woolf examples
Organic carbon mass fraction on dry matter varies from as low as ~7% (gasified biosolids) to ~79% (wood pyrolysed >600 °C) in Woolf’s abstract range (Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI). Table 2 class means (open PDF):





































Feedstock / processApprox. FCWood pyrolysis (mean of T classes)0.76Wood high-T (≥600 °C)0.81Wood low / medium0.70 / 0.77Manure pyrolysis (all T ≈)0.39Sewage sludge pyrolysis mean0.37Gasification wood0.63Gasification manure / sludge~0.14 / 0.10
Full feedstock grid: Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks · Feedstocks. Biomass ash/lignin priors: Woolf Table 1 from Phyllis2 (phyllis.nl/).

4. Process effects on quality and permanence (summary)
Higher pyrolysis T → lower H/C_org & O/C_org, higher aromatic condensation, generally higher (F_\mathrm{perm}), often higher pH/surface area (then possible decline at very high T), lower volatile matter, sometimes lower mass yield (Keiluweit 2010; Woolf 2021; Permanence). Gasification residues can be very high-ash / low FC; permanence of the organic C may still be high if H/C_org is low, but C per tonne product is lower (Gasification Residues).
PAH risk is driven more by vapor management than feedstock identity (PAHs; EBC 10.5E §7.11).

5. EBC process floor (sustainability, not just chemistry)
For EBC-certified production (EBC 10.5E §8): recover/use excess heat or liquid/gaseous products; do not release pyrolysis gases without a dedicated combustion chamber; meet national emission limits; document homogeneous batch quality (temperature typically held within ±20% of declared set-point — §5); energy-efficiency target ≥60% of feedstock+expenditures recovered in useful products (with transitional exemptions).

Production/Pyrolysis-Systems-and-Tempera.title: Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures
Production/Pyrolysis-Systems-and-Tempera.content:
Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures
Chapter on reactor modes, temperature classes, residence time, and heat management—the controllable engineering variables that set biochar yield and chemistry. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Production · Biochar Quality from Process · Gasification Residues · Feedstocks · Woolf IPCC Fperm · PAHs · Production Hub · Key Sources

1. Temperature classes used in inventories
Woolf et al. 2021 / IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix permanence and FC tables use:

























ClassPeak temperatureTypical roleLow350–450 °CHigher yield, higher H/C_org, lower (F_\mathrm{perm})Medium450–600 °CCommon agronomic / CDR operating windowHigh≥600 °CMore condensed aromatics; often lower mass yield
(Woolf DOI; IPCC PDF). Materials <350 °C excluded from these permanence methods (Woolf §2.1.1).
EBC batch rule of thumb: declared pyrolysis temperature may fluctuate by up to ±20% (e.g. 600 °C → short-term 480–720 °C) without breaking the batch, if documented (EBC 10.5E §5.5). EBC-FeedPlus / Swiss-style agricultural rules often require ≥500 °C for ≥10 min, proxied by H/C_org < 0.4 (EBC §10.4).

2. Heating rate and residence time

























ModeHeating rate / solids residenceProduct emphasisSlow pyrolysisLow °C/min; minutes–hoursMaximize biocharFast / flashVery high heating; secondsMaximize liquidsGasificationLimited oxidant; often >700–800 °C bedMaximize syngas; solid = residue
Residence time at peak T matters as much as the peak number for condensation (Keiluweit et al. 2010; Woolf notes T is a weaker condensation proxy than H/C_org because time also matters — DOI).

3. Reactor families (descriptive)
Commercial and farm-scale systems span:

Continuous auger / rotary / screw pyrolyzers — steady T profiles, good batch documentation for MRV.
Fixed / moving bed and fluidized bed — industrial throughput; fluid beds favor fast heat transfer (often liquids if configured that way).
Kilns / retorts / flame-curtain (e.g. Kon-Tiki class) — farmer-scale; EBC cites flame-curtain examples as capable of low PAH when vapor handling is correct (EBC 10.5E §7.11; Cornelissen et al. 2016 emissions/char quality study cited therein · DOI).
Gasifiers (downdraft, updraft, fluidized) — see Gasification Residues.

EBC requires each pyrolysis unit certified individually (with limited exceptions for identical parallel lines sharing feedstock/output) (EBC §8.6).

4. Energy and emissions engineering
From Woolf life-cycle framing and EBC:

~35–60% of feedstock energy often ends in pyrolysis gas that is burned in-plant (EBC §8.5).
Modern plants should fully combust organics to CO₂; simple kilns may emit CH₄ and VOCs that erase climate benefit if unmanaged (Woolf 2021 §2.1.2 item 7; Woolf et al. 2017 open-source reactor).
EBC: no uncombusted pyrolysis-gas release; fossil fuel banned for reactor heat except preheat; electric heat must be renewable/surplus (EBC §8.1–8.4).


5. Link to permanence and contaminants



































Higher peak T / longer residenceTypical effectNotesH/C_org, O/C_org↓H-Corg and O-Corg(F_\mathrm{perm})↑Woolf IPCC FpermMass yieldOften ↓Trade-off vs C per tonne feedstockBET surface area↑ then may ↓ at very high TPropertiesPAHNot a simple T function—vapor condensation dominatesPAHs

6. Practice takeaway

Log peak T + residence + feedstock blend for every batch (EBC Biochar Tool culture).
Prefer measured H/C_org over T-class alone for CDR math (Woolf IPCC Fperm).
Design vapor–solid separation before cooling to control PAHs (PAHs).

Testing EBC IBI S668
Chapter on how biochar is tested and certified: European Biochar Certificate (EBC), IBI Biochar Standards, and ANSI/ASABE/USBI S668 test methods. Clarifies pass/fail product standards vs methods-only standards vs carbon methodologies. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Contaminants and Quality · Product Standards EBC IBI · ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · PAHs · Heavy Metals and Ash · PFAS and Emerging Contaminants · H-Corg and O-Corg · Properties · Key Sources

1. Three layers





























LayerInstrumentSets pass/fail limits?Vault homeProduct certificationEBC / IBI (and WBC-related EBC framing)Yes — H/C_org, PAH, metals, use classesProduct Standards EBC IBITest methodsANSI/ASABE/USBI S668 (Nov 2025)No — recommended methods onlyANSI ASABE USBI S668Carbon creditingVerra / Puro / Isometric / CSIEligibility + MRV (may require EBC/IBI)MRV Stack · methodology notes
CSI Global Biochar C-Sink requires EBC- or WBC-certified biochar (CSI docs · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink).

2. EBC (v10.5E, 14 Aug 2025)
Primary PDF: EBC Guidelines 10.5E · home european-biochar.org.
Classes: FeedPlus, AgroOrganic, Agro, Urban, Materials, Basic (each with purpose-specific limits).
Minimum analytical package ideas:

Elemental: C_tot, C_org, H, N, O, S, ash → H/C_org (and O/C_org)
Physical: moisture, bulk density, WHC, pH, salt/EC, solid EC
Nutrients: N, P, K, Mg, Ca, Fe
Contaminants: heavy metals; PAH (Σ16 + Σ8); PCB/PCDD/F when triggered
FeedPlus extras: dioxin/PCB packages, F, crude ash, etc. (§10)

Batch & sampling culture: register batches in Biochar Tool; endorsed sampler; endorsed lab; retention samples; T within ±20%; feedstock blend within ±20% (§5–6).
Key numeric gates duplicated in contaminant chapters: PAHs, Heavy Metals and Ash, H-Corg and O-Corg.

3. IBI Biochar Standards
Portal: biochar-international.org/biochar-standards · org home biochar-international.org.
IBI standards define biochar material criteria (including H/C_org ≤ 0.7 classically, O/C thresholds, and contaminant declaration/limits by grade) used widely in North American commerce and lab report interpretation. ABI’s interpreting-lab-reports guidance points practitioners to IBI method packages (ABI lab report PDF · US Biochar Initiative). Exact grade tables should be read from the current IBI document before diligence—vault does not invent versioned limit tables beyond EBC full-text extracts and the ≤0.7 / ≤0.4 ratios already in Properties.

4. ANSI/ASABE/USBI S668 (NOV2025ED)
Source note: ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · PDF · doc page.
Scope highlights:





































TopicS668 pointerPermanence metrics§10 — H:C_org, O:C_org formulas; Ro per ISO 7404-5Organic C§9 — C_org = total C − inorganic CPhysical§11 — bulk density ISO 17828; PSD sieves; BET ISO 9277 guidancePAHs / PCBs / PCDD/F§12.1 — EPA extraction/analysis methodsPFAS§12.1.4 — EPA 1633A; no pass/failTrace metals§12.2 — EPA methods for U.S. useAg parametersNutrients, pH, liming, salinity
Front matter: ASABE standards are informational/advisory/voluntary. S668 does not replace NRCS CPS 336 or registry MRV.

5. How to choose a stack

























GoalPractical stackSell soil amendment in EU / EBC marketsEBC class certification + endorsed labSell in U.S. with transparent methodsIBI-aligned report + S668/EPA methods; consider EBC if buyer/CDR requiresIssue carbon creditsFollow methodology; many paths expect EBC/IBI + production MRV (Permanence Science for Credits)Research / R&D onlyS668 methods + publish FC, H/C_org, PAH, metals

6. Practice takeaway

Never treat a methods standard (S668) as a certificate.
Match class to end use before comparing PAH/metal numbers.
For PFAS, report method + jurisdiction—there is no universal biochar PFAS limit in S668.

Production/Woody-vs-Manure-Ag-Feedstocks.title: Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks
Production/Woody-vs-Manure-Ag-Feedstocks.content:
Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks
Chapter contrasting woody / lignocellulosic vs manure and other high-ash agricultural feedstocks for carbon fraction, nutrients, contaminants, and eligibility. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Feedstocks · Production · Gasification Residues · Heavy Metals and Ash · Contaminants and Quality · Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry · Production Hub · Key Sources

1. Why the contrast matters
Feedstock sets baseline ash, lignin, and nutrient loads that pyrolysis concentrates or transforms. Woody biomass → high-C, low-ash chars optimized for CDR mass per tonne product. Manures / sludges → lower FC, higher ash and nutrients, tighter contaminant and certification constraints (Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI; EBC 10.5E §4).

2. Biomass priors (Woolf Table 1 / Phyllis2)
Mean dry-matter ash and DAF carbon for feedstock classes (Woolf open PDF Table 1; database Phyllis2):





















































Feedstock classAsh (DM) meanC (DAF) meanLignin meanWood2.2%50.7%24.7%Herbaceous7.0%48.9%11.8%Wheat straw7.2%48.8%12.3%Manure28.5%45.2%11.3%Sewage sludge39.4%51.1%6.0%Rice residues17.9%48.3%17.9%Pits/shells/stones3.8%50.6%33.2%
Ash is largely conserved into the solid, so high-ash feedstocks produce high-ash biochars even when organic matter carbonizes fully (Woolf eqs. 2–4).

3. Biochar carbon fraction (Woolf Table 2)















































FeedstockPyrolysis FC (mean)High-T pyro FCGasification FCWood0.760.810.63Herbaceous0.640.660.38Manure0.390.390.14Sewage sludge0.370.380.10Rice residues0.470.480.20Pits/shells0.720.760.52
(DOI). CDR implication: one tonne of manure char stores much less organic C than one tonne of wood char at similar permanence of that C.

4. Nutrients and agronomy
EBC notes nutrient contents can reach ~one-third of biochar mass; first-year plant availability often roughly ~15% of P, ~1% of N, ~50% of K in cited ranges (EBC 10.5E §7.4). Manure chars are therefore more “fertilizer-like”; woody chars are nutrient-poor sponges that often need inoculation (Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer). EBC encourages keeping manure-derived nutrients in agricultural cycles rather than locking them into industrial materials (EBC §4.8).

5. Certification / safety contrasts



































TopicWoody / plant residuesManure / animal by-productsBiosolidsEBC soil classesPositive-list biomass; forest wood needs FSC/PEFC/etc.Allowed except Feed; H/C_org < 0.4 requiredGenerally EBC-Basic only; metals often too high for Agro/UrbanHeavy metalsUsually low if clean biomassWatch Cu/Zn; concentration effectOften limitingPFASLow unless contaminatedVariableElevated risk → test (PFAS and Emerging Contaminants)Feed gradePossible (FeedPlus plant biomass)Not for FeedPlusNo
(EBC 10.5E §4.7–4.9). Credit methodologies add their own feedstock eligibility—see MRV Stack / methodology notes, not duplicated here.

6. Practice takeaway

Match feedstock to goal: CDR mass → clean woody/low-ash; nutrient recycling → manures with metals/PFAS controls.
Always measure FC and H/C_org on high-ash chars rather than assuming wood defaults (H-Corg and O-Corg).
Track competing uses (feed, bedding, soil OM, energy) for additionality narratives (Feedstocks).

CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting
IPCC inventory method
IPCC 2019 Refinement Vol. 4 Appendix 4 provides a method for estimating biochar C in mineral cropland/grassland soils (PDF · IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix).
F_perm after 100 years (conservative ~20 °C basis in appendix notes):





















Temperature classF_permLow (350–450 °C)0.65Medium (450–600 °C)0.80High (>600 °C / high-T gasification)0.89
Uncertainty roughly ±11–15%. Guidance / basis for future Tier 1—not a credit methodology. See Verra VM0044, Puro CORC200+, etc. for market methods.
Woolf et al. (2021) extends this with H/C_org and soil-temperature predictors. DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.1c02425.
Mitigation / CDR potential estimates





























SourceEstimateWoolf et al. 2010Max 1.8 Pg CO₂-Cₑ yr⁻¹ (≈ ~6.6 Pg CO₂e if ×44/12); century total 130 Pg CO₂-Cₑ. Prefer Lehmann 2021 / Weng 2025 for updated framing.Lehmann et al. 2021Emission reductions 3.4–6.3 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹ (~half CDR); residues-only 2.4–3.9; with land sparing + CCS up to ~7.4–10.3Weng & Cowie 2025Literature 0.03–11; credible multi-Gt scaleState of CDR 2026 (Fuss & Lunstrum) · Fuss & Lunstrum 2026Sustainable removal ≤~2.7 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹; total mitigation ≤~10.3; IAM 2050 <0.1–1.1Costs (Fuss & Lunstrum 2026)Often ~70–360/tCO₂** (recent); broader historical **~10–345
LCA / system boundaries
Net climate benefit is dominated by biochar C permanence vs baseline biomass fate, modulated by methane avoidance (rice, landfill), energy co-products, transport, and kiln CH₄ if poorly engineered (Roberts et al. 2010 onward; Matuštík et al. 2020 review; Lehmann 2021).
State of CDR (2026) and Weng & Cowie (2025) place biochar as largest current novel CDR contributor with gigaton-scale technical/sustainable potential but much lower near-term economic/IAM deployment.
MRV accounting insight (science side)
MRV can focus on mass produced × C fraction × permanence factor at the kiln/gate, with application verification—cheaper than full soil flux monitoring (Lehmann 2021). Markets implement this differently—see MRV Stack.

Science/Consensus-vs-Debates.title: Consensus vs Debates
Science/Consensus-vs-Debates.content:
Consensus vs Debates
Broad consensus

Well-made biochar (adequate T / low H/C_org) is much more persistent than raw biomass; fused aromatics are the mechanistic basis.
Sustainable feedstock (wastes/residues; no deforestation) is required for net climate benefit.
Biochar can raise yields especially in acid/degraded/tropical soils, but responses are context-specific.
N₂O reductions are real in many systems in year 1; magnitude and multi-year persistence less certain.
MRV can focus on mass × C fraction × permanence factor at the kiln/gate, with application verification—cheaper than full soil flux monitoring (Lehmann 2021 · DOI).
Quality control for PAHs/heavy metals and process emissions (kiln CH₄) matters for safe deployment.

Open debates / uncertainties

Long-term decay model form: Two-pool fits from ≤few-year incubations may mis-estimate millennial recalcitrant pools; newer proxies (HyPy, conductivity, Ro) and policy commentaries argue for refined permanence metrics.
CH₄ in paddies: Direction and magnitude still study-dependent.
Priming ceiling: Decade-scale negative priming is promising but long-term saturation and organic-soil risks remain.
Energy vs CDR trade-off: Relative benefit depends on what energy is displaced (coal vs renewables); as grids decarbonize, soil biochar becomes relatively more attractive (Lehmann 2021).
Economic vs technical potential: Technical/sustainable multi-Gt ≠ near-term deployable; IAM/economic potentials often ≪1 Gt by 2050.
Non-soil uses (concrete, asphalt, animal feed, materials): permanence pathways differ; soil-amendment science does not automatically transfer.
Climate feedback on permanence: Warmer soils accelerate decay (Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI Q10 framework)—future warming reduces F_perm relative to today’s tables.

Science/H-Corg-and-O-Corg.title: H-Corg and O-Corg
Science/H-Corg-and-O-Corg.content:
H/C_org and O/C_org
Chapter on molar hydrogen-to-organic-carbon and oxygen-to-organic-carbon ratios as the primary chemical proxies for biochar aromatic condensation and soil persistence. Companion to Permanence · Woolf IPCC Fperm · Properties. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Reflectance Ro and HyPy · Biochar Quality from Process · Product Standards EBC IBI · Testing EBC IBI S668 · Permanence Science for Credits · ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. Why elemental ratios track permanence
Pyrolysis drives condensation reactions that grow fused aromatic domains. As aromatic sheets enlarge, C–C bonds replace C–H and C–O bonds, so H/C_org and O/C_org fall (Keiluweit et al., 2010 · DOI; Woolf et al., 2021 · DOI). Lower ratios therefore indicate a more condensed, typically more persistent solid—relative indicators, not absolute half-lives by themselves (Schmidt et al., 2025).
IUPAC’s biochar glossary frames biochar as a pyrolysis solid with molar H/C_org < 0.7 and O/C_org < 0.4 to ensure abundant fused aromatics and distinguish inadequately carbonized materials (Bilias et al. 2024 · DOI).

2. Definitions and calculation

























SymbolMeaningNotesC_orgOrganic carbon mass fraction (dry basis)Total C minus inorganic C (carbonates); see ANSI ASABE USBI S668 §9 · PDFH/C_org (also H:C_org)Moles H / moles C_orgPreferred condensation proxy in Woolf inventory model (DOI)O/C_org (also O:C_org)Moles O / moles C_orgClassic Spokas predictor (DOI); O often calculated by difference
ANSI/ASABE/USBI S668 formulas (PDF §10.1–10.2):
[
\mathrm{H{:}C_{org}} = \frac{(%\mathrm{H}/1.0079)}{(%\mathrm{C_{org}}/12.011)}
\qquad
\mathrm{O{:}C_{org}} = \frac{(%\mathrm{O}/15.999)}{(%\mathrm{C_{org}}/12.011)}
]
S668 notes that high-ash chars need care on oxygen (alternate calculation in §14.2)—important for manure/sludge/gasification residues (Gasification Residues, Heavy Metals and Ash).
EBC accepts calculating O from C, H, N, S, and ash when direct O measurement is expensive (EBC 10.5E PDF §7.3).

3. H/C_org as inventory input (Woolf)
Woolf et al. 2021 recommends H/C_org over pyrolysis temperature when elemental analysis is available, because H/C_org correlates more tightly with condensation (temperature alone ignores residence time and other process factors) (DOI; open PDF §3.2).
Permanence is fit as a linear regression:
[
F_\mathrm{perm} = c_\mathrm{hc} - m_\mathrm{hc},(H/C_\mathrm{org})
]
Coefficients (c_\mathrm{hc}), (m_\mathrm{hc}) depend on soil temperature and time horizon (Woolf Table 3). Example at 14.9 °C, 100 years: (c_\mathrm{hc}=1.04), (m_\mathrm{hc}=-0.64), (R^2=0.32) (open PDF Table 3). Full coefficient grid: Woolf IPCC Fperm.
Gasification chars often combine high process temperature with low H/C_org despite low carbon fraction—persistence of the organic C can still be high even when FC is low (Woolf 2021 §3.2; Gasification Residues).

4. O/C_org and Spokas half-life classes
Spokas (2010) reviewed biochar stability and proposed O:C molar ratio as a predictor of soil half-life. The review is foundational for standards language and practitioner rules-of-thumb; treat the binned half-lives as approximate, not inventory-grade alone (Quantitative Benchmarks, science report framing).
Widely cited interpretive bins from that literature (cite Spokas DOI when using):

























Approx. O/CInterpreted half-life classPractice reading< ~0.2Millennial-scaleHighly condensed / high-T chars~0.2–0.6Centennial-scaleTypical mid-range pyrolysis> ~0.6Decadal / shorterIncompletely carbonized / low-T
Woolf argues H/C_org is preferred over O/C_org for high-ash materials because inorganic oxygen in ash confounds O/C more than H/C (DOI §3.2).

5. Product-standard gates (not credit methodologies)















































FrameworkH/C_orgO/C_orgSourceIUPAC glossary< 0.7< 0.4Bilias et al. 2024 · DOIEBC all classes< 0.7should be < 0.4EBC 10.5E §7.2–7.3EBC-FeedPlus< 0.4 (proxy for ≥500 °C / ≥10 min)—Same PDF §10.4EBC manure chars< 0.4 required—Same PDF §4.8IBI Biochar Standards≤ 0.7 classically required for “biochar”often ≤ 0.4IBI standards · Product Standards EBC IBINRCS CPS 336H:C_org max 0.7 (practice eligibility)—NRCS CPS 336 Standard 2022 · PDF
Credit programs map these ratios into different permanence tables and horizons—do not copy thresholds here; see Permanence Science for Credits.

6. Lehmann H/C_org < 0.5 subset (use with care)
Lehmann et al. 2021 is widely cited for: among biochars with H/C_org < 0.5, 95% showed >50% C remaining after 100 years, with mean remaining ~82% in that subset (DOI). The vault’s source note flags these figures as not re-checked against the paywalled full text—confirm before diligence use (Lehmann et al. 2021). Abstract-checked claim that remains solid: persistence is 1–2 orders of magnitude longer than source biomass (same DOI).

7. Measurement pitfalls

Ash and inorganic C: Always use C_org, not total C, in the denominator (S668 §9–10).
Post-pyrolysis oxidation / additives: EBC notes O/C_org can exceed 0.4 after oxidative post-treatment or co-pyrolysis with catalysts; CSI may grant exemptions after plausibility checks (EBC 10.5E §7.3).
Lab method package: Pair elemental analysis with contaminant and ag packages when selling soil products (Testing EBC IBI S668).
Process link: Higher peak T and longer residence generally lower H/C_org (Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures, Biochar Quality from Process; Keiluweit 2010).


8. Practice takeaway

Measure H/C_org (and report O/C_org) on every batch destined for CDR accounting or EBC/IBI labeling.
Use H/C_org → Woolf (F_\mathrm{perm}) when soil T and horizon are known (Woolf IPCC Fperm).
Treat Spokas O/C bins as orientation, not as Verra/Puro/Isometric factors.
For high-ash manure/sludge/gasification solids, prefer H/C_org and direct C_org measurement over default FC tables (Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks, Gasification Residues).

Science/Overview-and-Definition.title: Overview and Definition
Science/Overview-and-Definition.content:
Overview and Definition
Definition
Biochar is a solid, porous, carbon-rich material produced by pyrolysis of biomass under oxygen-free or oxygen-limited conditions.
IUPAC (2024) defines it as a solid multi-functional porous carbonaceous product of agricultural biomass pyrolysis in the temperature range 350–1000 °C, with molar H/C_org < 0.7 and O/C_org < 0.4 to ensure abundant fused aromatic structures and distinguish it from inadequately carbonized materials (Bilias et al., 2024; DOI: 10.1515/pac-2021-0106).
IPCC (2019) inventory appendix defines biochar for GHG accounting as solid material from heating biomass >350 °C under controlled/limited oxidant (pyrolysis or gasification), applicable to mineral soils in cropland/grassland (IPCC 2019 Refinement, Vol. 4, Appendix 4 · IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix).
Not the same as

Science/Permanence-Debates.title: Permanence Debates
Science/Permanence-Debates.content:
Permanence Debates
Chapter on open scientific and policy debates about biochar permanence: decay-model form, inertinite/Ro claims, horizon choice, and what “permanent” should mean for CDR accounting. Complements the settled mechanism snapshot in Permanence and the proxy chapters. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Consensus vs Debates · Permanence Science for Credits · Reflectance Ro and HyPy · Woolf IPCC Fperm · Risks and Controversies · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. What is largely settled

Well-made biochar (adequate T / low H/C_org) persists far longer than raw biomass; fused aromatics are the mechanistic basis (Lehmann et al. 2021 · DOI).
Persistence is probabilistic and environment-dependent, not literal immortality (Schmidt et al. 2025; Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI).
Inventory practice can use mass × (F_C) × (F_\mathrm{perm}) with kiln/gate MRV (CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting).


2. Debate A — Do short incubations overestimate long-term decay?
Claim: Two-pool fits from incubations lasting only a few years may mis-estimate (often overestimate) millennial decay of the recalcitrant pool, because the “slow” pool is still a mixture and true inert fractions need other assays (HyPy, Ro, conductivity) (frontier discussion in science report 2026-09-14; Azzi et al. 2024 modelling work listed in Key Sources · DOI).
Counterweight: Woolf/IPCC deliberately use ≥1-year multi-pool fits and conservative exclusions (no priming credit, mineral soils only) so inventory factors are less likely to over-credit (Woolf 2021; IPCC PDF).
Vault posture: Active research—not settled. Prefer transparent horizon + method; cross-check high-permanence marketing claims against Reflectance Ro and HyPy and Schmidt policy commentary.

3. Debate B — Decomposition-model camp vs inertinite/Ro camp























CampCore toolsTypical horizonsExemplarsDecomposition-modelMulti-pool decay, H/C_org, T-class, soil T100y (IPCC/Woolf); “several centuries” / 200y in some marketsIPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix, Woolf et al. 2021, Puro CORC200+, Isometric 200yInertinite / RoRandom reflectance, HyPy-resistant CMillennial / “permanent” upper classesSanei et al. 2024, Isometric 1000y, CSI upper class
Sanei et al. 2024 IBRo2% (Ro = 2%) and modelled ~100 Myr half-life under stated oxidizing conditions (DOI) energize the Ro camp. Schmidt et al. 2025 push back: do not equate modern biochar with geological inertinite; refuse 100% permanence declarations; recommend policy definitions on the order of centuries with registered material properties, traceable application, conservative modelling, and long-term field validation.
Puro’s public permanence post (2025-07-03) explicitly chose centuries not millennia pending more integrated science (puro.earth permanence post)—a market illustration of Debate B, detailed on the credit side in Permanence Science for Credits / Puro CORC200+.

4. Debate C — Which time horizon is “the” permanence number?
UNFCCC GWP practice and IPCC biochar appendix center 100 years (IPCC PDF; Woolf discussion of GWP analogy DOI). Woolf also publishes 500- and 1000-year factors showing large further losses (e.g. high-T at 14.9 °C: 0.82 → 0.25 from 100y to 1000y — Table 3).
Choosing 100y vs 1000y changes both the number and the narrative. Neither is wrong if labeled; mixing them in marketing is.

5. Debate D — Climate feedback and non-soil uses

Warming feedback: higher future soil T lowers (F_\mathrm{perm}) (Soil Temperature and Environment).
Non-soil matrices (concrete, asphalt, polymers): oxygen/microbe exposure differs; soil (F_\mathrm{perm}) tables do not automatically transfer (Materials and Built Uses, Consensus vs Debates).


6. How this vault talks about permanence

Lead with mechanism + proxies + (F_\mathrm{perm}) chapters, not slogans.
Cross-link markets via Permanence Science for Credits without pasting registry tables into science notes.
Flag Lehmann H/C < 0.5 subset figures as full-text not re-checked (Lehmann et al. 2021).
Align with Schmidt 2025 on rejecting absolute millennial zero-decay claims unless a specific protocol’s evidence bar is met and disclosed.

Science/Permanence.title: Permanence
Science/Permanence.content:
Permanence
Hub for persistence / permanence science: how long biochar organic carbon remains in soil after application, which material and environmental factors control that longevity, and which laboratory proxies inventories and markets use. Credit-program thresholds and issuance rules live in Permanence Science for Credits — this cluster stays on the science. Report context: 2026-09-16.

Companion chapters (2026-09-16): H-Corg and O-Corg · Woolf IPCC Fperm · Reflectance Ro and HyPy · Soil Temperature and Environment · Permanence Debates. This note is the spine—definitions, mechanism snapshot, chapter map, and practice takeaway—without duplicating registry methodology text.

Related notes: Properties · Quantitative Benchmarks · CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting · Consensus vs Debates · Permanence Science for Credits · Production · Biochar Quality from Process · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. What “permanence” means here
Biochar carbon mineralizes 1–2 orders of magnitude more slowly than unpyrolysed biomass because pyrolysis builds fused aromatic structures that microbes oxidize poorly (Lehmann et al., 2021 · DOI; Woolf et al., 2021 · DOI). Persistence is not literal forever: it is probabilistic over centennial–millennial horizons for well-made chars, and it depends on material chemistry (aromatic condensation) and environment (soil temperature, moisture, minerals, microbes) (Schmidt et al., 2025; Woolf 2021).
Policy and inventory practice usually compress that dynamics into a single permanence factor (F_\mathrm{perm}) = fraction of biochar organic C still unmineralized after a chosen horizon—commonly 100 years for IPCC-style accounting (IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix · PDF). Always state horizon + soil temperature with any (F_\mathrm{perm}) number (Woolf IPCC Fperm, Soil Temperature and Environment).

2. Mechanism in one paragraph
During pyrolysis, cellulose/hemicellulose/lignin rearrange into condensed aromatic domains; H and O are lost relative to C, so H/C_org and O/C_org fall as condensation rises (Keiluweit et al., 2010 · DOI; H-Corg and O-Corg). Labile aliphatic / incompletely carbonized fractions mineralize in months–years; the recalcitrant aromatic pool decays much more slowly, so multi-pool (at least two-pool exponential) models are the inventory workhorse (IPCC App. 4; Woolf 2021). Aging in soil also includes stabilization pathways (organo-mineral associations, aggregation)—decomposition and stabilization run in parallel (Schmidt 2025).

3. Proxy map (science side)

5. Practice takeaway (science → project)

Prefer measured H/C_org + site soil temperature for (F_\mathrm{perm}) when elemental analysis is available (Woolf 2021).
Fall back to IPCC / Woolf temperature class when only production logs exist (IPCC PDF).
Do not claim “permanent” without a time horizon (usually 100 years in inventory policy; credit programs may use 200y / 1000y / “several centuries”—see Permanence Science for Credits).
Treat Ro / HyPy as complementary high-condensation indicators, not drop-in replacements for Woolf-style decay factors, unless a specific protocol says otherwise (Reflectance Ro and HyPy, Permanence Debates).
Warmer soils lower (F_\mathrm{perm}) for the same char (Soil Temperature and Environment).

Science/Recent-Research-2021-2026.content:
Recent Research 2021–2026
Major reviews & methods (climate / permanence / accounting)


Lehmann et al. (2021). Biochar in climate change mitigation. Nature Geoscience 14:883–892. DOI: 10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8. Global system potential 3.4–6.3 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹ emission reductions (~half CDR); with land sparing/CCS pathways up to ~7.4–10.3 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹. Emphasizes H/C_org, feedstock sustainability, energy vs sequestration trade-offs.


Woolf et al. (2021). Greenhouse Gas Inventory Model for Biochar Additions to Soil. Environ. Sci. Technol. 55:14795–14805. DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.1c02425. ~183 citations (S2). Operational EF model extending IPCC 2019; F_perm from T class or H/C_org; temperature-adjusted.


IPCC (2019). 2019 Refinement… Vol. 4 Appendix 4. PDF · IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix. F_perm after 100 yr: 0.65 / 0.80 / 0.89 for low / medium / high T.


Bilias et al. (2024). Glossary of terms used in biochar research (IUPAC Technical Report). Pure Appl. Chem. DOI: 10.1515/pac-2021-0106. Formal terminology (178 terms).


Weng & Cowie (2025). Estimates vary but credible evidence points to gigaton-scale… Commun. Earth Environ. DOI: 10.1038/s43247-025-02228-x. Literature range ~0.03–11 Pg CO₂e yr⁻¹; credible centering around multi-Gt scale.


Fuss & Lunstrum (2026). Chapter 10: Costs and potentials. In The State of Carbon Dioxide Removal, 3rd ed. DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/FBZ4X. Sustainable removal up to ~2.7 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹; total mitigation up to ~10.3 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹; IAM Highest Ambition <0.1–1.1 GtCO₂ yr⁻¹ by 2050; costs often US$70–360/tCO₂.


Schmidt et al. (2025). Biochar Permanence—A Policy Commentary. GCB Bioenergy. DOI: 10.1111/gcbb.70092. Centuries–millennia for condensed fractions; multi-proxy discussion.


Soil amendments, crop yields, GHG fluxes


Jia et al. (2023). Global patterns… soil GHG fluxes and crop yield. Land Degradation & Development. DOI: 10.1002/ldr.4868. 3883 paired obs / 220 studies: yield +9.4%; CH₄ −13.0%; N₂O −26.8%; GWP −7.7%.


Global field vs lab synthesis (2022). Renewable & Sustainable Energy Reviews. Field: yield +15.7%, CH₄ −14.8%, N₂O −23.1%, SOC stocks +26.6%.


Jeffery et al. (2017). Biochar boosts tropical but not temperate crop yields. Environ. Res. Lett. 12:053001. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bd — still widely cited.


Ye et al. (2020). Biochar effects on crop yields with and without fertilizer… Soil Use Manage. 36:2–18 — used heavily in Lehmann 2021.


Weng et al. (2017). Biochar built soil carbon over a decade… Nature Climate Change 7:371–376. DOI: 10.1038/nclimate3276. ~344 citations — decade-scale negative priming / rhizodeposit stabilization.


Blanco-Canqui et al. (2020). Soil carbon increased by twice the amount of biochar carbon applied after 6 years… GCB Bioenergy 12:240–251.

Science/Reflectance-Ro-and-HyPy.title: Reflectance Ro and HyPy
Science/Reflectance-Ro-and-HyPy.content:
Reflectance Ro and HyPy
Chapter on optical random reflectance (Ro) and hydropyrolysis-resistant carbon (BC_HyPy) as advanced permanence proxies beyond elemental ratios and pyrolysis-temperature class. Positions the “inertinite / Ro camp” relative to Woolf-style decay models without duplicating credit rules (Permanence Science for Credits). Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Permanence · H-Corg and O-Corg · Woolf IPCC Fperm · Permanence Debates · Sanei et al. 2024 · ANSI ASABE USBI S668 · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. Why advanced proxies exist
Elemental ratios and T-class (F_\mathrm{perm}) are accessible but imperfect: short incubations may mis-estimate millennial recalcitrant pools, and H/C_org regressions leave substantial unexplained variance (Woolf 100-yr H/C (R^2 \approx 0.3) at 14.9 °C — open PDF Table 3). Petrography and selective chemical oxidation/hydropyrolysis aim to isolate the most condensed carbon fraction—analogous to inertinite in coal geology (Sanei et al. 2024 · DOI; policy framing in Schmidt et al. 2025).

2. Random reflectance (Ro)
2.1 What it measures
Random reflectance is the percentage of incident light reflected from polished carbonaceous particles under oil immersion—standard coal petrography (ISO 7404-5). Higher Ro tracks higher aromatic condensation / thermal rank. ANSI ASABE USBI S668 §10.3 specifies Ro per ISO 7404-5 (white-light microscopy) as a permanence assessment method (PDF)—methods only, not pass/fail.
2.2 Sanei et al. 2024 inertinite benchmark
Sanei et al. 2024 propose an inertinite benchmark at random reflectance Ro = 2% (“IBRo2%”) (DOI; abstract checked).





























Claim (abstract)ValueBenchmarkRo = 2%Commercial samples76% had their entire Ro distribution above 2%Modelled half-lifeOrder of ~100 million years for typical inertinite biochar under highly oxidizing conditions at constant 30 °COther poolsIncomplete carbonization may leave up to three less-stable pools (geochemical pyrolysis + Ro)Process inferenceRo can back-calculate peak particle temperatures
Use with care (vault source note): the multi-Myr half-life is a kinetic model for inertinite under stated conditions, not a field measurement of soil biochar decay (Sanei et al. 2024).
2.3 Policy / science tension
Schmidt et al. (2025) argue biochars and inertinite-ranked fossil coals must not be equated: geological inertinite experienced burial, mineral inclusion, high P–T over geologic time; modern pyrolysis chars are different materials. Field and lab studies show measurable though small mineralization across biochar types; declaring 100% permanence over millennia is inconsistent with current understanding. Analytical proxies indicate relative, not absolute, persistence.
Credit programs that use Ro (e.g. Isometric 1000y pathway, CSI upper class) make standards decisions—see Permanence Science for Credits, Isometric Permanence Pathways 200y and 1000y, CSI Global Biochar C-Sink—not automatic science conclusions.

3. Hydropyrolysis-resistant carbon (BC_HyPy)
Hydropyrolysis (HyPy) subjects organic matter to high-pressure hydrogen with a catalyst, destroying labile organic carbon while leaving a refractory carbon residue used as a black-carbon / pyrogenic-carbon assay in geochemistry. In biochar MRV discussions, the HyPy-resistant fraction (BC_HyPy) is treated as a high-permanence pool proxy (science report / Schmidt multi-proxy discussion; Woolf 2021 lists HyPy among emerging proxies in the broader permanence literature cited by later commentaries).
Practical points for this vault:

BC_HyPy is a material metric (fraction resistant to HyPy), complementary to H/C_org and Ro.
CSI Global Biochar C-Sink documentation discusses HyPy ≥90% (with Ro thresholds) for upper permanence classes—thresholds belong in CSI Global Biochar C-Sink / Permanence Science for Credits, not restated as science universal constants here.
Pair HyPy with elemental ratios and process data; do not treat any single proxy as absolute millennial proof (Schmidt 2025).

Method standardization for U.S. labs remains thinner than for H:C_org; S668 currently lists H:C_org, O:C_org, and Ro explicitly in §10 (PDF).

4. Solid electrical conductivity (brief)
EBC lists electrical conductivity of the solid biochar (not leachate EC) as an important indirect parameter for batch homogeneity and as a correlate of certain use effects; it is part of the EBC physical package (EBC 10.5E §7.8). Some permanence commentaries group solid EC with HyPy/Ro as multi-proxy toolkit entries (Schmidt 2025). It is not a substitute for (F_\mathrm{perm}) tables.

5. How to read Ro/HyPy next to Woolf (F_\mathrm{perm})

























ApproachStrengthLimitationWoolf / IPCC multi-pool decayEmpirically tied to mineralization data; T- and H/C-resolvedExtrapolates beyond incubation length; (R^2) modestRo inertinite benchmarkFast optical screen; ranks condensationGeological analogy contested; model half-lives ≠ field soilBC_HyPyChemically isolates refractory CLab capacity; mapping to (F_\mathrm{perm}(t)) still protocol-specific
Synthesis for this vault: use Ro/HyPy to document high condensation and to satisfy protocols that require them; use Woolf/IPCC when you need an explicit remaining-fraction vs time and soil T. Holding both without claiming identity is the conservative scientific posture (Permanence Debates).

6. Practice takeaway

If a buyer or methodology asks for Ro, specify ISO 7404-5 and report the distribution, not only a mean (S668; Sanei 2024).
Never equate “Ro ≥ 2%” with “zero decay forever” (Schmidt 2025).
For inventory-style tonnes CO₂e, still need (F_C \times F_\mathrm{perm}) logic (Woolf IPCC Fperm) unless the governing protocol replaces it.

Science/Soil-Temperature-and-Environment.title: Soil Temperature and Environment
Science/Soil-Temperature-and-Environment.content:
Soil Temperature and Environment
Chapter on environmental controls on biochar carbon persistence—especially soil temperature (Q10), with notes on moisture, minerals, microbes, and aging. Complements material proxies in H-Corg and O-Corg and Reflectance Ro and HyPy. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Permanence · Woolf IPCC Fperm · Permanence Debates · CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting · Consensus vs Debates · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. Material × environment
Persistence is jointly controlled by intrinsic chemistry (aromatic condensation) and extrinsic environment (temperature, moisture, mineralogy, biology) (Lehmann et al. 2021 · DOI; Schmidt et al. 2025). A high-T wood char in cool temperate mineral soil will outlast the same chemistry in warm tropical soil on a 100-year (F_\mathrm{perm}) basis (Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI).

2. Temperature and Q10 (Woolf framework)
Woolf et al. 2021 rescale mineralization studies to a common soil temperature using a temperature-dependent Q10:
[
Q_{10} = 1.1 + 12.0,e^{-0.19,T}
]
after Lehmann et al. (2015) persistence chapter (cited in Woolf Methods) (open PDF).
Reference climates in Woolf Table 3:

























ReferenceMean annual TUseGlobal croplands14.9 °CDefault headline (F_\mathrm{perm})US croplands10.9 °CRegional US inventoriesGrid5, 10, 15, 20, 25 °CSite-specific
Example: high-T class, 100 years — (F_\mathrm{perm}) falls from 0.94 at 5 °C to 0.76 at 25 °C (Table 3). IPCC App. 4 instead embeds a conservative ~20 °C basis into its single 100-yr table (PDF).
Climate feedback: future warming increases decay rates, so today’s (F_\mathrm{perm}) tables overstate permanence under warmer future soils if T is not updated (Consensus vs Debates; Woolf 2021).

3. Horizon length interacts with temperature
At fixed soil T, remaining fraction drops sharply from 100 → 500 → 1000 years (Woolf Table 3). At 14.9 °C, high-T (F_\mathrm{perm}) ≈ 0.82 / 0.44 / 0.25 for those horizons (open PDF). Warm soil + long horizon is the most punishing combination for decay-model accounting—and the main quantitative reason “millennial permanence” claims need Ro/HyPy-style arguments or different system boundaries (Permanence Debates, Reflectance Ro and HyPy).

4. Moisture, minerals, microbes, aging
Schmidt et al. (2025) emphasize that longevity is not chemistry alone: soil mineralogy, biological activity, and climate mediate both decomposition and stabilization (organo-mineral associations, aggregation with native OM) (DOI). Practical implications:



































FactorDirection of effect (qualitative)Evidence postureHigher soil TFaster mineralization → lower (F_\mathrm{perm})Quantified in Woolf Q10Mineral association / aggregationCan stabilize pyrogenic CMechanistic / field aging literature; not in IPCC Tier-1 factorMicrobial communityDegrades labile pools first; slow attack on aromaticsBasis for multi-pool modelsMoisture extremesCan limit or enhance oxidationSite-specific; sparse in inventory EFsOrganic soils / forest organic horizonsRisk of positive priming / out-of-scopeWoolf: do not apply method on Histosols or organic horizons (DOI §3.3)
Priming of native SOC is conservatively excluded from Woolf’s GHG method because meta-mean negative priming was not significant at p<0.05 (DOI; Wang et al. 2016 · DOI).

5. Scope limits that are environmental
From IPCC App. 4 and Woolf:

In: mineral soils, cropland/grassland applications of purpose-made pyrolysis/gasification biochar.
Out: wetlands (IPCC), forest organic horizons, Histosols (Woolf conservative), wildfire/open-fire chars (IPCC), non-soil matrices (concrete, etc.—different permanence pathways; Materials and Built Uses).


6. Practice takeaway

Always attach mean annual soil (or air-as-proxy) temperature to (F_\mathrm{perm}).
Prefer Woolf Table 3 (or SI spreadsheet) over a single global factor for project MRV (DOI).
Do not apply mineral-soil permanence factors to organic soils.
Treat mineral stabilization as a bonus narrative, not an automatic uplift to inventory (F_\mathrm{perm}), unless a methodology explicitly allows it.

Science/Terra-Preta-and-Pyrogenic-Carbon.title: Terra Preta and Pyrogenic Carbon
Science/Terra-Preta-and-Pyrogenic-Carbon.content:
Terra Preta and Pyrogenic Carbon
Amazonian Dark Earths (Terra Preta) are the cultural and historical inspiration for modern biochar research: anthropogenic soils enriched with pyrogenic carbon that remain fertile centuries after formation.
Foundational citation
Glaser et al. (2001). The ‘Terra Preta’ phenomenon: a model for sustainable agriculture in the humid tropics. Naturwissenschaften 88:37–41. DOI: 10.1007/s001140000193. ~1,145 citations (Semantic Scholar, 2026-09-14).
This historical analog underpins the idea that intentionally produced pyrogenic carbon can improve tropical soils and store carbon for long periods—later formalized in Lehmann (2006/2007) and modern CDR literature (see Foundational Papers).

Science/Woolf-IPCC-Fperm.title: Woolf IPCC Fperm
Science/Woolf-IPCC-Fperm.content:
Woolf / IPCC F_perm
Chapter on inventory permanence factors: how IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix and Woolf et al. 2021 turn production temperature (or H/C_org) into the fraction of biochar organic carbon remaining after a chosen time. Credit methodologies that cite these tables are mapped in Permanence Science for Credits—this note stays on the science/model. Report context: 2026-09-16.
Related notes: Permanence · H-Corg and O-Corg · Soil Temperature and Environment · CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting · Quantitative Benchmarks · Science Hub · Key Sources

1. What (F_\mathrm{perm}) is
[
F_\mathrm{perm}(t,T_\mathrm{soil}) = \text{fraction of biochar organic C still unmineralized after time } t \text{ at soil temperature } T_\mathrm{soil}
]
Both IPCC App. 4 and Woolf fit multi-pool exponential decay (minimum two-pool) to incubation and field datasets lasting ≥1 year, then evaluate remaining C at policy-relevant horizons (IPCC PDF; Woolf DOI).
Do not mix IPCC and Woolf tables in one calculation—Woolf re-derived factors with newer data and explicit soil-temperature adjustment; values differ (IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix “Use with care”).

2. Temperature classes (shared vocabulary)

























ClassPeak pyrolysis temperatureNotesLow350–450 °CIPCC / Woolf binMedium450–600 °CHigh≥600 °C (IPCC also flags high-T gasification)
Materials below ~350 °C (torrefaction, typical HTC) are out of scope for these permanence tables (Woolf 2021 §2.1.1; IPCC definition).
Process engineering context: Pyrolysis Systems and Temperatures.

3. IPCC 2019 Appendix 4 (100-year factors)
Source: IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix · PDF (full text checked in vault).

























Production class100-yr (F_\mathrm{perm})UncertaintyHigh (>600 °C)0.89±13%Medium (450–600 °C)0.80±11%Low (350–450 °C)0.65±15%
Temperature basis: factors adjusted to a conservative ~20 °C ambient (against ~10 °C mean land-surface temperature in the appendix background). Scope: mineral soils in cropland/grassland only—not organic soils, forests with organic horizons, wetlands, or wildfire chars (same PDF). Status: basis for future Tier 1 development, not complete good-practice inventory guidance yet.
Carbon content (F_{C_p}) is tabulated separately by feedstock/process (Neves et al. regressions + ash correction)—see Production, Woody vs Manure Ag Feedstocks.

4. Woolf et al. 2021 (temperature- and H/C-resolved)
Source: Woolf et al. 2021 · DOI · open PDF (full text checked).
4.1 Headline 100-year values at global cropland mean (14.9 °C)





















Class(F_\mathrm{perm}) (100 yr, 14.9 °C)Low0.63 (SE 0.045)Medium0.71 (SE 0.03)High0.82 (SE 0.028)
Abstract phrasing: 63–82% of initial biochar C remains after 100 years at that temperature (DOI).
4.2 Longer horizons at 14.9 °C (Table 3)























HorizonLowMediumHigh500 yr0.190.320.441000 yr0.0840.160.25
4.3 Soil-temperature sensitivity (100 yr, high class examples)





























Soil T (°C)High-class (F_\mathrm{perm}) (100 yr)50.94100.8814.9 (global cropland mean)0.82200.79250.76
US cropland mean 10.9 °C also tabulated (high 100-yr = 0.87). Full grid: Woolf Table 3 (open PDF). Deep dive: Soil Temperature and Environment.
4.4 H/C_org pathway
When H/C_org is measured, use Woolf eq. 5 with Table 3 regression coefficients rather than temperature bins (H-Corg and O-Corg). Preference order in Woolf §3.4: measured FC + H/C_org → else FC from Table 2 + T-class (F_\mathrm{perm}) → else conservative low-T (F_\mathrm{perm}).
4.5 Inventory equation (soil C term)
[
\mathrm{GHG_{bc}} \approx \frac{44}{12},M_\mathrm{bc},F_C,F_\mathrm{perm} ;+; \text{(optional year-1 N₂O term)}
]
(Woolf eq. 6). Optional N₂O: −23% first year only, only if application >10 Mg C ha⁻¹—usually small vs C sequestration; not the focus of this permanence chapter (GHG Fluxes).

5. Why Woolf numbers are lower than IPCC’s






























FactorIPCC App. 4Woolf 2021Dataset vintagePre-2019 appendix synthesisUpdated decay compilationClimate basis~20 °C conservativeExplicit T grid; headline at 14.9 °CH/C_org optionNoted as future optionFully parameterizedFCSeparate feedstock tableTable 2 by feedstock × T / gasification
Using IPCC 0.89 with a Woolf-style cool-climate narrative (or vice versa) silently mis-states certainty. Pick one method stack and document it.

6. Worked intuition (from Woolf §3.4.1)
Maize stover pyrolysed at 500 °C (medium), FC = 0.68 (Table 2), sequestered at 10 °C soil → (F_\mathrm{perm}=0.79). With 15,000 Mg biochar + conditional N₂O term, Woolf’s example yields 29,710 Mg CO₂e (open PDF §3.4.1). Scale and boundaries matter for LCA vs inventory (CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting).

7. Link to carbon markets (pointer only)
Registries interpret these science tables differently (100y vs 200y vs 1000y; T-class vs H/C_org vs Ro). Do not paste methodology thresholds here—use Permanence Science for Credits · Verra VM0044 Permanence and Quantification · Isometric Permanence Pathways 200y and 1000y · Puro CORC200+ · CSI Global Biochar C-Sink.

8. Practice takeaway

Quote horizon + soil T + method (IPCC vs Woolf) every time you cite (F_\mathrm{perm}).
Prefer Woolf + H/C_org when lab data exist; IPCC T-class when only kiln temperature is known.
Remember 1000-year remaining fractions are much lower than 100-year ones at the same T (Woolf Table 3)—central to Permanence Debates.

What it is: A narrative review of co-composted biochar (“COMBI”, biochar added at the start of composting). It covers production, soil and yield effects, and cleanup of soils contaminated with toxic metals.
Key figures

(2011) regressions, corrected for ash using yields from Woolf et al. (2014)Appendix PDF, Table 4Ap.1 notes✓ full textShorter horizonsEstimating carbon remaining over less than 100 years needs more detailed informationAppendix PDF, footnote✓ full text
Use with care

Woolf et al. 2021 re-derived temperature-specific factors, and its values (0.63 / 0.71 / 0.82 at 14.9 °C) are lower than this table’s. Don’t mix the two tables in one calculation.
This is inventory guidance, not a crediting standard. See Permanence Science for Credits for how credit programs use or depart from it.

Sources/Jeffery-et-al.-2011.title: A quantitative review of the effects of biochar application to soils on crop productivity using meta-analysis
Sources/Jeffery-et-al.-2011.content:
Jeffery et al. 2011
Citation: Jeffery S, Verheijen FGA, van der Velde M, Bastos AC (2011). A quantitative review of the effects of biochar application to soils on crop productivity using meta-analysis. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment 144(1): 175–187. doi.org/10.1016/j.agee.2011.08.015
What it is: The first widely cited meta-analysis of biochar effects on crop productivity (yield or above-ground biomass). Its subgroup results are where the vault’s liming and water-holding explanations come from.
Key figures



























































FigureValueWhereCheckGrand mean productivity effect+10% (small but statistically significant)Abstract (Europe PMC record)✓ abstractRange of subgroup means−28% to +39%Abstract✓ abstractSoil pH subgroupsAcidic +14%, neutral +13%Abstract✓ abstractTexture subgroupsCoarse +10%, medium +13%Abstract✓ abstractApplication rateLargest positive effect at 100 t ha⁻¹ (+39%)Abstract✓ abstractFeedstockPoultry litter +28% (strongest significant positive); biosolids −28% (only significant negative)Abstract✓ abstractStudy lengthAvailable studies limited to 1–2 yearsAbstract✓ abstractTypical research rates of ~5–50+ t ha⁻¹Used in vault rate tables—not re-checked (full text not accessible)
Use with care

The authors read the pH and texture subgroups as pointing to liming, better water holding, and nutrient availability. That’s an interpretation of subgroup means, not a tested mechanism.
The 100 t ha⁻¹ result is a research extreme, not a farm rate.
Every underlying study ran only 1–2 years, so this says nothing about long-term yield effects.

Related: Jeffery et al. 2017 · Crop Yield Effects · Key Sources

Sources/Jeffery-et-al.-2016.title: Biochar effects on methane emissions from soils: A meta-analysis
Sources/Jeffery-et-al.-2016.content:
Jeffery et al. 2016
Citation: Jeffery S, Verheijen FGA, Kammann C, Abalos D (2016). Biochar effects on methane emissions from soils: A meta-analysis. Soil Biology and Biochemistry 101: 251–258. doi.org/10.1016/j.soilbio.2016.07.021 · author manuscript: hau.repository.guildhe.ac.uk/id/eprint/15223/1/Simon%20Jeffery%20biochar%20effects%20on%20methane%20emissions%2023%20July%2016%20upload.pdf
What it is: Meta-analysis of biochar effects on agricultural soil CH₄ fluxes, separating flooded vs non-flooded systems and soil pH classes. The vault’s primary CH₄ chapter source.
Key figures





















































FigureValueWhereCheckDataset62 studies screened → 42 included; 189 pairwise comparisonsAuthor PDF✓ full textMetricHedge’s dsame✓ full textFlooded soilsd = −0.87 (increased sink / reduced source)Abstract / results✓ full textNon-flooded soilsd = +0.65 (decreased sink / increased source)Abstract / results✓ full textAcidic soils (pH < 6)d = −1.56Abstract / results✓ full textNeutral soilsd = +1.17Abstract✓ full textAlkaline soilsd = +0.44Abstract✓ full text
Use with care

Effect sizes are standardised mean differences, not percent reductions—don’t convert d to % without the paper’s own reporting.
Sink/source ambiguity: a positive d can mean a weaker sink or a stronger source.

Sources/Jeffery-et-al.-2017.title: Biochar boosts tropical but not temperate crop yields
Sources/Jeffery-et-al.-2017.content:
Jeffery et al. 2017
Citation: Jeffery S, Abalos D, Prodana M, Bastos AC, van Groenigen JW, Hungate BA, Verheijen F (2017). Biochar boosts tropical but not temperate crop yields. Environmental Research Letters 12(5): 053001. doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/aa67bd (open access)
What it is: A global meta-analysis that splits biochar yield effects by latitude. It’s the vault’s main evidence that yield benefits concentrate in acidic, low-fertility tropical soils.
Key figures















































FigureValueWhereCheckTemperate latitudesNo average effect on crop yieldAbstract✓ full textTropics~25% average yield increaseAbstract; results, fig. 1✓ full textTropical mechanismLiming and fertilizationAbstract✓ full textNutrient content of the charIn tropical soils, high-nutrient biochars raised yields substantially more than low-nutrient onesAbstract✓ full textpH gap behind the liming effectMedian biochar pH 9.0 vs median tropical soil pH 5.7Discussion✓ full textAdvice for temperate systemsFocus on non-yield benefits: lime and fertilizer savings, GHG control, other ecosystem servicesAbstract✓ full text
Use with care

“No effect on average” in temperate soils hides variation. The authors discuss over-liming, which can tie up micronutrients, as one possible reason for yield decreases.
Charged or enriched products are a different question; see Melo et al. 2022 and Schmidt et al. 2017.

Related: Jeffery et al. 2011 · Crop Yield Effects · Soil and Agriculture · Key Sources

Sources/Jia-et-al.-2023.title: Global patterns and controls of soil greenhouse gas fluxes and crop yield under biochar application
Sources/Jia-et-al.-2023.content:
Jia et al. 2023
Citation: Jia X, Yan W, Yang J, Chen W, Ma H, Chen X, Liu J, Zhong Y, Shangguan Z (2023). Global patterns and controls of soil greenhouse gas fluxes and crop yield under biochar application. Land Degradation & Development 34(17): 5622–5634. doi.org/10.1002/ldr.4868 (open access)
What it is: A global meta-analysis of biochar effects on soil CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O fluxes, warming potential, and crop yield. The vault uses it for recent GHG and yield averages.
Key figures

































































FigureValueWhereCheckDataset3,883 paired observations from 220 studiesAbstract✓ abstractCrop yield+9.4%Abstract✓ abstractN₂O emissions−26.8%Abstract✓ abstractCH₄ emissions−13.0%; CH₄ uptake unchangedAbstract✓ abstractCO₂ emissions+7.4% overall; the increase came mainly from incubation and pot experiments and wasn’t significant in field studiesAbstract✓ abstractGlobal warming potential−7.7%Abstract✓ abstractGHG intensity−14.3% overall (−18.7% upland, −14.5% paddy)Abstract✓ abstractSoil carbon pool+38.1% upland, +33.4% paddyAbstract✓ abstractStrongest driver of GHG responsesBiochar-induced change in soil pHAbstract✓ abstract
Use with care

These averages pool incubation, pot, and field experiments. GHG responses were more sensitive in incubation and pot studies than in the field, so field effects are likely smaller than the headline numbers. Earlier vault notes called this meta-analysis “field-focused”; it isn’t.
Warming potential and GHG intensity are bundled metrics. Check the paper’s system boundaries before comparing them with other studies.

Related: GHG Fluxes · Crop Yield Effects · Cayuela et al. 2014 · Key Sources

Sources/Kammann-et-al.-2015.title: Plant growth improvement mediated by nitrate capture in co-composted biochar
Sources/Kammann-et-al.-2015.content:
Kammann et al. 2015
Citation: Kammann CI, Schmidt H-P, Messerschmidt N, Linsel S, Steffens D, Müller C, Koyro H-W, Conte P, Joseph S (2015). Plant growth improvement mediated by nitrate capture in co-composted biochar. Scientific Reports 5: 11080. doi.org/10.1038/srep11080 (open access)
What it is: A greenhouse pot study with quinoa that compares untreated biochar with the same biochar after co-composting. It’s the vault’s clearest controlled contrast between “hungry” raw char and charged char.
Key figures



























































FigureValueWhereCheckDesignFull-factorial pot study, Chenopodium quinoa, sandy nutrient-poor soil; biochar at 2% (w/w)Abstract and methods✓ full textCo-composted biocharBiomass 139–305% of the control, depending on nutrient supply; the relative gain was largest at the lowest supplyResults, fig. 2✓ full textUntreated biocharBiomass cut to 60% of the control (significant at the low-N level, not at the high-N level)Abstract; results✓ full textTotal N in biochar particles1.04% co-composted vs 0.43% untreated (+6.2 g N kg⁻¹)Results✓ full textNitrate held in co-composted particles~2.1–2.2 g NO₃⁻-N kg⁻¹ by electro-ultrafiltration; 5.2 g kg⁻¹ by sequential washing (electro-ultrafiltration found only ~40% of the total)Results, figs. 3–4✓ full textMature compost, for comparison0.98 g nitrate-N kg⁻¹Discussion✓ full textOther nutrientsK loading 1.6-fold; Ca +63% (3,735 → 6,077 mg kg⁻¹); Mg low and slightly reducedResults✓ full textFate of captured nitrateLargely protected from leaching, partly plant-available, didn’t stimulate N₂OAbstract✓ full text
Use with care

Correction to earlier vault notes: “+305%” overstates the result. Co-composted biochar biomass reached up to 305% of the control, about 3× (roughly +205%). Untreated biochar reached 60% of the control.
The vault’s “~3–5 g NO₃⁻-N kg⁻¹” range isn’t this paper’s number. It reports ~2.1–2.2 g kg⁻¹ by the standard method and ~5.2 g kg⁻¹ by exhaustive washing.
A pot study in one soil at 2% w/w: a demonstration of mechanism, not a field yield estimate.

Related: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry · Antonangelo et al. 2021 · Key Sources

Sources/Lehmann-et-al.-2021.title: Biochar in climate change mitigation
Sources/Lehmann-et-al.-2021.content:
Lehmann et al. 2021
Citation: Lehmann J, Cowie A, Masiello CA, Kammann C, Woolf D, Amonette JE, Cayuela ML, Camps-Arbestain M, Whitman T (2021). Biochar in climate change mitigation. Nature Geoscience 14(12): 883–892. doi.org/10.1038/s41561-021-00852-8
What it is: A widely cited review of how biochar systems mitigate climate change: emission reductions versus CO₂ removal, energy trade-offs, persistence, and crop responses. The vault uses it for global potential and persistence framing.
Key figures















































FigureValueWhereCheckGlobal emission reductions from biochar systems3.4–6.3 PgCO₂e per year, about half of it CO₂ removalAbstract✓ abstractPersistence vs the source biomassOne to two orders of magnitude longerAbstract✓ abstractEnergy trade-offRelative to producing bioenergy, emissions from biochar systems rise 3% where the displaced energy is coal and fall 95% where it’s renewableAbstract✓ abstractCrop yieldsNo clear relationship between yield responses to fertilizer and to biocharAbstract✓ abstractResidue-only potential of 2.4–3.9 PgCO₂e/yr; up to 7.4–10.3 with land-sparing or CCS pathwaysUsed in CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting and Quantitative Benchmarks—not re-checked (full text paywalled)Of biochars with H/C_org < 0.5, 95% kept more than half their carbon after 100 years (mean ~82%)Used in Permanence and Quantitative Benchmarks—not re-checked (full text paywalled)
Use with care

Two of the vault’s most-quoted numbers from this paper, the H/C_org persistence subset and the land-sparing range, come from the full text, which wasn’t accessible. Check them before relying on them.
The energy trade-off means biochar’s climate advantage depends on what energy it displaces; it isn’t a fixed number.

Related: CDR Potential and IPCC Accounting · Permanence · Woolf et al. 2021 · Key Sources

Sources/NRCS-CPS-336-FAQ-2026.title: Planning CPS 336 – Soil Carbon Amendment: Frequently Asked Questions
Sources/NRCS-CPS-336-FAQ-2026.content:
NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026
Citation: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (2026). Planning CPS 336 – Soil Carbon Amendment: Frequently Asked Questions. National edition, April 2026. nrcs-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/2026-04/soil-carbon-amendment-ac-336-faq.pdf
What it is: NRCS’s question-and-answer guide for planners using the Soil Carbon Amendment practice (CPS 336): choosing biochar and compost, reading spec sheets, setting rates, and contracting payment scenarios. It’s the most-cited document in the vault’s farm notes.
Key figures











































































































FigureValueWhereCheckStarting application rate4–10 cubic yards per acre in generalFAQ PDF, rates✓ full textFY2024 payment scenarios, per acre100% biochar 4 yd³; 80/20 biochar/compost 3.2 yd³ + 1.1 t; 60/40 2.4 yd³ + 2.2 t; 40/60 1.6 yd³ + 3.3 t; 20/80 0.8 yd³ + 4.4 t; compost off-site 3 tFAQ PDF, Table 1, p. 13✓ full textWeight of biocharDry weight of 1 yd³ is roughly 135–540 lbFAQ PDF✓ full textPersistence vs compostRoughly 60–80% of biochar carbon remains after 100 years, vs 2–14% of compost carbon (the FAQ’s summary of research)FAQ PDF, biochar vs compost✓ full textSoil-carbon equivalenceSoil carbon gain from 10 yd³ of biochar equaled that from 40 yd³ of compost (research the FAQ cites)FAQ PDF, biochar vs compost✓ full textYield risk from biochar aloneCan reduce crop yields by binding and immobilizing nutrientsFAQ PDF, biochar vs compost✓ full textLiming example1 t/acre of biochar at 9% CaCO₃ equivalency cuts a 1-ton lime need by 9%, to 0.91 t; use caution on soils above pH 7FAQ PDF, pH✓ full textSaltsBiochar can intensify salinization, especially at high rates; look for spec-sheet EC under 8; manure-based biochar is higher in saltsFAQ PDF, salinity and spec sheets✓ full textSpec-sheet targetsOrganic carbon above 85% ideal; low ash; low EC; low liming equivalency unless liming is wantedFAQ PDF, spec sheets✓ full textPoultry-manure biochar exampleExtremely high in salts and nutrients; may suit very acidic, low-nutrient, high-rainfall soils; not neutral-to-basic soils with high P or saltsFAQ PDF, spec-sheet examples✓ full textCertificationAn IBI certificate alone isn’t enough; planners still need the spec sheet. A spec sheet ≤2 years old is probably fine if feedstock and temperature haven’t changedFAQ PDF, selecting biochar✓ full textExcluded materialsBiochar or compost from biosolids or municipal waste (PFAS concerns); humic and fulvic substances aren’t carbon amendments but can serve as inoculants; residues that would normally stay on the land can’t be used as feedstockFAQ PDF✓ full textManure as inoculantContract the 100% biochar scenario; the producer mixes in manure at their own expense under a nutrient management planFAQ PDF, contracting✓ full textWhere it can be usedPasture, yes; native rangeland only when facilitating Range Planting (550) or Critical Area Planting (342)FAQ PDF, contracting✓ full textContract termsPractice lifespan 1 year; can be contracted up to 5 times over a contractFAQ PDF, contracting✓ full textTimingAny time the ground isn’t frozen; most commonly early spring, or after harvest with a cover cropFAQ PDF, application✓ full text
Use with care

The persistence and soil-carbon figures are NRCS’s summary of research, not NRCS measurements. For permanence numbers use Woolf et al. 2021 or IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix.
Payment scenarios are FY2024 values and can change each fiscal year.
A text search of the FAQ found no mention of carbon credits. Claims that the FAQ calls CPS 336 “not a carbon credit” need a different source.

Related: NRCS CPS 336 Standard 2022 · NRCS CPS 336 and US Ag · Application Rates and Methods · Key Sources
