Sources/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial-2023.title: Oasis Vineyard Trial Results – Harvest 2023 (7th leaf) Summary
Sources/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial-2023.content:
Oasis Vineyard Trial 2023
Citation: Hunt J, McIntosh C, Beck D, Baltar R (2023). Oasis Vineyard Trial Results – Harvest 2023 (7th leaf) Summary. Final draft, 12 December 2023. pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Oasis-Vineyard-Trial_-5th-harvest_-Final-Draft_12.12.2023.pdf
What it is: A five-harvest summary of a vineyard trial on sandy, low-organic-matter soil in Monterey County, California, comparing compost, biochar, and both. It’s the vault’s best public dataset that combines yield and economics.
Key figures







































































FigureValueWhereCheckProjectBegan 2016 on a California Department of Water Resources grant: Sonoma Ecology Center (grant administrator), UC Riverside (principal investigator), Monterey Pacific (vineyard manager), Pacific Biochar (biochar supplier)Trial summary PDF, p. 1✓ full textSite8 acres; mainly Oceano sand at 0.7% organic matter; Pinot Noir clone 456 on 1103P, planted 2017Trial summary PDF, overview✓ full textTreatments (wet weight)Control; compost 15 t/ac; biochar 10 t/ac; compost + biocharTrial summary PDF, treatments✓ full textPlacementRipped down the vine row by GPS, mixed with a winged plow to 30 inches in a bowl about 2 ft wide × 2.5 ft deepTrial summary PDF, overview✓ full textAmendments as appliedBiochar 38% moisture, 75% organic matter (≈0.42% SOM gain in the row); compost 49% moisture, 43% organic matter (≈0.30%)Trial summary PDF, overview✓ full textFive-season total yieldCompost + biochar 41.7 t/ac; compost 40.1; biochar 38.2; control 31.7Trial summary PDF, results✓ full textAverage yield increase vs controlCompost + biochar +36%; compost +29%; biochar +25%Trial summary PDF, results✓ full textGrape qualityNo significant differencesTrial summary PDF, grape quality✓ full textEconomicsPositive return by the 2nd harvest. By the 5th, extra revenue per acre of 9,752** (biochar), **12,569 (compost), and **14,937** (both), at ~1,500/t grapes (October 2023) and 2016 delivered prices of 40/t compost and 240/t biochar (wet weight)Trial summary PDF, economic impact✓ full textPersistence claimWoody biochar made above 600 °C; more than 80% projected to persist at least 100 years, citing Woolf et al. 2021Trial summary PDF, carbon section✓ full text
Use with care

Not peer reviewed. The authors include McIntosh and Hunt, who also wrote the supplier’s Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023. The summary gives few statistical details.
Revenue depends on the grape price. Water and fertilizer inputs were the same across treatments, so no savings are counted.
Compost alone out-earned biochar alone; the combination did best.

Related: Agronomic Economics · Real World Soil Projects · Crop Yield Effects · Key Sources

Sources/Pacific-Biochar-Compost-White-Pa.title: Biochar + Compost
Sources/Pacific-Biochar-Compost-White-Pa.content:
Pacific Biochar Compost White Paper 2023
Citation: McIntosh C, Hunt J (2023). Biochar + Compost. Pacific Biochar Benefit Corporation, January 2023. pacificbiochar.com/wp-content/uploads/Pacific-Biochar_Biochar-Compost_white-paper.pdf
What it is: A practitioner synthesis from a biochar supplier on co-composting biochar and blending it with compost. It mixes the authors’ commercial experience with citations to peer-reviewed studies.
Key figures



































FigureValueWhereCheckRecommended loadingWood-based biochar at 5–10% by weight, added early in compostingWhite paper PDF, p. 1 and co-composting section✓ full textNitrogen losses during co-compostingMore than 50% lower in cited studies, with a shift toward nitrateWhite paper PDF, p. 1✓ full textComposting GHGs (some studies)CH₄ >80% lower, N₂O >50% lower, NH₃ up to 60% lowerWhite paper PDF, p. 1✓ full textLoading range across cited literature3–50% biochar (dry weight); optimum around 10%; significant benefits from 3–5%White paper PDF, literature summary✓ full text
Use with care

Not peer reviewed, and written by a biochar seller. The emission reductions are best cases from cited studies, so check the primary paper before quoting one as typical.
It restates Kammann et al. 2015 as a “yield increase of 305%“. That paper’s results put biomass at up to 305% of the control (about 3×).

Related: Biochar Compost and Manure Blends · Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Key Sources

Sources/Quilliam-et-al.-2013.title: Life in the 'charosphere' – Does biochar in agricultural soil provide a significant habitat for microorganisms?
Sources/Quilliam-et-al.-2013.content:
Quilliam et al. 2013
Citation: Quilliam RS, Glanville HC, Wade SC, Jones DL (2013). Life in the ‘charosphere’ – Does biochar in agricultural soil provide a significant habitat for microorganisms? Soil Biology and Biochemistry 65: 287–293. doi.org/10.1016/j.soilbio.2013.06.004
What it is: A study of field-aged biochar that tested the popular idea that biochar pores are a “microbial hotel”. It’s the vault’s main counterweight to habitat claims for raw biochar.
Key figures





















































FigureValueWhereCheckMaterial and settingWood-derived biochar buried in an agricultural soil for 3 yearsAbstract (Europe PMC record)✓ abstractColonizationVery sparse, with no obvious difference between internal and external surfaces (scanning electron microscopy)Abstract✓ abstractBiochar’s share of topsoil pore space at 50 t ha⁻¹6.52% ± 0.11% (0–30 cm)Abstract✓ abstractBiochar’s share of topsoil surface area at 50 t ha⁻¹7.35% ± 0.81%Abstract✓ abstractBiochar pores too small for most microbes (<1 µm)17.46%Abstract✓ abstractMicrobial activityInitial ¹⁴C-glucose mineralization faster in bulk soil and in soil next to the char than on char surfacesAbstract✓ abstractConclusionIn the short term (≤3 years) biochar isn’t a significant microbial habitat; effects on the surrounding soil (the “charosphere”) may matter moreAbstract✓ abstract
Use with care

One wood biochar, one site, up to three years. It doesn’t rule out habitat effects for other chars, or for biochar charged with compost (Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer).
Attribution fix: the clover-nodulation finding cited in Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry comes from a different paper: Quilliam, DeLuca & Jones (2013), Plant and Soil 366: 83–92, doi.org/10.1007/s11104-012-1411-4.

Related: Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology · Ross & Emery 2025 · Key Sources

Sources/Ross--and--Emery-2025.title: Microbial inocula enhance effects of biochar amendments on crop productivity, soil health, and microbial communities: A meta-analysis
Sources/Ross--and--Emery-2025.content:
Ross & Emery 2025
Citation: Ross AT, Emery SM (2025). Microbial inocula enhance effects of biochar amendments on crop productivity, soil health, and microbial communities: A meta-analysis. Soil Science Society of America Journal 89(1): e20792 (online 5 Dec 2024). doi.org/10.1002/saj2.20792
What it is: The meta-analysis behind the vault’s claim that adding microbial inocula to biochar helps on average, but mainly with local or research-grade inocula and mainly in greenhouse studies.
Key figures















































FigureValueWhereCheckStudies56Abstract✓ abstractBiochar + inoculum vs biochar aloneHigher soil N, soil organic carbon, and crop productivityAbstract✓ abstractInoculum sourceGains limited to locally sourced and research-grade inocula; commercial products only slightly raised soil PAbstract✓ abstractInoculum typeFungal inocula stronger than bacterialAbstract✓ abstractExperiment typeStrongest in greenhouse studies (N, productivity, fungal abundance); field studies raised only plant productivityAbstract✓ abstractAuthors’ conclusionActivating biochar with inocula on farms may not deliver the intended benefits; other activation methods may be neededAbstract✓ abstract
Use with care

The effect sizes are in the full paper, which wasn’t re-checked. Quote directions of effect from this note, not magnitudes.
The first author’s surname is Ross (given names Aysha Tapp); some vault notes cite “Tapp Ross”.

Related: Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology · Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Key Sources

Sources/Sanei-et-al.-2024.title: Assessing biochar's permanence: An inertinite benchmark
Sources/Sanei-et-al.-2024.content:
Sanei et al. 2024
Citation: Sanei H, Rudra A, Przyswitt ZMM, Kousted S, Sindlev MB, Zheng X, Nielsen SB, Petersen HI (2024). Assessing biochar’s permanence: An inertinite benchmark. International Journal of Coal Geology 281: 104409. doi.org/10.1016/j.coal.2023.104409 (open access)
What it is: The petrography paper behind the “inertinite / random reflectance” camp in the permanence debate. It proposes a reflectance threshold for classing biochar carbon as inertinite-like, and therefore effectively permanent.
Key figures









































FigureValueWhereCheckProposed benchmarkRandom reflectance Ro = 2% (“IBRo2%“)Abstract✓ abstractCommercial samples meeting it76% of studied commercial biochars had their entire Ro distribution above 2%Abstract✓ abstractModelled persistence~100 million years for a typical inertinite biochar to lose half its carbon, assuming a highly oxidizing environment at a constant 30 °CAbstract✓ abstractOther carbon poolsIncompletely carbonized biochar may hold up to three less-stable pools, measurable with geochemical pyrolysis plus RoAbstract✓ abstractCarbonization temperatureRo can be used to back-calculate the peak temperature biochar particles reachedAbstract✓ abstract
Use with care

The half-life comes from a kinetic model for inertinite under stated conditions. It isn’t a field measurement of biochar decay.
Crediting reflectance is a standards decision; see Permanence Science for Credits and Puro vs Other Standards. Critiques of the approach: Risks and Controversies.

Related: Permanence · Reflectance Ro and HyPy · Permanence Debates · Woolf et al. 2021 · Key Sources

Sources/Schmidt-et-al.-2015.title: Fourfold Increase in Pumpkin Yield in Response to Low-Dosage Root Zone Application of Urine-Enhanced Biochar to a Fertile Tropical Soil
Sources/Schmidt-et-al.-2015.content:
Schmidt et al. 2015
Citation: Schmidt H-P, Pandit BH, Martinsen V, Cornelissen G, Conte P, Kammann CI (2015). Fourfold increase in pumpkin yield in response to low-dosage root zone application of urine-enhanced biochar to a fertile tropical soil. Agriculture 5(3): 723–741. doi.org/10.3390/agriculture5030723 (open access)
What it is: A single pumpkin field trial in Nepal. It compared compost plus urine, compost plus biochar, and compost plus urine-loaded biochar, all placed in the root zone. It’s the vault’s reference for low-dose, urine-charged biochar.
Key figures

































































FigureValueWhereCheckBiocharEupatorium adenophorum (invasive shrub), flame-curtain kiln; met European Biochar Certificate premium criteriaAbstract✓ abstractChargingMixed 1:1 by volume with fresh cow urineAbstract✓ abstractDose and placement750 kg ha⁻¹ biochar dry matter, root zone, before seedingAbstract✓ abstractBackground amendmentCow-manure compost in every treatmentAbstract✓ abstractUrine-biochar yield82.6 t ha⁻¹ pumpkinAbstract✓ abstractvs urine onlyMore than +300%Abstract✓ abstractvs biochar only+85%Abstract✓ abstractSoilFertile silt loamAbstract✓ abstractSoak urine and biochar at least 1 hour before applyingProtocol detail used in Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer—not re-checked (full text blocked to automated download)
Use with care

One site, one crop, one season: a strong demonstration, not an average effect. The multi-site follow-up is Schmidt et al. 2017.
The authors tentatively attribute the gain to an organic coating that urine loading forms on pore surfaces. The abstract offers this as an explanation, not a measured cause.

Related: Schmidt et al. 2017 · Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Biochar Nutrients and Fertilizer Chemistry · Key Sources

Sources/Schmidt-et-al.-2017.title: Biochar-Based Fertilization with Liquid Nutrient Enrichment: 21 Field Trials Covering 13 Crop Species in Nepal
Sources/Schmidt-et-al.-2017.content:
Schmidt et al. 2017
Citation: Schmidt H-P, Pandit BH, Cornelissen G, Kammann CI (2017). Biochar-based fertilization with liquid nutrient enrichment: 21 field trials covering 13 crop species in Nepal. Land Degradation & Development 28(8): 2324–2342. doi.org/10.1002/ldr.2761
What it is: A program of 21 on-farm trials in Nepal. Biochar from flame-curtain kilns was loaded with cow urine or dissolved NPK and placed in the root zone at low doses. Controls got the same nutrients without biochar, so the trials isolate biochar’s role as a nutrient carrier.
Key figures





















































FigureValueWhereCheckTrials and crops21 field trials, 13 crop speciesAbstract✓ abstractEnriched-biochar dose0.5–2 t ha⁻¹ into the root zoneAbstract✓ abstractNutrient load per tonne of biochar60–100 kg N, 5–60 kg P₂O₅, 60–100 kg K₂OAbstract✓ abstractNPK-enriched biochar vs the same NPK without biochar+20% ± 5.1% yield (4 trials)Abstract✓ abstractUrine-enriched biochar + compost vs farmer practice (urine-blended compost)+123% ± 76.7% yield (13 trials)Abstract✓ abstractUrine-enriched vs NPK-enriched biochar, same nutrient dose+103% ± 12.4% (4 trials)Abstract✓ abstractSoilsDescribed as rather fertile silt loamsAbstract✓ abstract
Use with care

The large gains come from enriched biochar placed in the root zone at ≤2 t ha⁻¹, not from bulk raw char. Don’t transfer them to broadcast applications.
The +123% comparison is against local organic practice, not mineral NPK, and its spread (±76.7%) is wide.
The full text wasn’t accessible for this check. Trial-level details (crop list, sites, enrichment timing) still need confirming against the paper.

Related: Schmidt et al. 2015 (the pumpkin trial before this program) · Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · Key Sources

Sources/USBI-Ag-Guidelines-2023.title: Biochar Guidelines for Agricultural Applications: Practical insights for applying biochar to annual and perennial crops
Sources/USBI-Ag-Guidelines-2023.content:
USBI Ag Guidelines 2023
Citation: Aller D, Trippe K, Smith B, Seman-Varner R, Delaney M, Miles T (2023). Biochar Guidelines for Agricultural Applications: Practical insights for applying biochar to annual and perennial crops. United States Biochar Initiative, in partnership with the Nebraska Forest Service. farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/06/usbi-biochar-guidelines-for-ag-application.pdf
What it is: An 8-page practitioner guide from the US Biochar Initiative on choosing, charging, and applying biochar on farms. The vault uses it for the “charge before use” rule.
Key figures





















































FigureValueWhereCheckWhat charging doesInoculating, charging, activating, or blending fills biochar’s surface functional groups with nutrients and microbesGuide PDF, post-processing✓ full textWhy it mattersInoculating is described as critical to minimize nutrient immobilization after applicationGuide PDF, post-processing✓ full textInoculant sourcesCompost, manure, compost tea, fertilizer, urine, microbial inoculantsGuide PDF, post-processing✓ full textActivation timeVaries; 1–3 weeks has been recommendedGuide PDF, post-processing✓ full textPasture timingApply right after livestock rotate through a paddock, so biochar mixes with residual manure and urineGuide PDF, pasture✓ full textPrilled biochar–N fertilizersAcross more than 20 studies: 15–69% slower N release and 25–65% better fertilizer-use efficiency, citing Gao et al. 2022Guide PDF, fertilizer products✓ full textCase history: Shamrock Christmas Tree Farm, Mattituck, NY20-acre Douglas fir farm on sandy soil at 1.7% organic matter. A 3-year trial starting 2019 applied compost-tea-inoculated biochar at 5, 10 and 15 t/acre plus a control: 10 trees per plot, 5 replicates, raked into the top 4 inchesGuide PDF, p. 7✓ full text
Use with care

Practitioner guidance, not peer reviewed. The 1–3 week window is a recommendation, not a tested optimum.
The prilled-fertilizer ranges come from Gao et al. 2022 (doi.org/10.1007/s42773-022-00160-3); cite that review for them.

2026 ABI republication
ABI hosts an updated Biochar Guidelines for Agriculture Applications PDF (Nebraska Forest Service partnership) that retains the same charging / rate framing: biochar.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Biochar-Guidelines-for-Agriculture-Applications-2026.pdf · org note US Biochar Initiative · comparison USBI Guidance vs Vault Notes.
Related: Biochar Inoculation for Fertilizer · NRCS CPS 336 FAQ 2026 · Key Sources

Sources/Wang-et-al.-2016.title: Biochar stability in soil: meta-analysis of decomposition and priming effects
Sources/Wang-et-al.-2016.content:
Wang et al. 2016
Citation: Wang J, Xiong Z, Kuzyakov Y (2016). Biochar stability in soil: meta-analysis of decomposition and priming effects. GCB Bioenergy 8(3): 512–523 (online 2015). doi.org/10.1111/gcbb.12266 (open access)
What it is: Two meta-analyses in one paper. The first asks how fast biochar itself decomposes, using isotope-labelled studies. The second asks whether biochar speeds up or slows down decomposition of native soil organic matter (“priming”).
Key figures





















































FigureValueWhereCheckDecomposition dataset128 observations from 24 ¹³C/¹⁴C studiesAbstract✓ abstractBiochar carbon poolsLabile ~3% (mean residence ~108 days); recalcitrant ~97% (mean residence ~556 years)Abstract✓ abstractPriming dataset116 observations from 21 studiesAbstract✓ abstractOverall primingSoil organic matter mineralization −3.8% (95% CI −8.1% to +0.8%): a slight slowdown whose interval includes zeroAbstract✓ abstractSignificant negative primingStudies shorter than half a year −8.6%; crop-derived biochar −20.3%; fast pyrolysis −18.9%; lowest pyrolysis temperature −18.5%; small application amounts −11.9%Abstract✓ abstractPositive primingSandy soils: soil organic matter mineralization +20.8%Abstract✓ abstractConclusionBiochar persists on a centennial scaleAbstract✓ abstract
Use with care

Correction to earlier vault notes: several notes cited this paper for “short-term positive priming is common”. For short studies it found the opposite: significant negative priming under six months. Its positive priming was in sandy soils, and the overall −3.8% isn’t statistically different from zero.
Decade-scale field evidence of negative priming comes from other work, such as Weng et al. 2017 (doi.org/10.1038/nclimate3276).

Related: Permanence · GHG Fluxes · Biochar Microbes and Soil Biology · Key Sources

Sources/Woolf-et-al.-2021.title: Greenhouse Gas Inventory Model for Biochar Additions to Soil
Sources/Woolf-et-al.-2021.content:
Woolf et al. 2021
Citation: Woolf D, Lehmann J, Ogle S, Kishimoto-Mo AW, McConkey B, Baldock J (2021). Greenhouse gas inventory model for biochar additions to soil. Environmental Science & Technology 55(21): 14795–14805. doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c02425 · open copy: Canada federal science repository PDF
What it is: A greenhouse-gas accounting method for biochar added to mineral soils. It extends the IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix approach with soil temperature and H/C_org. It’s the most-cited source in the vault: permanence tables, carbon-market methodologies, and N₂O accounting all lean on it.
Key figures

























































































FigureValueWhereCheckCarbon content of biocharFrom 7% (gasified biosolids) to 79% (wood pyrolysed above 600 °C)Abstract✓ full textCarbon fraction (FC) of wood biocharLow / medium / high temperature 0.70 / 0.77 / 0.81; mean 0.76; gasification 0.63Table 2 (open PDF)✓ full textTemperature classesLow 350–450 °C; medium 450–600 °C; high ≥600 °C§3.1 (open PDF)✓ full text100-year permanence factor (F_perm) at 14.9 °C, the global cropland meanLow / medium / high 0.63 / 0.71 / 0.82; this is the abstract’s “63–82% remains after 100 years”Table 3 (open PDF)✓ full textF_perm at 14.9 °C over longer horizons500 years: 0.19 / 0.32 / 0.44; 1,000 years: 0.084 / 0.16 / 0.25Table 3✓ full textF_perm vs soil temperature (100 years, high class)0.94 at 5 °C; 0.88 at 10 °C; 0.79 at 20 °C; 0.76 at 25 °CTable 3✓ full textTemperature sensitivity usedQ10 = 1.1 + 12.0·e^(−0.19T)Methods✓ full textN₂O adjustment−23% (95% CI 5–41%), first year only, only where more than 10 Mg C ha⁻¹ is applied; fitted to field trials, with pot and incubation studies excluded§3.3.2✓ full textEarlier N₂O meta-analyses it weighs−54% (Cayuela et al. 2014), −12.4% (Verhoeven), −38% (Borchard); Verhoeven’s reanalysis correcting for non-independent treatments gave −9.2%, not significant§3.3.2✓ full textCH₄No effect assumed; too few field data to predict size or direction§2.4 and §3.5✓ full textPriming of native soil carbonNot credited, because net negative priming wasn’t statistically significant in meta-analyses§3.3✓ full textWhere the method appliesMineral soils only; not organic soils (Histosols) or forest soils with an organic horizon, where positive priming is possible§3.3✓ full textWorked exampleMaize stover pyrolysed at 500 °C: FC 0.68, F_perm 0.79 at 10 °C; 15,000 Mg biochar plus the N₂O term → 29,710 Mg CO₂e§3.4.1✓ full text
Use with care

The abstract’s 79% carbon content and Table 2’s FC of 0.81 for high-temperature wood aren’t the same statistic. Quote the table when you need a class value.
F_perm drops quickly in warmer soils and over longer horizons, so always state the temperature and time horizon with a permanence number.
The N₂O term is small and conditional. Don’t apply it at typical farm rates below 10 Mg C ha⁻¹.

Related: Permanence · Woolf IPCC Fperm · H-Corg and O-Corg · Soil Temperature and Environment · IPCC 2019 Biochar Appendix · GHG Fluxes · Permanence Science for Credits · Key Sources

Sources/Ye-et-al.-2020.title: Biochar effects on crop yields with and without fertilizer: A meta-analysis of field studies using separate controls
Sources/Ye-et-al.-2020.content:
Ye et al. 2020
Citation: Ye L, Camps-Arbestain M, Shen Q, Lehmann J, Singh B, Sabir M (2020). Biochar effects on crop yields with and without fertilizer: A meta-analysis of field studies using separate controls. Soil Use and Management 36(1): 2–18 (online December 2019). doi.org/10.1111/sum.12546 · author-hosted PDF
What it is: A meta-analysis of field studies that compares biochar against separate fertilized and unfertilized controls, so biochar’s effect isn’t confused with the fertilizer’s. It’s the vault’s reference for the right comparison when biochar goes on with fertilizer.
Key figures





















































FigureValueWhereCheckBiochar + inorganic fertilizer vs fertilizer alone+15% yield (CI 11–19%)Abstract (author PDF)✓ full textFertilizer alone vs unfertilized control+26% (CI 15–40%)Abstract✓ full textBiochar + fertilizer vs unfertilized control+48% (CI 30–70%)Abstract✓ full textBiochar aloneDid not increase yield, whichever control was usedAbstract✓ full textApplication rateRates above 10 t ha⁻¹ added no yield, at least in the short term; 5–10 t ha⁻¹ out-yielded 10–20 t ha⁻¹ against fertilized controlsResults and conclusions✓ full textSoil pHBiochar shouldn’t be applied to high-pH soilsConclusions✓ full textLargest responsesSandy and low-CEC soilsResults✓ full text
Use with care

DOI correction: Key Sources listed this paper as 10.1111/sum.12555, which is a different article. The correct DOI is 10.1111/sum.12546.
The +15% is biochar’s added effect on top of fertilizer. It doesn’t apply to biochar used instead of fertilizer.

Related: Crop Yield Effects · Lehmann et al. 2021 · Melo et al. 2022 · Key Sources
